trials.methods: Review of retrospective studies
trials.results:
Radiation provides very good control and with low adverse effects

Dose 20-45 Gy/ 10-25 fx

trials.commentary:
Treating amyloidosis is similar to the concept of treating plasmacytoma/multiple myeloma. The disease is caused by amyloid light chain secretion by monoclonal plasma cells.

trials.patients:
Unruptured AVM

(Characteristics: Spetzler-Martin grade I-III in ~30% each, and grade IV in ~10%)
trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 medical management
vs.
➜ medical management + intervention
(can include SRS, embolization, neurosurgery, or combination)
trials.results:
-Mean f/u of 50 mos
-Death or stroke 3.39 vs. 12.32 per 100 pt-years
-Deaths: n=2 vs. 4
-Adverse events 59% vs. 79%

•Neurosurgery in 21%. 95% of these had eradication, 41% had an event
•SRS in 54%. 21% had eradication, 37% had an event
•Embolization in 62%. 52% had eradication, 50% had an event
trials.interpretation: Medical management alone results in less death, stroke, and adverse effects compared to interventional therapy (SRS, surgery, or embolization) in unruptured AVM.
trials.commentary:
This is the first randomized trial evaluating intervention in unruptured AVM. Follow-up may be too short - closure can occur later. It should still give some caution toward interventional therapy.

SRS, a less invasive option, might possibly be preferred. The trial seems to show that events are fewer with SRS than other modalities. However, the rate of eradication is lower. Recognize that outcome data by modality is non-randomized and non-stratified. Deep and larger tumors would be more likely to undergo SRS. This would favor the surgical and embolization groups. Even so, SRS showed less adverse effects.
trials.reference: 1. Mohr JP, Overbey JR, Hartmann A, et al. Medical management with interventional therapy versus medical management alone for unruptured brain arteriovenous malformations (ARUBA): final follow-up of a multicentre, non-blinded, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Neurol 2020. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30181-2

trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 15 Gy/5 fx + 15 Gy/5 fx, each 1 week, separated over 10 weeks
vs.
➜ sham radiation
trials.results:
⬆️1-yr pain relief 74% vs. 56%
⬆️QOL scores with RT

RT had higher mean walking speed and step rate with barefoot speed walking
trials.interpretation: Radiation therapy is an effective treatment for pain relief and QOL in Ledderhose disease.
trials.commentary:
Planning: mark all Ledderhose nodules and/or cords on the sole then add 2.5 cm sup/inf margin and 1.5 cm lateral margin

8 MeV electrons used for size ≤1 cm, and 10 MeV for size >1 cm. The authors wrote that the dose was chosen because it's the most common used.

The study was conducted in the Netherlands. Other treatment options include cortisone injections or extracorporeal shock wave therapy. Surgery is also an option but not routinely performed.

DEGRO 2022 guidelines: Radiation therapy can be performed in Ledderhose disease when symptoms are clearly increasing, both primarily and secondarily after surgery. Evidence level 4, recommendation level C

Dupuytren’s contracture and Ledderhose disease are the same pathological process, which is why the same dose is used for both. Ledderhose is eponymous of the surgeon who first described the disease. Lederhosen on the otherhand is a popular traditional German attire, often worn for Oktoberfest.

trials.citation: Fazilat-Panah et al, Int J Radiat Biol, 2026
trials.patients:
Knee OA

age ≥65
trials.methods:
➜ sham RT
vs.
➜🏆 3.0 Gy/ 6 fx

Endpoints: Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and Lysholm 100-point Scale
trials.results: AS pain score, Lysholm scale, PS and analgesic consumption were improved p<0.01
trials.interpretation: LDRT improves pain and joint function in knee OA.
trials.commentary:
On X Koneru writes that there are no randomized trials comparing total knee replacement vs placebo or sham. On the other hand, LDRT has two positive two positive sham controlled trials (LORD-KNEA and Iranian), extensive prospective evidence, 4.5x difference in pain scores at 36 months across every domain (pain, stiffness, function, quality of life), and plain-film radiography and MRI at 10 years showing a statistically significant reduction in marked progression.

Other OA treatments have significant downsides: NSAIDs: known cardiovascular, renal, and Gl harm at chronic doses. Corticosteroid injections: evidence of accelerated cartilage loss with repeat use (Wernicke 2025).
trials.reference: 1. Fazilat-Panah D, Javadinia SA, Shabestani Monfared A, et al. Int J Radiat Biol 2025;101:541-548. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1080/09553002.2025.2473975

trials.patients:
Knee OA

by Altman’s criteria (1991) and Kellgren – Lawrence radiographic stages 0-2
trials.methods:
➜ symptomatic slow acting drugs
vs.
➜🏆 LDRT up to 4.5 Gy/ 10 fx QOD plus standard therapy
trials.results:
9-yr f/u total knee arthroplasty 7.5% vs. 4.1%

3-yr MRI score better with LDRT, with less cartilage destruction and bone marrow edema

LDRT reduced disability by 67%, p<0.001

Those with baseline KL2 disease had best benefit:
Disability reduced 61% vs. 31%
TKA 36% vs. 14%
trials.interpretation: LDRT for knee OA resulted in less TKA, less progression on MRI, and reduced disability. Results were best in KL2.
trials.commentary:
Kellgren – Lawrence radiographic staging

•grade 0 (none): definite absence of x-ray changes of osteoarthritis
•grade 1 (doubtful): doubtful joint space narrowing and possible osteophytic lipping
•grade 2 (minimal): definite osteophytes and possible joint space narrowing
•grade 3 (moderate): moderate multiple osteophytes, definite narrowing of joint space, some sclerosis and possible deformity of bone ends
•grade 4 (severe): large osteophytes, marked narrowing of joint space, severe sclerosis and definite deformity of bone ends

The DEGRO guidelines quote an additional risk of basal cell carcinoma 0.1% and of leukemia of 0.03% with 3 Gy dose

Yu (2025) also provides useful instructions for sim and field design. An atlas from HM Hospitales, Madrid gives useful anatomical and CT based instructions (Alvarez 2021).

On X Koneru writes that there are no randomized trials comparing total knee replacement vs placebo or sham. On the other hand, LDRT has two positive two positive sham controlled trials (LORD-KNEA and Iranian), extensive prospective evidence, 4.5x difference in pain scores at 36 months across every domain (pain, stiffness, function, quality of life), and plain-film radiography and MRI at 10 years showing a statistically significant reduction in marked progression.

Other OA treatments have significant downsides: NSAIDs: known cardiovascular, renal, and Gl harm at chronic doses. Corticosteroid injections: evidence of accelerated cartilage loss with repeat use (Wernicke 2025).

trials.methods: Evaluated those treated with lumpectomy, with and without RT, and mastectomy. 1:1 matching
trials.results:
15-yr BCM 2.33% with lumpectomy, 1.74% lumpectomy+RT, and 2.26% with mastectomy
[NNT: 170]

On subanalysis, clear benefit with grade 3 (HR 0.59), benefit in ER negative and ER positive, and benefit in tumors 1-1.9 cm and >5.0 cm. Tumors 2-2.9 cm were p=0.24, tumors 3.0-4.9 were p=0.07, and tumors <1.0 cm were p=0.58.

trials.commentary: Importantly, BCM is the endpoint used. The subanalysis of pathologic factors strengthens the findings. A trial large enough to show survival benefit in DCIS will likely not be performed. Do exercise caution using large population observational studies: A review found that the conclusions of these were not better than chance at matching randomized trials, and no factors were found to improve conclusions (Soni 2019). This does not necessarily mean the reports worthless - they still contain more data than a single insitution retrospective report for example - but that the eras and parameters should be carefully selected, that the results should be considered something in the realm of hypothesis generating and exploratory, and that results absolutely cannot replace or disprove a randomized trial unless perhaps it was poorly undertaken.

trials.commentary:
73% of tumors were <1 cm. Note that if the recurrence rate is 1% per year, a patient will have a 15% chance of recurrence in 15 years and so on. There was no subanalysis of effectiveness hypofractionation vs. WBRT. The trial was in the 2D era and thus no dose constraints were included.

Note that RT is first choice per NCCN. It is more effective than TAM, is completed in a shorter time period, and has higher compliance, especially with hypofractionation. TAM causes cognitive decline (TAILORx, Wagner 2020). TAM adherence is unreliable: 20-60% will discontinue (Shinn 2019). In other trials such as UKCCCR, LC is superior with WBRT over TAM (Houghton 2003).  On the other hand, it should be acknowledged that there is no OS advantage to either WBRT or TAM. Recurrences can be salvaged, but often with mastectomy. Regarding the lack of OS benefit, it should to be emphasized that many women with breast cancer "don't want to go through this again" and value the benefit of LC. One in ten women at 10 years is not a small number for all.

These trials emerged from an era when radiotherapy was 6 weeks. Noninferior regimens of 5 or 15 fractions have since been developed. A provocative essay entitled "Endocrine Treatment for 5 Years or Radiation for 5 Days" (Naoum 2022) makes a succinct point regarding the durations of the therapies.

trials.commentary:
Although the trial's stated purpose was to enroll "non-low-risk" DCIS, low risk DCIS were in reality included as well due to eligibility criterion of any DCIS with margins <10 mm in ages ≥50. 25-29% were grade 1-2 without comedonecrosis (specific numbers for grade 1 or 2 were not shown). Thus the trial can support boost for any kind of DCIS including low risk.

Only 13% had endocrine therapy. Favorable LC can be achieved with RT plus boost in the absence of ET in DCIS. The trial reported endpoint of LC, but this is rephrased as LR here to be consistent with other trials.

Taking into account the small but present increase in adverse effects with a 16 Gy boost for benign disease, a middle ground for some could be to limit indicators for boost, treat a smaller volume, 10 Gy, or SIB boost as per UK IMPORT HIGH. Additional f/u might also aid in decision making. At long term f/u in EORTC 22881, fibrosis was 4% at 10 years and 5% at 20 years.

trials.commentary:
Early stage overview
-Landmark study NSABP B06, and the Milan I study and others, showed that lumpectomy plus WBRT was not different than total mastectomy
-Other randomized trials also confirmed the benefit of WBRT, and the landmark EBCTCG meta-analysis of these trials was the first to show a BCM benefit with WBRT. Since then treatment is more nuanced based on subtypes, age, and new developments in chemotherapy and sequencning
-NSABP B21 and PMH, and other studies not listed here, established the benefit of TAM
-EORTC 22881 and Lyon, as well as some other studies, showed  LC benefit with boost. Due to risk of fibrosis, many use risk factors to help guide boost
-Later studies developed SIB boost: UK IMPORT HIGH, RTOG 1005, IMRT-MC2
-PRIME II and CALBG showed that ages >65-70 have good results without RT, but RT does still provide some additional LC and should be used case by case
-Moderate hypofractionated WBRT to 13-16 fractions was developed by START A&B and Canadian OCOG, as well as other trials
-FIve fraction WBRT was then developed with UK FAST and UK FAST FORWARD, now with 10-yr follow-up
-Various trials show the benefit of extended endocrirne therapy, confirmed in EBCTCG meta-analysis

SLNB and ALND
-ACOSOG Z0011 reconfirm NSABP B04, showing that ALND is not required after 1-2 SLNB+
-ACOSOG Z1071 and SENTINA showed that SLNB isn't as reliable after neoadjuvant chemo, but dual tracer technique and sampling of more nodes can improve results
-INSEMA and SOUND authors concluded no benefit to SLNB in T1, but RNI was prohibited in this study, leading to questionable methodology and conclusions

trials.methods:
Analysis of prospective Swedish database

OS in BCS+RT, Mx, Mx+PMRT

stepwise adjusted by tumor, chemo, endocrine therapy, age, year, region, prognostic group, Nottingham grade, subtype, socioeconomic factors
trials.results:
OS and BCSS worse with Mx and Mx+PMRT than with BCS+RT

M+RT had increased mortality in T1N0, T1N1, T2N0, but not T1N2. For T2N1 and T2N2 there was nonsignificant increase
trials.interpretation:
In this largescale database analysis with adjustment for confounders, mastectomy and mastectomy with PMRT were associated with worse OS and BCSS compared to BCS+RT.

This is contradictory to the randomized trials that show no difference in OS between mastectomy and BCS.
trials.commentary:
The benefit in BCS could be due to stage nuances that are not captured by the staging system. It seems that patients were adjusted by T stage and N stage, not by exact size of tumor and # nodes. If this is the case, the mastectomy group likely consisted of "bigger" T2s (and possibly T1s) and N1s and N2s with more nodes. It is obvious that there is a difference between a T2 that is 2.1 cm and one that is 4.9 cm. The same holds for N stage.

Other explanations for the benefit of RT may be due to RT generating an immune response or targeting occult disease that is missed by mastectomy. There is a possibility that this difference is only detectable with large numbers of patients.

The authors name possible confounders that are not recorded in the database: smoking, body habitus, alcohol, drug abuse, and psychiatric disorders. But it would seem that these features would favor the mastectomy group.

trials.commentary: Bernie Fisher revolutionized breast cancer care. He was a surgeon advocating against surgery, for chemo and endocrine therapy, and for women's autonomy. These were some of the first ever randomized trials. At the time there was fierce oppositon to his ideas, and the trial was run mainly in community centers. Surgeons were so opposed to the findings that practice took years to change even after the trial, and the axillary portion was repeated in multiple other trials. He was advised by some not to attend conferences in order to avoid physical altercations. Later in his career he became a political target and his reputation was ruined due to a witch hunt highlighting one enrolling physician who falsified data. NSABP-06 received a cautionary label of "Scientific Misconduct." The falsified data however didn't change the results, and the label was later removed. For more on Bernie Fisher, listen to Stacy Fisher's podcast Less Radical (2024). https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/less-radical/id1767700499

trials.interpretation: WBRT in elderly patients with low risk tumors improves IBTR. IBTR continues to rise with f/u. There is no benefit in OS or DM. Observation may be reasonable in some populations. Treatment should be individualized.
trials.commentary:
Results may not apply to grade 3. The distribution of grades enrolled was not revealed in the CALGB study, and in PRIME II there were only 2-3% grade 3. Should there be a standard age or subtype cutoff for RT for breast cancer? A personalized approach calls practioners to assess goals, comorbidities, life expectancy, and competing risk with a discussion with the patient. Regarding the lack of OS benefit, it should be emphasized that many women with breast cancer "don't want to go through this again" and value the benefit of LC. One in ten women at 10 years is not a small number for all. A minimalist view is that in the defined subset with the data we have there is no confirmed OS benefit, and DM control via ET may be higher priority than LC.

These trials emerged from an era when radiotherapy was 6 weeks. Noninferior regimens of 5 or 15 fractions have since been developed. A provocative essay entitled "Endocrine Treatment for 5 Years or Radiation for 5 Days" (Naoum 2022) makes a succinct point regarding the durations of the therapies.

trials.commentary:
Although age ≥55 was permitted, the median IQR age was 67. 32% were age 70 or older and 59% were age 65 or older. They report that 83% were still receiving endocrine therapy if their last follow-up visit was "at 5 years or earlier." Subanalyses of any kind were not performed.

If the recurrence rate in luminal A is so low, can we also omit all adjuvant therapy altogether, or treat with radiation alone without endocrine therapy? Radiation is better tolerated and completed in a shorter time period than ET. This idea will be tested in EUROPA. Another attractive approach is evaluation of treatment guidance by Oncotype. Should there be a standard age or subtype cutoff for RT for breast cancer? A personalized approach calls practioners to assess comorbidities, life expectancy, and competing risk with a discussion with the patient.

trials.commentary:
Like the TAILORX and RXPONDER trials before it, IDEA seeks to identify what is overtreatment and spare patients from unneeded therapy. The follow up might be considered short, but may be appropriate for some situations. The Oncotype score required here of ≤18 is lower than that of TAILORX and RXPONDER, which have Oncotype ≤25 as indication. The DEBRA trial is a phase III trial to randomize this question.

Future directions perhaps should include evaluating omission of endocrine therapy in those with low Oncotype.

trials.interpretation:
16 Gy boost improves local control after whole breast radiation for lumpectomy. Fibrosis is increased. OS is unchanged.

On exploratory subanalysis, 16 Gy boost reduces LR in all age groups. Younger age benefits the most. Grade 3 benefits in earlier f/u, and those with adjacent DCIS benefit at long term f/u.
trials.commentary:
10 Gy or 16 Gy. Since the innovation of SIB boost, the choice between 10 and 16 Gy is less of a discussion, but may still be relevant for some centers and some regimens. The 48 Gy SIB dose is equivalent to a 13-16 Gy sequential boost. Interestingly, 10 Gy boost seems to have become commonplace, but 16 Gy has overwhelmingly better phase III evidence. The phase III trial that evaluated 10 Gy, Lyon, was single institution and found only a 1% benefit at 5 years. Some hold concerns for fibrosis with 16 Gy: the EORTC study shows 5% vs. 2% severe risk at 20 years, and 15% vs. 30% risk of moderate-severe. The EORTC study also benefits from longer-term f/u and subanalyses.

An intriguing question is, how should one view all the subanalyses? These are all post-hoc and not intentionally powered; in the era of this clinical trial, standards for subanalyses had not yet been developed. The subanalyses performed do meet a rational hypothesis however, so they seem reasonable to perform. Cancer cells don't know if an analysis was preplanned or not.

One could make a statistical argument that boost should be recommended in all lumpectomy patients based on the results of EORTC given that results in the entire cohort are positive, and that splitting the patients by subanalysis was not prespecified or intentionally powered. But, what matters is not if the analysis was planned, but whether it is rational and its degree of power - and most are not powered, but are still meaningful. Interestingly, in UK IMPORT HIGH, no such specific eligibility criteria were required, and that trial used 16 Gy boost as the control. For many rad oncs, boost recommendations are a balance between LR risk and fibrosis.

Likewise one should be cautious of fragmenting boost recommendations by decade as in the subanalysis: in addition to being exploratory, different patients of different life expectancies and comorbidities may have differing chances of benefit. Also recognize that division by decade is fully arbitrary: if boost in age 51-60 gives a significant benefit, there is more than likely also benefit in ages 51-62. Boost recommendations should be personalized just like RT vs. observation recommendations in DCIS and elderly invasive, or any medical decision.

On MVA, the p values for DCIS were p=0.001, for age p=<0.001, and for diameter p=0.5. TROG BIG confirmed that boost for DCIS alone also results in LC benefit.

trials.commentary:
Results shown here include the addendum to the meta-analysis, adding UK IMPORT LOW, published in an appendix of a Lancet letter to the editor. In the initial analysis, there were slight differences in p values when the random effects vs fixed effects models were used. It is unclear which statistical model is employed in the updated analysis. (In the initial analysis, the fixed effects model did lead to p=0.13 for non breast cancer mortality.)

How can the difference in non BCM be explained? Radiation exposure to the heart may be an answer. From Darby (2013) and van den Bogaard (2017) we know that cardiac events do occur within 5 years. But detailed causes of death are typically not reported. Another hypothesis is that less fractions may lead to less impairment of the immune system (Sun 2020). IBTR results were not provided in the meta-analysis. An subanalysis of left vs. right tumors was not included but would be enlightening. A later EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis (2023) shows worse OS with older RT techniques, but no worsening of OS with newer techniques. Perhaps 2D breast tangents cause similar effects.

Some might assert that the meta-analysis is weighted by TARGIT, or that each technique may have different effects, but a Higgins test shows no heterogeneity.
trials.notes:
PBI overview
-Almost all PBI studies show that PBI is noninferior or equivalent to WBRT
-There are mixed results with EBRT PBI. RAPID study showed worse cosmesis with EBRT PBI in 10 fx BID, and RTOG 0413/B39 (PBI EBRT and catheter) showed small increase in adverse effects. The Christie's study also did not show noninferiority. UK IMPORT LOW showed less adverse effects with ABPI EBRT in 15 fx daily
-TARGIT showed that IORT is noninferior to WBRT in the pre-pathology group and less non-cancer deaths late
-UK Meta-analysis shows no difference in BCM between PBI and WBRT. There is actually a worsening of OS with WBRT. The reasons why are debated
-PMH Meta-analysis shows PBI has worse LR over WBRT
-McMaster meta-analysis shows LR rates not different when excluding 2DCRT and IORT
-Combining PBI data with UK FAST FOWARD, 26 Gy/5 fractions PBI is another regimen

📌 Delayed second-procedure IORT (post-pathology)

trials.commentary:
TARGIT is a potential disruptor in oncology, and there have been questions related to the design of its arms, statistics, benefit, and mechanism of action. TARGIT is applied using a spherical applicator of 50 kV RT. This rapidly attenuates to 5 Gy at 1cm, leading some to question how it could provide adequate coverage (Polgár 2021). TARGIT authors have proposed biologic mechanisms related to avoiding seroma that may lead to increased effectiveness at lower depth (Belletti 2008).

Pre-path. 20% who had IORT crossed-over to receive WBRT for high risk features, which some say biases in favor of IORT. In the pre-path group, the authors did provide separate HR analyses for treatment received (IORT only, or IORT + WBRT) and found no difference in long term LRFS HRs. While some may question this methodology of allowing WBRT for high risk features, consider the alternative, where those with PBI-unsuitable risk features are withheld WBRT - an arguably unethical approach. Some remark that only the results of the delayed cohort matter - when surgical pathology is known - because this is the only way the arms can be truly balanced. A concern with delayed IORT is that there may be issues locating the original site, possibly different biologic mechanisms, and delayed IORT also isn't quite the point. The other alternative is to replicate the trial with more favorable eligibility upfront.

Statistics. Some had concerns that LRFS was reported in initial publication rather than LC. The authors eventually reported that LC is not different in the 2023 publication, p=0.28. Vaidya explains that LR does not censor those who have died, leading to misleading data (Vaidya IJROBP 2023). Some guidelines now do recommend that RFS type endpoints be standard (Vaidya BJC 2021, IJROBP 2023). A later meta-analysis by McMaster University evaluated IBTR and found that IORT and 2DCRT led to worse recurrence rates (Goldbergy 2022).  Some have compared the results to PRIME II, asserting that IORT is no better than observation, but this is not sound: the populations are obviously different and such a comparison is not randomized or even propensity matched. TARGIT's population was higher risk and younger than PRIME II (Kunkler 2015, Vaidya 2021).

Some commented that the noninferiority margin or methodology was inappropriate (Cuzick 2015, Polgár 2021). The authors responded that appropriate statisitical methods were indeed used (Vaidya 2015). Later f/u was not planned, and rarely is, and thus noninferiority margins are not prespecified for late f/u.

Adverse effects. Can non-breast cancer deaths be explained by subtle adverse effects of EBRT? From Darby (2013) and van den Bogaard (2017) we know that cardiac events can occur within 5 years with RT. A later EBCTCG RNI 2023 meta-analysis shows how RT technique can impact later OS. Yet RT techniques have advanced, including with more sophisticated 3DCRT, VMAT, surface tracking, protons, etc.

Most of the statistical issues have been addressed, but some still have concerns regarding the mechanism and treating before final pathology. What if after final path you would have done something different? It is to be acknowledged that overall results seem favorable regardless, and costs are markedly reduced. In one editorial, Vaidya reiterates the comment by Zeitman (2016) that the "elephant in the room" of criticism of TARGIT is that revenue for many facilities will be impacted. TARGIT is allowed on multiple national guidelines (Vaidya 2021).
(Commentary last updated Nov 2025, Estes)

trials.commentary:
Overview. Given that the EBCTCG 2023 RNI meta-analysis showed benefit of RNI in 1-3 nodes, INSEMA and SOUND are perplexing clinical trials. Prior to release of the meta-analysis, when INSEMA and SOUND were designed, some doubted the existence of benefit of RNI, though some studies offered support. INSEMA did not permit RNI for 1-3 nodes positive, and in SOUND there were no instructions for RT or record of RNI use, nearly eliminating any chance of benefit from SLNB. A rationale for the study is that for many oncologists an elevated Oncotype is what indicates chemotherapy for 1-3 nodes, not node positive disease itself. However if that is the case and SLNB already plays no role in determining treatment, then there is no need for SLNB or a trial. Like a PET scan or xray, SLNB is a diagnostic tool, not a treatment, and would not be expected to have any survival benefit by itself. The only meaningful endpoint in a SLNB trial is the detection rate. Consider if a trial was designed to randomize PDL1 immunohistochemistry, but treatment with immunotherapy was forbidden. Some might advocate for omission of SLNB in T1 age >70, but there is no trial of RNI vs. obs in N+ age >70 to support this practice, and the EBCTCG meta-analysis even found a benefit with RNI in N0. Treatment should be individualized after staging. NSABP B51, although likely underpowered, also appears to reaffirm the benefit of RNI in ER+ Her2- on subanalysis in those who have CR in nodes from neoadjuvant chemo.

The SOUND authors write in the discussion that the trial was not powered to detect differences from adjuvant treatments. In other words the study tested if SLN removal itself has any intrinsic benefit. The INSEMA authors write that omission of SLNB was must be weighed against potential benefit of RNI. If RNI was a requirement in those with 1-3 nodes, and the trial was properly powered, EBCTCG 2023 suggests the results would have been in favor of SLNB.

PBI and mastectomy. Another question that arises is whether PBI should be offered after omission of SLNB and if the findings should extend to post-mastectomy - a setting where RT would then be omitted completely. PBI was not permitted in INSEMA, and mastectomy was not allowed in either study. WBRT tangents and PMRT allow for at least some radiation to axillary levels I-II. One might also choose to exercise caution with IMRT SIB boost regimens targeted to breast only and add contours for axillary I and/or II.

Even in T1, SLNB still resulted a 14% detection rate. Efficacy outcomes are coincidental and related to the era and prohibition of RNI. A diagnostic method serves its role when it leads to a change in treatment that leads to benefit. It is also to be acknowledged that there is some good cause to avoid SLNB, most importantly an easier post-op recovery. The authors are applauded for their goal to eliminate potentially unnecessary procedures, and it is recognized that the trial was designed before the release of the EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis, when RNI was more controversial. Omission of SLNB is probably reasonable in T1a. Ultimately the EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis confirms the benefit and continued practice of SLNB.
(Commentary last updated Jan 2026, Estes)

trials.commentary:
This trial was prior to the era of ultrasound, SLNB, and chemotherapy. Once ultrasound was developed, many used it as cause to once again doubt the findings, but the ALND portion of the trial continues to be reproduced even in the ultrasound era (ACOSOG Z0011 Giulano 2017, AMAROS Donker 2014).

Bernie Fisher revolutionized breast cancer care. He was a surgeon advocating against surgery, for chemo and endocrine therapy, and for women's autonomy. These were some of the first ever randomized trials. At the time there was fierce oppositon to his ideas, and the trial was run mainly in community centers. Surgeons were so opposed to the findings that practice took years to change even after the trial, and the axillary portion was repeated in multiple other trials. He was advised by some not to attend conferences in order to avoid physical altercations. Later in his career he became a political target and his reputation was ruined due to a witch hunt highlighting one enrolling physician who falsified data. NSABP-06 received a cautionary label of "Scientific Misconduct." The falsified data however didn't change the results, and the label was later removed. For more on Bernie Fisher, listen to Stacy Fisher's podcast Less Radical (2024). https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/less-radical/id1767700499

trials.commentary:
With ALND, suprisingly 21% had ≥3 positive nodes, which suggests that RT and possibly ET can control nodal disease in the RT arm. Nonetheless the regimens were noninferior and OS even appears to be in favor of no ALND. Although the trial was not originally powered for OS, there is a possibility of unknown mechanisms ocurring. Although mastectomy was excluded, there is no reason the results shouldn't apply to mastectomies of similar tumor characteristics. The trial did not complete accrual. There is some question as to whether the trial is powered appropriately. Z0011 had n=856 and AMAROS had n=1425 that were SLN+.

On secondary analysis (Jagsi 2014) high tangents did not have benefit over standard tangents, but this was nonrandomized, and those who had high tangents had more nodes. High tangents might have compensated for increased recurrence. 89% received WBRT and 15% had axillary RT, which was a protocol violation.

trials.commentary:
The trials were prior to the era of Her2. The authors comment in the discussion that since these trials techniques have improved including in targeted systemic therapy, nodal dissection and sectioning, endocrine therapy, and also RT techniques. All therapies have improved, including RT, especially in techniques to avoid the heart. This meta-analysis is the highest level of evidence and remains so until more specific trials are undertaken.

For this analysis the authors limited evaluation to those with full lymph node dissections to address concerns that benefit of RT may have been due to inadequate LNDs. However it is now known that there is often no benefit to full LND over SLND in 1-2+ nodes. From that standpoint these patients are actually overtreated with LND (ACOSOG Z0011, Giuliano 2010).
trials.notes:
Advanced overview
-Landmark trial NSABP B04 shwed that RT can treat the axilla, and patients can undergo total mastectomy instead of the morbid radical mastectomoy
-Many doubted the study, and the findings have been reproduced and furthered in varioous trials such as NSABP B32, AMAROS, and ACOSOG Z0011, showing that ALND is not needed in 1-2 SLNB+
-LC and OS benefit of PMRT was established in Danish 82bc and British Columbia studies, as well as others
-EBCTCG PMRT meta-analysis showed benefit with PMRT in 1-3 nodes and ≥4 nodes. Some doubt the benefit in 1-3 nodes given advancementt in chemotherapy in some subtypes. Treatment may be individualized
-There is no randomized trial to confirm the benefit of scar boost. A large retrospective study from Mass Gen showed no benefit

trials.commentary:
About 70% were N1. RNI was not routine in the study, which may explain the lack of benefit. Axillary RT was completely prohibited. SCV and IMN RT were optional and performed in 12% and 1.5%. A prior EBCTCG PMRT meta-analysis (2014) showed benefit in BCM with PMRT in 1-3 nodes positive. The EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis (2023) showed benefit wth RNI in 1-3 nodes.

There were fewer than expected events. An update to the EBCTCG meta-analysis may be warranted. It should also be recognized that the trials within the 2014 EBCTCG meta-analysis may not apply in the modern era. Consistent with this, radiation itself has advanced since SUPREMO, including arc IMRT and the development of comprehensive RNI to include IMNs, which showed benefit in the EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis published in 2023. The EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis even showed a benefit with RNI in those N0, perhaps limited to medial and central tumors. LC was very low in both arms, but SUPREMO's 10-yr DMFS of about 80% in both arms does leave room for improvement and might have been better with RNI.

About 20% had Her2+ therapy.

trials.interpretation:
Regarding the primary endpoint of the study, hypofractionation did not result in improved physical well-being in mastectomy patients with reconstruction. But there appeared to be no difference. About 90% received RNI.

A secondary endpoint, chest wall adverse effects, was lower than expected and similar between arms.
trials.commentary:
After this study, the DBCG SKAGEN large randomized trial showed that breast cancer mortality worsened by 2% with hypofractionated RNI compared to conventional.

The FABREC trial did not meet its endpoints per the prespecified design. Although one may wish for a different design of the study, including higher power or other endpoints, the trial nicely illustrates that both conventional and hypofractionated radiation can be performed in those with reconstruction with low adverse effects. Grade ≥3 chest wall effects was only 10% and lower than expected. Capsular contraction was not included in chest wall adverse effects as the investigators considered it too subjective.

Bolus use and technique varied and was not associated with adverse effects (Rinaa PA, email communication, Sept 2024). Practice patterns vary. An ESTRO international Delphi consensus guideline recommends bolus only for skin involvement, inflammatory, or anterior margin (Kaidar-Person 2021). ASTRO allows for variation of practice.

🚫 Non BCM is increased. No improvement in BCR or BCM.
trials.interpretation: In modern studies, RNI reduces BC recurrence, BCM, DM, and overall mortality in both node positive and node negative patients. The effects may be greater in those with medial or central tumors. Non BCM is not increased.
trials.commentary:
Different types of RNI were used between the studies. Those that included IMNs would be expected to provide more benefit (DBCG-IMN, MA.20).

It is uncertain which node negative tumors benefit from RNI. Additional subanalysis was not undertaken. One could use the inclusion criteria from the EORTC and MA.20 trials:

EORTC 22922/10925 allowed node negative tumors that were medially or centrally located. These comprised 44% of patients in the study.  On subanalysis at 15 years there was no heterogeneity within treatment groups. The stages were not reported, but 60% were T1, 40% were medial, 44% were N0, and 43% were N1.

MA.20 allowed node negative tumors of size >5 cm or size >2 cm with <10 axillary nodes removed with either ER-, grade 3, or LVI.

Per the authors the most common technique used in older trials, AP IMN fields, delivered a typical mean heart dose of 15 Gy for left sided and 10 Gy for right sided.

In an editorial Recht (2024) elaborates on the findings, including benefit vs possible increase in non BCM, and different effects from different types of RNI as outlined in the supplementary data (Figs S3-7, and Table 1 in commentary). The bottom line is that 15 year follow-up is outstanding for any trial, and breast cancer mortality is improved at 15 years, without any significant change in non-breast cancer mortality. A secondary publication from the DBCG authors concluded that IMN RT to left sided patients outweighs risk to the heart (Thorsen 2014). Techniques such as arcs may lower the risk of cardiac disease further. Another EBCTCG meta-analysis showed that even T1N0 have a late DM risk of 13% at 5-20 years after endocrine therapy (Pan 2017). Investigation into additional therapy is still warranted - one could speculate that RNI with IMN RT for T1N0 medial tumors could help reduce these late failures; some others may want more evidence.
(Commentary last updated 2024, Estes)
trials.notes:
RNI overview
-Historical trials showed OS detriment with IMN RNI
-Later more modern trials EORTC 22922, MA.20, AMAROS, DBCG IMN, KROG 0806 showed various small benefits with RNI in DM and OS
-An eventual EBCTCG meta-analysis on RNI showed a BCM benefit in 1-3 nodes and even in N0 (possibly limited to medial and central tumors, orr other high rirsk tumors
-NSABP B51 showed no benefit with RNI after CR in nodes after neoadjuvant chemo, but the trial may be underpowered

Characteristics: 57% were Her2+ and 23% triple negative

trials.interpretation:
Overall there was no benefit with RNI for those with pCR in nodes after neoadjuvant chemo for cN1 disease. The study may be underpowered. The CIs are wide and nearly all cross 1, and results vary by subtype.

RNI should continued to be administered to those ER/PR+ Her2-. On subgroup analysis there was benefit in ER/PR+ Her2-.

For lumpectomy, WBRT without RNI is otherwise still recommended in this setting.
trials.commentary:
NSABP B51 highlights advancements in chemotherapy and shows that some patients might be able to safely avoid radiation therapy. LR RFS is outstanding at 99%. However due to low events the trial is underpowered in some aspects, and probably should have been separate trials for each subtype. 57% were Her2+.

Statistical design. There are concerns that the trial is underpowered. The study was powered for superiority, not noninferiority, there were less than expected events for analysis, and specific results were not reported by subtype. Some have commented that the analysis should have been event driven rather than time driven. The EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis (2023) showed BCM benefit with RNI - when some of the studies within it did not - and NSABP B51 could be a reproduction of those underpowered trials that need a larger meta-analysis. The authors reported time driven analysis rather than event driven as intended. On subgroup analysis ER/PR+ Her2- did favor benefit with RNI. Triple negative had worse outcomes with RNI. There also appears to be benefit in ages 50-59. Results are excellent in both arms but CI intervals are wide, and authors have not reported efficacy endpoints for each subtype. Nearly all CIs cross 1 except ER/PR+ Her2-. Although possibly underpowered, this is not to say the results have no meaning. It should be acknowledged that if results are excellent in all arms and subtypes, we may not need extraordinary power to detect small differences, but results do appear to differ by subtype. The authors plan to report longer follow-up.

SLNB. The results of NSABP B51 support the continued practice of SLNB for ER/PR+ Her2-. INSEMA and SOUND concluded no benefit to SLNB in T1, but RNI for 1-3 nodes was forbidden in those trials, so there would be no benefit to SLNB. The EBCTCG RNI meta-analysis (2023) shows BCM benefit with RNI in 1-3 nodes.

Patient population. Enrollment selection favored Her2+ and triple negative, those who were expected to have good response from chemotherapy. Axillary cN1 prior to neoadjuvant chemo was required, and the specific number of clincally positive nodes was not documented. Remember, cN1 status is positive level I-II axillary nodes and is not determined on quantity like pN1. The study does not outline what diagnostic methods were used. Even at the time of publication, NCCN recommends to "consider" imaging such as CT and PET, thus patients may be understaged.

WBRT & Oncotype. In BCS, WBRT was required in both arms, not omitted after pCR. Thus WBRT is still required, but investigation of omission of WBRT or surgery might be warranted in Her2+. This study was prior to RXPONDER, therefore some ER/PR+ with low Oncotype now would have only had radiation. A post-hoc subanalysis of effects by Oncotype would be enlightening.

Contouring. The contoured volumes and coverarge required in the trial were larger than what was covered with clinically marked 2D/3D tangents (Fontanilla PRO 2012), and VMAT was not in widespread use at the time. Nonetheless adverse effects are low.

Dose constraints: mean heart ≤4 Gy (VA mean ≤5 Gy)
Left sided heart V25 ≤10%

trials.patients: Early stage breast cancer without neoadjuvant treatment
trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 0.5% lidocaine peritumoral injection 7-10 mins prior to surgery
vs.
➜ no lidocaine
trials.interpretation: Peritumoral lidocaine injection prior to surgery improves DFS and OS and should be standard of care.
trials.commentary: The old wive's tale: "surgery lets the air in." Were the conspiracy theorists in the right this whole time? This landmark trial asserts yes. In the background of the paper, the authors provide a number of sources for their rationale. Lidocaine modulates receptor tyrosine protein (Src) kinases and sodium channels. This in turn can inhibit cell proliferation, motility, invasion, and promote focal adhesion, which could reduce metastatic potential. Possible critcisms: a 4% benefit in both DFS and OS is unusual, and an OS benefit is not normally seen so early. Regardless lidocaine is a simple and cost effective intervention with few adverse effects.

trials.methods:
Retrospective study to identify those who benefit from dose escalation.

➜ Various doses used, but generally 51 Gy/1.5 Gy BID then boost 9-15 Gy
trials.results:
5-yr LRC 84% full course vs. 51% if not completing full therapy
5-yr DMFS 47% vs. 20%
5-yr OS 51% vs. 24%

-Dose escalation up to 66 Gy from 60 gave LRC benefit in: less than partial response to neoadjvant chemo, close, positive, or unknown margins, or <45 yrs old

grade 3-4 effects 29% with 66 Gy, 15% with 60 Gy.
Lymphedema 9% vs 2%.
Fibrosis 6% vs 4%.
Brachial plexopathy 2% vs 0%.
trials.interpretation: In inflammatory breast cancer, completion of mastectomy, RT, and chemo leads to high LC. Dose escalation to 66 Gy appears to mitigate failure in partial responders, young age, or positive or close margins.
trials.commentary:
This study is among the largest series for inflammatory breast cancer. At the same time, don't view in isolation. Also note that it and others are retrospective. Other series show other conclusions or no differences. In a editorial review of IBC series, Woodword (2015) infers that the data is mixed, but either acceleration, bolus, or dose escalation is called for in all IBC. Randomized trials seem unlikely to be undertaken.

Consider also the difficulty in classifying outcomes. IBC often recurs just outside the radiation field. Is this a local, regional, or distant recurrence?

Mean tumor size 1.7 cm, range 1.2-2.0

trials.interpretation: WBRT for palliation of brain mets is noninferior to observation in QALY outcomes in these poor prognosis patients. Most had ≤4 lesions. On subanalysis OS favors WBRT for ≥5 mets or age <60.
trials.commentary:
On subanalysis, ≥5 mets did favor WBRT for OS. WBRT seems to be more of use in those with greater numbers of mets, while SRS could help preserve QOL in those with fewer lesions.

QOL metrics can be unreliable (Amdur 2019), and may especially tend to be negative in poor prognosis patients regardless of the therapy. This is imporant to note, but it should not be suggested that QOL results are to be ignored. Physician assessed symptoms might have been a useful endpoint. There is a better possibility that QALYs would be improved if SRS was used (RTOG 1270, Brown 2017). Over 50% of patients had only 1-4 mets, and 30% had 1 met! It is unclear why these were not suitable for SRS in the trial but likely due to poor KPS perceived as a contraindication or logistical issues such as setup and treatment time.

The patients were poor prognosis: median OS was 2 mos. The lack of OS benefit was not suprising, and it was not a primary endpoint. Palliative therapies, in general, and also perhaps by definition, are not expected to improve OS. On the other hand since this study we know that some patients with oligometastasis and limited brain metastasis can have more favorable prognosis. The subanalysis results showing OS benefit in ≥5 mets are actually new findings to support RT. WBRT did have neurologic death benefit in Patchell II (1998). An endpoint of neurologic death might have been useful. There is consistent LC benefit across trials.

Since the trial's design, memantine and hippocampal sparing are innovations to improve QOL. The dose used in this study, 20 Gy/5 fx, is routine in UK, Europe, Asia, Canada, and Australia. It was as effective as other regimens in RTOG 6901 & 7361 (Tsao 2012, Borgelt 1980 and 1981).

Individualized approaches are called for. Although some concerns with the trial may exist regarding the role of RT, it should not be dismissed. It is the only randomized trial evaluating WBRT vs. observation in multiple brain mets. The trial provides support for hospice in limited life expectancy.

trials.commentary:
GammaTile is a bioresorbable collagen implant embedded with four cesium-131 seeds. Half life 9.7 days. Collagen implants are already used in neurosurgery and act as scaffold grafts for dura repair.

About five patients in each arm were found to have glioblastoma on final pathology and were excluded from analysis. In the SRS group 92% received 3-5 fractions. MRI review was central and blinded by two ACR certified neuroradiologists who had 100% agreement. Regarding logistics, the radiation oncologist no longer is required to be present during the procedure, but there is a billing code for supervision.

How could survival be so markedly improved? OS was a secondary endpoint and only evaluated because the study met predetermined thresholds. Benefits of GammaTile include improved LC, less radiation necrosis, faster time to begin systemic therapy, and better adherence. Recall that cavity LC with post-op SRS is 70-80% in RTOG 1270 & MDACC randomized trials, which allows for opportunity for improvement (Brown 2017 and Mahajan 2017). There are some differences in histologies between arms, but generally they seem balanced. It's indeed possible that improved LC and less radiation necrosis did improve survival though the magnitude of benefit seems astonishing, or in other words possibly some contribution of Type 1 error. There was higher compliance since 18% weren't able to even undergo postop SRS. Per protocol analysis was performed, and results were still in favor of GammaTile. For comparison in RTOG 1270, only 5% did not receive postop SRS, in the MDACC trial all received postop SRS, and in the JCOG study only 2% did not receive postop SRS (Kayama 2017). The ROADS population may have been higher risk, and this still supports GT's use. Explanations for nonadherence are of interest and could reveal processes that could be improved upon. Perhaps extra collagen grafting also contributed to survival, but this would be purely speculative; placebo collagen without cesium was not used in the control arm. Some results exceed conventional wisdom, but the results are persuasive and the trial was rigorous.

With SRS, OS is maintained compared to WBRT alone. QOL is improved with SRS.

On post-hoc central review, there was no difference in LC between SRS and WBRT. However, SRS continued to show worse LC in lesions >3 cm. On the initial report, LC was worse with SRS

When comparing 37.5 Gy to 30 Gy, 37.5 Gy led to more adverse effects. There was some trend to benefit in LC, cranial control, and OS, but not significant.
trials.commentary:
The defined primary endpoints of the study were QOL and OS, but LC is shown here first due to its interest to practitioners and to make parallel to other similar studies here. If the study is powered for OS, it should also be powered for LC as a primary endpoint.

The initial report showed inferior LC with SRS. This finding was contrary to the conventional wisdom that SRS should result in superior LC due to its higher BED (But note similar LC of 70% in MDACC post-op study, as well as EORTC and Alliance looking at SRS without surgery [Chang 2009, Kocher 2011, Brown 2016]). Are these failures or necrosis? Unlike the MDACC study, RTOG 1270 did not require central review: A post-hoc central review of LF was later reported at ASTRO 2022 and showed less of a difference, LC 79% vs. 87%, p=0.099. The trending p value of 0.099, however, may not provide complete confidence for some, especially since tumors of size >3 cm still had better results with WBRT. At the very least, the trial illustrates the difficulty in assessing LF after SRS and distinguishing LF from radiation necrosis. There is no consensus or reliable method to do so. But even if SRS indeed tends to worse LF, OS is maintained and QOL is superior. Indeed, some data even suggest that radiation necrosis-like findings are correlated with improved OS, perhaps a sign of immune response (Lehrer 2022).

Results for SRS could be improved with fractionation, better conformality, protons, or higher dose. Or perhaps better criteria are needed to assess LF vs. radiation necrosis. And the elephant in the room: perhaps brain metastasis, especially larger ones, are better treated with 30-37.5 Gy focal IMRT in 10-15 fractions. Or maybe some necrosis is ideal if it represents an immune response.

This protocol provides useful doses to prescribe SRS based on size. Note 15 fx has higher BED than the 10 fx regimen.

trials.subtopic: SRS for post op cavity STR vs. WBRT
trials.patients:
1-4 brain metastasis and resection of all, GTR or STR (73% had single met)

One lesion >3 cm allowed
trials.methods:
Resection of all brain mets →

➜🏆 SRS to cavity for STRs & observation of GTRs (termed "salvage SRS")
vs.
➜ WBRT 37.5 Gy

40% in SRS arm had STR and SRS; 60% had GTR and obs

SRS doses: 24 Gy for ≤4 cc, 18 Gy for >4 cc
trials.results:
-cavity LC 51% vs. 78%
(crude, calculated using table A2)
-LF as sole first recurrence 51% vs. 45%
-LF as any first recurrence 64% vs. 48%
-Median intracranial PFS 4.0 vs. 10.4 mos
-Median OS 15.6 mos, not different
-Neurologic death ~22%, not different
-Leptomeningeal mets 13%, not different
-Radiation necrosis 2.6% vs. 1.6%

Grade 2-4 cognitive adverse effects 7.7% vs. 16.4%
trials.interpretation: SRS for STR only in resected brain mets is noninferior compared to WBRT in OS. However LR is increased.
trials.commentary:
Crude LC is hand calculated by myself using supplemental table A2. Note the high rate of LF and low PFS in the SRS arm. Despite the poor control, there is still no change in OS or neurologic death.

This study requires resection of all brain mets. SRS was given only when resection was subtotal (40%), but not for GTR (60%), which may explain the poor LC in this study.

WBRT was 15 fractions (higher BED than 30 Gy in 10 fx).

trials.patients:
1-3 brain metastases and GTR of ≥1 lesion (~62% had single met)

Resection cavity ≤4 cm and unresected lesions ≤3 cm
trials.methods:
➜🏆 SRS to cavity
vs.
➜ Obs to cavity

Unresected lesions treated with SRS in both arms

SRS doses: 16 Gy for ≤10 cc, 14 Gy for >10.1-15 cc, 12 Gy for >15 cc
trials.results:
LC improved with SRS over obs
12-mo cavity LC 72% vs. 43%
12-mo distant brain control 58% vs. 67% (NS)
Time to WBRT 15 mos (NS)
Median OS 17 mos, not different
Neurologic death 64% vs. 48%, p=0.13
12-mo leptomeningeal 28% vs. 16% (NS)
No radiation necrosis events with SRS

-Larger tumor size was associated with LR (in obs and SRS arms). SRS improved LC even in small resected lesions over obs.

-Factors not associated with LR: histology (lung, breast, melanoma, other), extracranial disease status, GPA score, # brain mets
trials.interpretation: SRS improves LC compared to observation in resected brain mets. OS and neurologic death are unchanged.
trials.commentary:
An unexpected finding was that LC after post-op SRS was only 72%; was assumed to be higher. See commentary on RTOG 1270 (Brown 2017). All follow-up MRIs were reviewed centrally by the study neuroradiologist. Still, there is no consensus on how to diagnose rad necrosis by imaging. Similar finding in RTOG 1270, LC 61%. Note similar LC of 70% in EORTC and Alliance looking at SRS without surgery (Kocher 2011, Brown 2016). Does surgery add benefit in LC when SRS is given?

Larger tumors had worse LC in both arms. Investigation may be warranted toward higher dose or multi-fractionation in these tumors. Lower doses were used in this study than in RTOG 9005 (Shaw 2005). It should be recognized that WBRT has the best lesion specific LC (Andrews 2004).
trials.reference: 1. Mahajan A, Ahmed S, McAleer MF, et al. Post-operative stereotactic radiosurgery versus observation for completely resected brain metastases: a single-centre, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Oncol 2017;18:1040-8. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(17)30414-X

trials.citation: Guo et al, JAMA Netw Open, 2023
trials.patients:
High grade glioma
(54% were grade 4)
trials.methods:
➜🏆 adj TMZ + IFN-α
vs.
➜ adj TMZ

Maximum 12 cycles of TMZ was allowed, but median 6.0 was given in both arms
trials.results:
Overall (grade 3 & 4)
⬆️ Median OS 26.7 mos vs. 18.8 mos
⬆️ 2-yr OS 57% vs. 37%
⬆️ 5-yr OS 18% vs. 9%

WHO Grade 4
⬆️ Median OS 20.5 mos vs. 17.7 mos

WHO Grade 3
⬆️ Median OS 39.6 mos vs. 20.5 mos

Unmethylated MGMT
⬆️ Median OS 24.7 mos vs. 17.4 mos

Methylated MGMT
No improvement in OS

No overall difference in PFS. On subanalysis PFS is improved in grade 3, and trend to improvement in unmethylated, p=0.06. No PFS improvement in grade 4 or methylated.
trials.interpretation: Adjuvant IFN-α improves OS in high grade glioma. On subanalysis the effect seems to be present only in unmethylated.
trials.commentary:
The rationale for the study was that research has shown that IFN-α downregulates MGMT. 54% were grade 4. It is unknown how many grade 4 were GBM, but epidemiologically, it would be expected to be a large majority. The OS for grade 3, 20.5 mos in the control arm, suggests these may have actually been grade 4 and were miscategorized; OS for grade 3 in CATNON was 82 mos. This may mean that the trial results apply more to grade 4. Detailed molecular studies are not yet available. A post-hoc eval of even simply IDH status would be enlightening. Some may wish to see findings reproduced in their home nation; commentary on why this is so deserves its own investigation. Some might speculate that the trial is underpowered. A positive partially underpowered phase III trial is still equal to higher level evidence than a phase II or ongoing trial.

Interferon administration is resource intensive, with risk of seizure, and requires admission to ICU.

The results of the trial do show fairly good results, with statistical odds that would be outstanding at a casino. Few interventions have shown OS benefit in GBM. In pathologies such as glioblastoma, especially unmethylated, risk tolerance may be wider for some. If you were in this situation, would you want interferon?
trials.reference: 1. Guo C, Yang Q, Xu P, et al. Adjuvant Temozolomide Chemotherapy With or Without Interferon Alfa Among Patients With Newly Diagnosed High-grade Gliomas: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open 2023;6:e2253285. trials.patients: Glioblastoma with methylated MGMT
trials.methods:
➜ 60 Gy + conc & adj TMZ x6 cycles
vs.
➜ 60 Gy + TMZ + lomustine
trials.results:
Median OS 31 vs. 48 mos (ITT)
Median OS 30 vs. 40 mos per protocol
Stratified by center and RPA: log rank, p=0.0492, & Cox regression, p=0.0641
Median PFS 16.7 mos, not different (ITT)
Grade ≥3 adverse effects 51% vs. 59%
trials.interpretation:
Adding lomustine to TMZ and RT in GB with methylated MGMT improves OS.
Some critics question if these results will be reproducible.
trials.commentary: The trial may be underpowered. The modifed ITT analysis leads to patients being excluded and even lower power. Some call for a multi-institutional trial with larger numbers (Stupp 2019). It is unclear how there can be a change in OS without a change in PFS. Perhaps lomustine has a later effect, or lomustine creates more pseudoprogression that was called progression. There were some small differences in 2nd line therapies but not major. Nevertheless, GBM is a deadly disease, and some may be willing to accept treatments from a possibly underpowered trial for a chance of benefit.

RT + conc TMZ →

➜ 🏆 tumor treating fields (until 2nd progression or 2 years) + adjuvant TMZ x6-12 cycles
vs.
➜ adjuvant TMZ x6-12 cycles
trials.results:
OS improved with TTF
⬆️ Median OS 20.9 mos vs. 16.0 mos (24.5 vs. 19.8 mos from diagnosis)
⬆️ 2-yr OS 43% vs. 31%
⬆️ 5-yr OS 13% vs. 5%

trials.commentary:
Tumor treating fields (TTF) mechanism: low amplitude alternating electric fields that disrupt cell division and organelles. Required to wear ≥18 hrs in protocol.

Sharp dropoff of treatment effect if device worn <50% of time. At 75% of time (18 hours), a greater benefit occurs.

trials.patients: High grade glioma (95% GB), age >65, KPS≥60
trials.methods:
Noninferiority, margin 0.25

➜ 54-60 Gy
vs.
➜ dose dense TMZ (every other week)
trials.results:
RT and TMZ noninferior:
Median OS 9.6 mos vs. 8 mos
Median EFS 4.7 vs. 3.3 mos

MGMT methylated
Median OS 9.6 vs. 18.4 mos
Median EFS 4.8 vs. 8.5 mos

MGMT unmethylated
Median OS 10.2 vs. 6.7 mos, p=0.099
Median EFS 4.6 vs. 3.0 mos, p<0.001

TMZ is ideal for methylated MGMT and RT is ideal for unmethylated MGMT.
trials.commentary: The noninferiority margin was 25%, which is generous for a noninferiority trial. The HR & CI for OS was HR=1.09 (0.84-1.42). EFS curves appear in favor of radiation, and the CI only slightly crossed 1, HR=1.15 (0.92-1.43). Hypofractionated RT in recurrent GBM with bev improves PFS. There is no added adverse effects.

On subanalysis, there was OS improvement with RT in KPS score 90-100, 1st vs. 2-3rd relapse, and methylated MGMT.
trials.commentary:
A primary endpoint of OS was too ambitious, but this trial should be considered positive based on its improvement in PFS. On subanalysis there was OS improvement with RT in KPS score 90-100, 1st vs. 2-3rd relapses, and methylated MGMT. Imaging assessment prior to 6 weeks was recommended against for pseudoprogression. No therapies at this time have shown OS benefit in recurrent GBM. There is no OS benefit with bev in the phase III EORTC 26101, but it did benefit PFS. Drugs are often FDA approved based on phase II trials or for showing improvement in PFS. If PFS was the primary endpoint, this trial would be considered positive, and it should be considered so. 13% in the bev arm received salvage RT.

The trial had wide inclusion criteria. Although large size was allowed, median GTV was 18 cc and median PTV 54 cc. The trial used 3DCRT, IMRT, or protons. IMRT was used in 86%. RT plans were per protocol in only 61%. Low protocol compliance is not necessarily representative of negligence, and might be an indicator that many rad oncs are not comfortable prescribing such a dose in reirradiation or that elements of the protocol weren't widely feasible. SRS is another attractive therapeutic approach.

Brainstem 0.03 cc <35 Gy, or <24 Gy if overlap
No CTV, except 0.5 cm CTV optional for lesions ≤3.5 cm or new lesions. 90% coverage of PTV was variation acceptable

There is no definition of what should be considered overlap in the protocol

At 54 months follow-up, 78% patients completed salvage RT, and 48% completed salvage chemo. The molecular outcomes are reported in Table S1 (2016).

Interestingly median OS in this study appears better than RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951. However those studies did show an OS benefit with combination therapy compared to RT alone. And the CATNON trial for astrocytoma showed better benefit with RT + adj TMZ compared to RT monotherapy. Cross trial comparisons may have imbalanced populations. CODEL for oligodendroglioma results are pending.

This was one of few studies to include anaplastic astrocytoma at the time, however the term anaplastic is no longer in use. Although they sought to include aggresive tumors, the IDHwt rate in this study is similar to other trials for grade 3.

IDHwt was labeled as CIMP. IDHwt tumors require further testing and can include glioblastoma and diffuse pediatric-type high-grade glioma H3wt & IDHwt per WHO 2021. pHGG has variable prognosis with additional subtypes within it (Korshunov 2017, Tauziède-Espariat 2024). Although IDHwt had better OS with TMZ and relatively favorable OS compared to other trials, this subanalysis is probably underpowered. A nearly identical trial EORTC 22033-26033 showed no difference but similar relatively favorable survival for IDHwt. Perhaps sequential treatment warrants investigation in certain IDHwt. A meta-analysis of IDHwt tumors in six phase II/III trials of low grade gliomas showed that alkylating chemotherapy improved PFS not OS (Kinslow 2024).

trials.interpretation:
Radiation followed by TMZ or PCV is preferred as first line therapy.

Results from RTOG 9802 are more favorable than in this study for both astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma, and showed an OS benefit in the combination arm, even when progression or symptoms weren't required for entry.

There is no difference in OS or HRQOL between radiation and TMZ. HRQOL was more associated with tumor progression. PFS in astrocytoma was better with radiation.

Age ≥40 had better prognosis, reinforcing that molecular prognosis matters most.

IDHwt had better outcomes with TMZ, but this analysis may be underpowered, and IDHwt require futher testing for final diagnosis.
trials.commentary:
The trial was activated before results of RTOG 9802. NOA-4 was a similar trial for grade 3 and showed similar findings. A rationale of the study was to delay what was believed to be worse HRQOL with radiation, and to avoid hypothetical malignant transformation after treatment. This approaches glioma as a chronic disease, awaits symptoms or progression for any treatment, and separates and extends treatment options. However HRQOL was not different between the two arms, and was actually more associated with tumor progression, supporting RT+TMZ/PCV. RTOG 9802 may have had a more favorable population (progression or symptoms weren't required) but the bottom line is that this approach showed an OS benefit in 9802 vs. RT alone. 80% in EORTC had 3DCRT. IMRT could improve HRQOL. About 2/3rds crossed over in both arms. EORTC 22845 Nonbelievers' had already shown that radiation does not increase malignant transformation compared to observation.

The study also supports RT+TMZ/PCV upfront rather than vorasidenib. Although vorasidenib improved PFS, it did not improve HRQOL or shrink the tumor. RT+TMZ/PCV is standard, and discussion in low grade glioma should center around cure and local control upfront rather than delay of radiation.

Who should have treatment? NCCN 2026 recommends RT+chemo for those with STR or progression after surgery. For GTR, observation is recommended, or to consider vorasidenib. Some may advocate to only treat for progression. However STR is also a negative prognostic factor especially since an STR will be adjacent to sensitive structures. Astrocytoma has worse prognosis and may warrant treatment earlier.

EORTC 22033-26033 (RT vs. TMZ) showed that worse HRQOL was most associated with progression, not type of treatment. Although some may use this to support treating only at progression, it also supports treatment earlier before progression occurs. In glioma infiltration can be diffuse and subclinical before being noted on imaging. The study also showed that in the molecular era age is no longer a prognostic factor.

IDHwt. 13% were IDHwt. IDHwt tumors require further testing and can include glioblastoma and diffuse pediatric-type high-grade glioma H3wt & IDHwt per WHO 2021. pHGG has variable prognosis with additional subtypes within it (Korshunov 2017, Tauziède-Espariat 2024). Although IDHwt had better OS with TMZ and relatively favorable OS compared to other trials, this subanalysis is probably underpowered. A nearly identical trial NOA-4 showed no difference but similar relatively favorable survival for IDHwt. Perhaps sequential treatment warrants investigation in certain IDHwt. A meta-analysis of IDHwt tumors in six phase II/III trials of low grade gliomas showed that alkylating chemotherapy improved PFS not OS (Kinslow 2024).

trials.interpretation: Vorasidenib improves PFS in grade 2 IDHmut glioma. There was no improvement in HRQOL. OS is not yet reported.
trials.commentary:
Vorasidenib is a mutant IDH1/2 inhibitor. The drug is an option for those who are opposed to or have contraindications for RT+PCV/TMZ, but should not be considered preferred. NCCN advises to consider the drug for GTR (or observation), but not for STR or progression. Some of these patients had indications for RT+chemo including progressive tumor, but were not permitted to receive it. The radiogaphic PFS here is substantially worse than in RTOG 9802, 12 yrs vs. 2.3 yrs. RTOG had similar eligibility and progression was not required. Only median PFS was reported. Those in the placebo arm were allowed to crossover to vorasidenib if they met eligibility criteria and were "not in need of immediate chemotherapy or radiotherapy." Denying access to RT+PCV/TMZ twice is probably unethical, unless this was considered phase II. In the protocol the investigators show bias against radiation, referring to it as "aggressive", "intensive," and "noncurative." The adverse effects of both chemotherapy and radiation are to be acknowledged, but radiation reduces rates of recurrence and death, and better than vorasidenib.  One might call vorasidenib passive, palliative, procrastination, and noncurative. The median PFS of just 1 year improvement from observation suggests it is not durable for most, but could be in some. 2- and 5-yr PFS is not yet reported. We don't have long term information regarding if the drug increases malignant transformation. Vorasidenib may be best suitable for the pediatric population, who can have more adverse effects from radiation.

Should vorasidenib be used to delay RT to improve QOL? Because of the subtle infiltrative nature of low grade gliomas, delay may have the opposite effect - QOL may worsen before clear radiographic progression. Trials have shown stable to improved HRQOL and MMSE after RT, and that HRQOL is most associated with progression (Kinslow 2024). In EORTC 22033 there was no difference in HRQOL between RT and TMZ, and the authors concluded that QOL does not support delay of RT over treatment with RT+chemo. In INDIGO there is no difference in HRQOL with vorasidenib - no worsening and no improvement, which could support its use in some - however followup is limited and HRQOL could change with additional followup as tumors progress. An easy way to achieve a prolonged "time to next intervention" is to tell the patient they don't need treatment or radiation even when displaying progression, but EORTC 22033 does not support this this practice. NCCN 2026 recommends RT+chemo for all with progression or STR, not progression only.

RTOG 9802 vs. INDIGO PFS results:
IDH-mutant median PFS 12 yrs vs. 2.3 yrs
astrocytoma PFS 10.4 yrs vs. 1.4 yrs
oligodendrogliomas >12 yrs (not reached) vs. 2.3 yrs

trials.notes:
Low grade glioma overview:
-EORTC Nonbelievers shows PFS benefit with RT over obs. High risk "SATAN" criteria outlined in Believer's trial
-Believers and INT/NCCTG show that 45-50.4 Gy is adequate over higher dose
-RTOG 9802. New era. PCV gives large OS benefit in high risk (STR or age≥40), especially for oligo and IDH mutant
-RTOG 0424 phase II shows TMZ is also effective. TMZ has never been compared to PCV, but many prefer TMZ for its ease of use
-The INDIGO study shows a modest PFS with vorasidenib, but subpar compared to adjuvant radiation
-EORTC 22033-26033 confirmed RT+chemo as best treatment. HRQOL is most related to tumor progression. No OS or HRQOL difference with RT alone vs TMZ alone. RT+chemo is recommended.

s/p LN dissection for clinically palpable nodes [SLN detected only not eligible]

Must be node positive in ≥1 LN parotid, ≥2 LNs cervical or axilla , ≥3 groin, ECE, ≥3 cm LN cervical, or ≥4 cm LN axilla/groin
trials.methods:
➜ 48 Gy/20 fx
vs.
➜ obs

Primary endpoint: LN field relapse as first relapse and late adverse effects
Secondary endpoints: adjacent relapse, DM, OS, PFS, time to infield progression
trials.results:
RT improved LN relapse
6-yr LN relapse 21% vs. 36%
RFS and OS unchanged, 5-yr OS 35%

22% with RT had grade 3-4 adverse effects, 20% grade 3 (skin in 10% and subcutaneous tissue in 7%). 7.7% with increased limb volume in RT group
trials.interpretation:
Adjuvant radiation therapy for clinically detected LNs in melanoma improves LN relapse but has no confirmed benefit in RFS or OS.

Immunotherapy, clinical trials, or observation are alternative treatment options that may be more ideal.
trials.commentary:
The trial may be underpowered to detect OS benefit, or better eligibility criteria may be needed. A major past concern with RT after ALND was the potential of profound lymphedema, but now ALND is performed less frequently since studies showed no benefit with ALND after SLNB+. Now that there is less risk for lymphedema, a stronger case can perhaps be made for radiation. In the S1801 trial evaluating neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, pCR was only 21%. In the EORTC study evaluating adjuvant immunotherapy, DMFS was still only about 50%, indicating that additional therapy of some kind is warranted. Radiation could play a role. It's possible that radiation could work better in combination with immunotherapy and that there is a benefit with radiation with careful selection criteria. Genetic testing such as DecisionDX Melanoma (Durgham 2024) could help to stratify patients.

The study was prior to PET era. To be eligible for the study nodes were required to be palpable. Some may extrapolate the findings to SLN-detected nodes or image-detected nodes, or a genetic prognostic score, though this was not specifically the study design.
(Commentary updated June 2026, Estes)

trials.patients: locally advanced unresectable BCC
trials.methods:
Phase II, multicenter

➜ neoadj vismodegib then RT plus concurrent vismodegib
trials.results:
ORR 63% from induction
ORR 83% after radiation

1-yr LC 91%
5-yr LC 70% (calculated by me from text)
5-yr PFS 78%
5-yr OS 83%

No grade 4-5 adverse events
trials.interpretation: Neoadjuvant vismodegib then RT plus concurrent vismodegib seems to be effective for unresectable BCC in this small study.
trials.commentary: Vismodegib is FDA approved for those who are not candidates for surgery or radiation. However in practice some may use the drug neoadjuvantly, and with good intent such as to spare the eye or lid. Vismodegib might be able to delay radiation for some, but most will eventually benefit from radiation therapy. In the STEVIE trial 88% discontinued vismodegib. Since the medication is not cytotoxic, radiation should probably still cover the initial extent of disease. Vismodegib can heal ulcerations and may act as a radiosensitizer, perhaps improving tolerability and effectiveness of radiation.
trials.reference: 1. Barker CA, Dufault S, Arron ST, et al. Phase II, Single-Arm Trial of Induction and Concurrent Vismodegib With Curative-Intent Radiation Therapy for Locally Advanced, Unresectable Basal Cell Carcinoma. J Clin Oncol 2024;42:2327-2335. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.23.01708

trials.citation: Basset-Séguin et al, Eur J Cancer, 2017
trials.patients: metastatic and locally advanced unresectable BCC
trials.methods:
Phase II

➜ vismodegib
trials.results:
Median duration of response 23 mos
Median PFS 23 mos
ORR in locally advanced 69%
CR 33%
PR 35%
Stable 25%
PD 2%

Median treatment duration 8 mos
At median follow-up of 18 mos, 88% had discontinued, mainly due to adverse effects

ORR in metastatic 37%

Adverse events
98% had a side effect
Most common muscle spasm, alopecia, ageusia, dysgeusia and weight loss

Serious adverse effects in 24%. Majority resolved by 12 mos
Deaths 4%
trials.interpretation: Vismodegib has response in BCC. Adverse effects should be taken into account.
trials.commentary:
Vismodegib is FDA approved for those who are not candidates for surgery or radiation. However in practice some may use the drug neoadjuvantly, and with good intent such as to spare the eye or lid. Vismodegib might be able to delay radiation for some, but most will eventually benefit from radiation therapy. In the STEVIE trial 88% discontinued vismodegib. Since the medication is not cytotoxic, radiation should probably still cover the initial extent of disease. Vismodegib can heal ulcerations and may act as a radiosensitizer, perhaps improving tolerability and effectiveness of radiation.

Although median treatment duration of treatment was 8 months, the median duration of response was 23 months, suggesting that response can be maintained even long after discontinuation.

Regarding deaths the authors write that "seven were considered related to vismodegib by the investigator but showed presence of comorbidities/risk factors in each case (Supplementary Table S5). The DSMB determined these cases to be unrelated to vismodegib (n = 6) or not assessable because of insufficient clinical data (n = 1)." Vismodegib has not been tested in a randomized trial, therefore treatment related deaths and OS compared to control are unknown.
trials.reference: 1. Basset-Séguin N, Hauschild A, Kunstfeld R, et al. Vismodegib in patients with advanced basal cell carcinoma: Primary analysis of STEVIE, an international, open-label trial. Eur J Cancer 2017;86:334-348. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejca.2017.08.022

trials.commentary:
At the time of its publication, the trial was considered conclusive, and a phase III was not designed. 3DCRT planning for anal cancer was tedious, which certainly generated enthusiasm for the transition. Today expectations are that randomized trials are performed. In this case, results have been reproduced in phase III gyn trials (TIME C, PARCER, INTERTECC). The other view is the "just so" perspective, that IMRT is better just because it is, and this can be seen plainly on the DVH, and a randomized trial isn't always needed.

There was never a trial to confirm a benefit of dose escalation in anal cancer over the Nigro regimen (1981). Trials are ongoing to de-escalate (PLATO ACT IV, DECREASE). A lower dose of radiation and chemotherapy could profoundly reduce skin and heme adverse effects and improve treatment tolerance.

On a secondary analysis of bowel dose contraints, there was lower GI adverse effects with the following small bowel doses:
V25<185 cc
V30<155 cc
V35<40 cc
V40<30 cc

Schrag et al, NEJM, 2023
Basch et al, JCO, 2023
trials.patients: Rectal T2N1, T3N0, T3N1, >5 cm from anal verge, >3 mm radial margin, who are candidates for LAR
trials.methods:
Noninferioriy

➜ Standard: pre-op long course chemoRT → TME → suggested FOLFOX x8
vs.
➜ 🏆 Selective arm: FOLFOX x6 → response assessment with MRI → if response ≥20%, omit RT → TME → suggested FOLFOX x6

if response <20% or <5 cycles completed → long course chemoRT → TME → FOLFOX x2

•post-op chemoRT given for +margin
trials.results:
93% in FOLFOX arm had ≥20% response
✅ 5-yr DFS 81% vs. 79%, noninferior
5-yr LR 1.8% vs. 1.6%, not different
pCR 24% vs. 22%
R0 97% vs. 99%
5-yr OS 90% both arms

In the FOLFOX selective arm, 9% had pre-op RT and 1% had post-op RT

📌Adverse effects
During neoadjuvant: grade ≥3 adverse effects 23% vs. 41%
(neuropathy worse with FOLFOX, 17%, vs. 83%)
During any adjuvant treatment:
Grade ≥3 adverse effects 26% vs. 33%

📌QOL
•During neoadjuvant treatment:

chemoRT: worse diarrhea and bowel function

FOLFOX: worse anxiety, appetite loss, constipation, depression, dysphagia, dyspnea, edema, fatigue, mucositis, neuropathy, N/V

•1-yr after treament: chemoRT had worse fatigue, neuropathy, sexual function
trials.interpretation: The two approaches are noninferior in those that meet PROSPECT eligibility criteria.
trials.commentary:
Overview. The trial supports chemotherapy→TME in those that meet PROSPECT eligibility criteria. LR rates were very low in both arms. Nearly double the amount of chemotherapy was permitted in the selective arm. Radiation may be useful for those who wish to undergo less chemotherapy. Another alternative for this population is avoidance of surgery through organ preservation with chemoradiation.

Adverse effects. Neoadjuvant QOL was reported as worse overall with FOLFOX. ChemoRT QOL showed worse acute diarrhea as well as later fatigue, sexual function, and neuropathy, though neuropathy may be secondary to how chemotherapy was administered. For adverse effects chemo has worse neuropathy during neoadjuvant treatment. Patients who do not wish to undergo chemotherapy, or are unsure if they will complete it due to its difficultly, may elect for chemoRT.

FOLFIRINOX and sequencing. There are questions regarding application of other trials. PRODIGE 23 showed OS and DM benefit with FOLFIRINOX. In that study 7-yr LR was 5% with TNT, indicating a potentially continuing role for radiation. Selective use of radiation has not yet been evaluated with FOLIRINOX (though might be a reasonable extrapolation). The two trials will have different patient populations and should not be directly compared. Sequencing trials with FOLFOX found that chemoradiation should be given first for better pCR, and is recommended by ASCO 2024 rectal guidelines (Scott). This approach is especially useful for organ preservation.

Other stages. Those ineligible in PROSPECT were T4, N2, tumors <5 cm from anal verge, ≤3 mm radial margin, and requiring APR, though some were eligible for FOWARC. If strictly following PROSPECT, these should continue to receive chemoradiation. Additionally LR was 5% with chemoRT in PRODIGE 23. A similar population of advanced tumors were enrolled in RAPIDO, which showed improved LRC in this subset with long course chemoRT compared to short course. Prior to this study, the ASTRO 2020 guidelines already conditionally recommended to omit pre-op RT for T3a/b N0 located >10 cm from anal verge with mrCRM ≥2 mm and no mrEMVI.
