trials.commentary:
Results at one year are favorable and additional follow-up is awaited. Based on feedback to avoid surgery, the protocol was amended to allow randomization between only long course RT or short course RT. The study used a limited mesorectum as the CTV for these early stage tumors. This CTV may not be applicable for higher stages, but if results show low isolated regional nodal recurrence, this could be adopted.

Although the trial's goal is to address organ preservation, this simple randomization shows clearly the benefit long course radiation over short course, without other confounders in the arms such as extra systemic chemotherapy or changes in sequencing.

Radiation planning
The CTV consists of a limited mesorectum. It does NOT include internal and external iliac nodes.
Superior: S2/3 or 2 cm superior to GTV, whichever is greater
Inferior: 2 cm inferior to GTV (or 1 cm if below mesorectum)
Anterior: anterior mesorectum
Posterior: sacrum, coccyx, puborectalis muscle
Lateral: mesorectum or pyriformis, puborectalis muscle

Dose constraints for long course
Bowel Cavity V20 <180 cc, V30 <130 cc, V45 <90 cc
Bladder V35 <22%, V50 <7%

Dose constraints for short course
Bowel Cavity V10 <180 cc, V18 <110 cc, V23 <85 cc
Bladder V21 <15%, V25 <5%

TNT = total neoadjuvant therapy. Could outcomes have been improved even more with a TNT arm of pre-op 50 Gy/25 fx + cape → CAPOX x4? Another interpretation of the trial could be that less CAPOX cycles are needed. Interestingly IMRT was required in the study. Although similar numbers of patients did not undergo surgery in both groups, there were more that refused surgery in the CRT arm, n=17 vs. 36; reasons why were not reported. Since STAR TREC trial, there is less controvery regarding fractionation. This organ preservation study had a simple randomization between short and long course chemoRT and clearly showed superior response with long course chemoRT.

A word of caution when comparing this to the RAPIDO study: the RAPIDO population was more advanced and adjuvant chemo was optional in the CRT arm. RAPIDO was a superiority trial vs the non-inferiority trial for STELLAR so trial and statisical design differences need to be considered.  The trial was powered for noninferiority in DFS, not OS. A benefit in OS is difficult to explain without an improvement in MFS or LRR, as well as lower compliance rates. It could signal that chemo is best given pre-operatively. The POLISH II trial similarly showed an OS improvement with short course RT compared to long-course CRT without DFS benefit at 3 years but not at 8-year follow-up.

trials.methods:
➜ TNT: pre-op 25 Gy/5 fx → CAPOX/FOLFOX → TME
vs.
➜ pre-op 50-50.4 Gy + cape → TME → optional CAPOX/FOLFOX (given in 59%)

Surgery at 6-10 weeks
Primary endpoint: disease failure
trials.results:
3-yr disease failure 24% vs. 30%
3-yr DM 20% vs. 27%
3-yr OS 89% in both arms

5-yr LRF 12% vs. 8%, p=0.07
5-yr LRR (LRFs minus those resected with R0/R1) 10% vs. 6%, p=0.027

pCR 28% vs. 14%

75% completed chemo in 84% vs. 58%
serious adverse effects 38% vs. 34% (34% with chemo and 34% without)
trials.interpretation:
There was less disease failure and DM, better pCR, but worse LRC with [short course RT → chemo → TME] compared to [long course RT → TME → optional chemotherapy].

There was higher tolerance of chemotherapy when delivering chemo pre-op.
trials.commentary:
Local failure was worse with short course RT → chemo pre-op (vs. long course chemoRT → surgery → optional chemo) even though pCR was higher. Apparently pCR is not a surrogate for LRR. The optionality of systemic chemotherapy in the long course arm (given in 59%) limits the interpretation of this trial. (Optional chemo was given per predefined hospital policy.) It's unsurprising that mandating systemic chemo in the short course arm gives better DFS. Causation in the trial is unclear: are the results due to addition of chemo, compliance, short vs. long course RT, or sequencing? Chemo compliance was oddly counted as those who achieved 75% chemo dosing, not those that actually completed it. CAO/ARO/AIO 12 was another sequencing trial and showed that long course RT first → FOLFOX → TME gave better pCR than FOLFOX first → long course chemoRT → TME.  Since STAR TREC trial, there is less controvery regarding fractionation. This organ preservation study had a simple randomization between short and long course chemoRT and clearly showed superior response with long course chemoRT.

Taking the present findings into account, [long course RT → chemo → TME] seems to be a useful option. Numerous short course vs. long course trials exist, with varying designs and results. STELLAR was a similar trial, and showed no difference in LC but worse pCR with [long course RT → surgery → optional chemo]. STELLAR had less patients and lower-risk, more typical inclusion criteria (cT3-4, N+). Two early trials, Poland (Bujko 2006) and TROG 01.04 compared short course vs. long course RT in clean randomizations and both found nonsignificant trends toward worse LR with short course.

For short course RT planning, the target is the pelvis. The RAPIDO protocol provides detailed instructions for nodal contouring that allow more tissue sparing than RTOG.

trials.patients: Rectal cancer
trials.methods:
Retrospective database comparison

➜ watch and wait with gross LR after CR (IWWD database)
vs.
➜ TME with ≤10% viable cells (VIKINGO database)
trials.results:
DM 23% vs. 10%
3-yr DMFS 75% vs. 87%
trials.interpretation:
In this retropspective database analysis, those with LR after watch and wait have worse outcomes and more DM than those with ≤10% viable cells after TME.

Randomized trials and careful patient counseling prior to organ preservation are warranted.
trials.commentary:
The comparison is reasonable but may not be equal: one cannot say that those with gross LR after WW are the same group as those that would have had ≤10% viable cells after TME. Some with ≤10% viable cells may have had cells that were still undergoing mitotic death, inactive, or that would have had later CR if observed for longer. Although adjustment can correct for some imbalances, this also cannot replace random assortment in a randomized trial. It is also possible however that leaving those cells present for longer periods of time in WW provides them more opportunity to spread, or that chemoradiation could select for the worse clonogens in some histologies.

Randomized trials are warranted for TME vs. organ preservation. Still the study here should not be dismissed and may be useful for counseling and decision making. Both ASCO (Scott 2024) and NCCN guidelines allow for rectal preservation. ASCO's consensus is that the procedure has moderate evidence, strength conditional. NCCN also allows rectal sparing for dMMR/MSI-H or POLE/POLD1 ultra-hypermutated treated with immunotherapy based on phase II data. It should be acknowledged that if considered a toxicity, colostomy from APR is grade 4 RTOG. Framing colostomy as treatment does not remove its detriment to QOL. Ask the patient: what would they like to do? Early data is more acceptable to implement in scenarios of poor prognosis or excess adverse effects. See also commentary on OPRA.

Phase II organ preservation

Arm B:
➜  🏆 long course chemoRT 54 Gy → consolidation FOLFOX/CAPEOX

→Response assessment at 8-12 weeks with EUS, MRI, and DRE. If CR or nearCR → watchful waiting

5-yr organ preservation 39% vs. 54%

trials.commentary:
The trial is phase II and compared to historical control. Most were T3 and N+, and 10-15% were T4, a wide range of eligibility. Some may wish to see a randomized trial of TME vs. organ preservation. Both ASCO (Scott 2024) and NCCN guidelines allow for rectal preservation. ASCO's consensus is that the procedure has moderate evidence, strength conditional. NCCN also allows rectal sparing for dMMR/MSI-H or POLE/POLD1 ultra-hypermutated treated with immunotherapy based on phase II data.

It should be acknowledged that if considered a toxicity, colostomy from APR is grade 4 RTOG. Framing colostomy as treatment does not remove its detriment to QOL. Ask the patient: what would they like to do?

Those dMMR are best treated with immunotherapy alone if rectal sparing is the objective. Data suggests that dMMR may not respond to radiation (Ye 2020), and in endometrial cancer molecular data suggests that dMMR is both radio- and chemoresistant (Clements 2024, León-Castillo 2020)

Some may question why the organ preservation rate is higher than typically reported pCR for rectal cancer, such as 22% in STELLAR. This may be due to longer interval after surgery, 8-12 weeks, allowing the tumor more time to respond. The OPRA protocol has detailed instructions on how to assess CR. pCR rates may further increase if dMMR patients are excluded from upfront chemoRT. Likewise in CROSS, overall pCR is 29%, yet esophageal sparing LRPFS & LC range from 45-70% in trials (CONCORDE, ARTDECO, RTOG 0246, RTOG 9405). Similarly in the MISSILE trial in NSCLC evaluating SBRT followed by surgery, pCR was only 60%, contrasting with typical LC of 90-95% with SBRT. (RTOG 0236, 0915).
(Commentary last edited Oct 2025, Estes)

10-yr DFS 3% vs. 63% vs. 61% not dfferent
10-yr OS 63% vs. 72% vs. 73%, not different
trials.interpretation: RT can be omitted if extended FOLFOX is given.
trials.commentary:
A multi-institutional study from China. See also the PROSPECT trial, which had narrower inclusion criteria, and more detailed QOL reporting. Results differ. In that trial, DFS was not different between arms similar to 1 and 3. In FOWARC, pCR is improved with radiation, but not LRR, possibly supporting its role, and especially for non operative management.

A variety of substages were included in FOWARC, and a subanalysis was not done. Some of the lower stages may be overtreated and could have chemoRT alone, less FOLFOX, or even surgery alone for favorable T3. About 65% were T3, 25% T4a, and 9% T4b. About 52% were N1, 21% N2a, and 7% N2b. PROSPECT and FOWARC allow more options for patients.

The RAPIDO trial evaluated more advanced tumors with cT4a-b, N2, extramural vascular invasion, involved mesorectal fascia, or enlarged lateral nodes. There was better LRC with long course chemoRT vs short course in that study. This suggests that long course chemoRT is still a necessary component for this subset, as well as improved pCR in FOWARC, an Asian trial. The ASTRO 2020 guidelines already conditionally recommended to omit pre-op RT for T3a/b N0 located >10 cm from anal verge with mrCRM ≥2 mm and no mrEMVI.

trials.interpretation: Neoadjuvant mFOLFIRINOX with 3 months adjuvant FOLFOX improves OS, pCR, DFS, and MFS compared to 6 months adjuvant FOLFOX.
trials.commentary:
After years without innovation, PRODIGE 23 finally established a new standard of care in advanced rectal cancer for improvement of OS and MFS. LR of 5% is low, though not as low as in PROSPECT, indicating perhaps a continuing role for radiation therapy in this population. PRODIGE allowed entry of patients of higher stage than PROSPECT, but also anything that was eligible for PROSPECT. Because of a higher risk patient population, and use of different chemotherapy, it is unclear if radiation can be omitted with FOLFIRNOX. In PRODIGE 92% completed all cycles of FOLFIRINOX, and 81% in that arm completed adjuvant chemo as well, either 6 cycles of FOLFOX or 4 cycles of capecitabine. 83% were T3, and 17% were T4.

A more equal comparison would have entailed comparing FOLFOX and FOLFIRINOX without alteration of sequencing and without the extra 3 months of adjuvant FOLFOX in the FOLFIRINOX arm. The patient characteristics were not as advanced as RAPIDO and the trials should not be directly compared. FOLFIRINOX is a new standard of care in this setting.

trials.commentary: Should the trial have been powered for OS? One view is that PFS/DFS is a surrogate for OS, but this is met with critcism. If DFS leads to OS benefit later, confirmation of causation is difficult. Third, the mechanisms of the interventions leading to PFS in each trial may be very different. There is OS benefit with oxaliplatin in the MOSAIC trial in colorectal cancer (André 2015). Nonetheless, the US FDA does approve drugs based on PFS/DFS.

trials.patients: T2-4a or any N+, M0, adenocarcinoma only
trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 perioperative docetaxel, oxaliplatin, 5FU, LV (FLOT4)
vs.
➜ pre-op chemoRT to 41.4 Gy + carbo/paclitaxel weekly (CROSS)
trials.results:
FLOT vs. chemoRT

Median OS 66 vs. 37 mos
3-yr OS 57% vs. 51%
3-yr PFS 52% vs. 35%
3-yr DM 32% vs. 47%

3-yr LRR 20% vs. 17%, not different
pCR 17% vs. 8%
trials.interpretation: Peri-operative FLOT improves OS and DM compared to pre-op chemoRT for locally advanced esophageal adenocarcinoma. LRR was not improved with chemoRT.
trials.commentary:
ESOPEC and NeoAEGIS were pre-op trials for adenocarcinoma only. Results in ESOPEC show an impressive OS benefit with FLOT in esophageal cancer, an entity with few advancements over years other than nivolumab for those with partial response. ChemoRT did not improve LRR or pCR in ESOPEC. ChemoRT did have better pCR in NeoAEGIS. Neither trial investigated radiation with FLOT or nivolumab (Checkmate 577, Kelly 2021).

Fojo et al (2025) explain a statistical bias called skimming the median that overestimates survival gains by not taking into account the full dataset, and provide ESOPEC as one of their teaching examples. 3-yr OS of 57% and pCR of 4-17% is certainly short of reliable cure, and there is the potential that radiation and nivolumab could add benefit to FLOT, if they can be tolerated. The FLOT authors write that nivolumab was less effective in adenocarcinoma in Checkman577, supporting FLOT in adenocarcinoma, but in the Fig 2 forest plot the confidence intervals of squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma plainly overlap, and the subanalysis is not specifically powered. The pCR results in ESOPEC and NeoAEGIS with chemoRT, 8-12%, are less than in the CROSS trial itself for adenocarcinoma, 23%, for reasons unclear. In NeoAEGIS both MAGIC and FLOT regimens were permitted after an amendment, making the findings difficult to interpret. Allowing access to standard of care FLOT was absolutely the right decision by the authors, while many others resist altering their protocols to allow new interventions or crossover.

Chemoradiation is still standard for non operative management. Although not supported by a trial, it may be reasonable to follow chemoRT with some FLOT or nivolumab, especially for incomplete response. Furthermore those undergoing nonoperative management are typically less medically fit and often not good candidates for FLOT.

trials.patients: Esophagus or GEJ adenocarcinoma T2-3 N0-3
trials.methods:
Noninferiority

➜ perioperative chemo (ECF/ECX/EOF/EOX or FLOT)
vs.
➜ 🏆pre-op chemoRT to 41.4 Gy + carbo/paclitaxel weekly
(CROSS)
trials.results:
3-yr OS 56-57%, noninferior

MAGIC/FLOT vs. chemoRT
R0 82% vs. 96%
LRR not different, 20-25%
pCR 4% vs. 12%

Neutropenia, sepsis slightly worse with MAGIC/FLOT
trials.interpretation: The CROSS regimen leads to superior pathologic response and R0 resections over MAGIC/FLOT. In regards to OS, CROSS and MAGIC/FLOT are noninferior.
trials.commentary:
ESOPEC and NeoAEGIS were pre-op trials for adenocarcinoma only. Results in ESOPEC show an impressive OS benefit with FLOT in esophageal cancer, an entity with few advancements over years other than nivolumab for those with partial response. ChemoRT did not improve LRR or pCR in ESOPEC. ChemoRT did have better pCR in NeoAEGIS. Neither trial investigated radiation with FLOT or nivolumab (Checkmate 577, Kelly 2021).

Fojo et al (2025) explain a statistical bias called skimming the median that overestimates survival gains by not taking into account the full dataset, and provide ESOPEC as one of their teaching examples. 3-yr OS of 57% and pCR of 4-17% is certainly short of reliable cure, and there is the potential that radiation and nivolumab could add benefit to FLOT, if they can be tolerated. The FLOT authors write that nivolumab was less effective in adenocarcinoma in Checkman577, supporting FLOT in adenocarcinoma, but in the Fig 2 forest plot the confidence intervals of squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma plainly overlap, and the subanalysis is not specifically powered. The pCR results in ESOPEC and NeoAEGIS with chemoRT, 8-12%, are less than in the CROSS trial itself for adenocarcinoma, 23%, for reasons unclear. In NeoAEGIS both MAGIC and FLOT regimens were permitted after an amendment, making the findings difficult to interpret. Allowing access to standard of care FLOT was absolutely the right decision by the authors, while many others resist altering their protocols to allow new interventions or crossover.

Chemoradiation is still standard for non operative management. Although not supported by a trial, it may be reasonable to follow chemoRT with some FLOT or nivolumab, especially for incomplete response. Furthermore those undergoing nonoperative management are typically less medically fit and often not good candidates for FLOT.

trials.commentary: Criteria for judging a cCR in this study involved contrasted CT, upper gasteroenterography, and endoscopy with at least 3 locations biopsied at the primary tumor site. Note that PET scan was not used for restaging. Assessing CR at 1 week is intriguing, and, given no change in DFS, might be as long an interval as needed. The authors stopped at a dose of 40 Gy to assess for cCR and then randomized to surgery or definitive CRT. Would the outcomes in both arms be improved if the authors assessed cCR at 50-50.4 Gy and avoided split course radiation? The FFCD 9102 trial (Bedenne 2007) randomized patients to either surgery or definitive chemoRT after 46 Gy nCRT and showed there was higher local control and freedom from local progression in the surgery arm, so it could be possible the surgrical arm in this study received too low of a dose. This is a small single center study of 71 patients but their larger prospective multicenter study (NCT03708042) may be more conclusive.

trials.interpretation: Proton radiation therapy reduces adverse effects compared to IMRT.
trials.commentary: Arcs were not required. There is a possibility there would be no difference if IMRT arcs were used. Some have commented that for the Bayesian analysis, a highly skeptical prior should have been used instead of weakly uniform prior. Some have also commented that the endpoint of total adverse effects burden should be validated first (similar to the controversy surrounding PFS as an endpoint). On the other hand, the trial here is higher level than that used to support IMRT in many cases. Many may use the "just so" rationale for protons (it simply meets constraints when IMRT doesn't, and is more conformal than IMRT on screen). Obviously, the cost-benefit ratio of proton treatment is a consideration as well.

Some assert that RT would be sensitized better with 5-FU/cape or with FOLFIRINOX. SBRT trials are ongoing.

3DCRT in all. ENI was not done
There was no dose constraint for small bowel
trials.notes:
-There is some controversy regarding the role of radiation in unresectable pancreatic cancer
-An early trial, GITSG, showed OS benefit with addition of RT. Another trial, FFCD-SFRO, found worse OS with RT
-The best powered trial, LAP07, shows no OS difference with addition of RT
-LAP07 did show LC benefit with RT
-Better advances have been made in chemotherapy than with RT, such as with FOLFIRINOX and nab-paclitaxel
-Data supporting the role of SBRT in pancreatic cancer is emerging, with phase II data now available
-Potential roles for RT include: borderline tumors, unresectable tumors not receiving chemo, or positive margin after completion of chemo

trials.commentary:
Was the trial powered and designed appropriately? The only 2 patients to achieve pCR in the trial were in the RT arm, even after the chemo only arm reached full accrual. The arms were imbalanced, which may be reflected in the higher OS for the no RT arm. Several factors favored the no RT arm including age, CA19-9 at diagnosis, hepatic artery resections, and disease progression before completion of therapy (Chuong 2022).

Because the RT arm did not reach full accrual, the outcomes here cannot be directly statistically compared; this is why no p-values are provided in the study. The author's conclusion that RT impaired OS is a stretch given that this trial was phase II and not powered for OS, but it is to be acknowledged that the OS difference is wider than one might predict.

In CONKO-007, a trial for nonresectable & borderline pancreatic cancer in which most received FOLFIRINOX - and with more power than Alliance - conventional RT improved pCR and R0 CRM- rates. The worsening of R0 on the Alliance trial with SBRT remains concerning, and could represent a type of radiation fibrosis or necrosis that leads to a more difficult resection. If so, this could perhaps could be remedied by a different dose or moving the timing of surgery. mFOLFIRINOX has added a profound contribution to neoadjuvant therapy, but radiation may still serve a role in those with incomplete response.

trials.commentary:
Large tumor volume was permitted in this study: total tumor volume up to 20 cm, single size 15 cm, and up to 5 mets! SBRT easily can be delivered first, followed by immunotherapy, or the two could potentially be given confurrently. RTOG 1112 was terminated early, possibly due to enthusiasm for immunotherapy at the time. The statistical power of 1112 was modified.

How could SBRT improve OS? If radiation is clearing tumor thrombus, this would improve overall hepatic function. Since TACE is reliant on circulatory pathways, it likely is less effective in clearing thrombotic tumor.

In a study evaluating pre-op immuntherapy in HCC, pCR was only 18% (D'Alessio 2024). The IMBrave trial, randomizing atezolumab + bev vs. sorafenib showed OS & PFS benefit with immunotherapy, median OS 19.2 vs. 13.4 mos and median PFS 6.9 vs. 4.3 mos. Although certainly an achievement in cancer therapy, a 6 month improvement in OS falls short of cure and does not justify omission of five days of radiation. The authors also point out that immunotherapy was not as effective in those with macrovascular invasion.

Other immunotherapy trials showed a similar benefit in OS to SBRT in 1112 but unlike SBRT did not show a PFS benefit (KEYNOTE 240, pembro; HIMALAYA, tremelimumab + durva; Checkmate 459, nivolumab)

trials.commentary:
The ORR was only 44%, which seems worse than SBRT (2-yr LPFS 93% in Xi 2024, disease control 75% in RTOG 1112, and 2-yr LC 100% in TRENDY). There is concern that bevacizumab masks true progression. In the HIMALAYA trial tremelimumab + durvalumab, without TACE, shows an OS benefit compared to sorafinib.

Refer to the Discussion section of the study for commentary on adverse effects. According to the authors, the investigator determined whether an adverse event was due to treatment or not. For example bevacizumab has risk of hemorrhage, and many liver patients already have esophageal varices, and others for example have comorbidity of cirrhosis. Thus the authors reported treatment related adverse effects and "possible" treatment related adverse effects. The reader will notice that the "possible" adverse effects and deaths do increase with durvalumab and D+B combination therapy. This is why randomized trials must be performed. OS was not reported, but based on the number of deaths, seems that OS is worse with D and D+B.

In the HIMALAYA trial, tremelimumab + durvalumab, without any TACE, did show OS benefit. In that study however, durvalumab alone was noninferior to sorafinib.

The authors write that adverse effects doesn't seem in excess when comparing to prior TACE, Bev, and durvalumab studies. They also note that there were no deaths from hemorrhage in the study.

trials.interpretation:
Reduced volume high dose RT (RHDVRT) was not noninferior for LC and did not reduce late effects. However overall outcomes seemed favorable.

Chemotherapy improves LC and bladder preservation rates. There is a trend to improved OS, CSS, DFS, and MFS when adding 5FU and MMC to radiation; however this is not significant long-term.
trials.commentary:
Although the radiation randomization addressed a question of volumes, the trial's primary innovation is its use of hypofractionation. Hypofractionation was physician's choice and not randomized. A later combined propensity matched type analysis of BC2001 and BCON showed no difference between hypofx vs. conventional RT. There are limitations since neither trial originally randomized the dose regimens (Choudhury 2021). A propensity or adjusted analysis is not a replacement for a randomized trial and cannot create fully balanced arms. Hypofx shows generally favorable results prospectively and stands as a useful regimen for many, especially patients who are unfit for long course or have a limited schedule.

Results for all endpoints at 2, 5, and 10 years are found in the supplemental material of the 2022 publication. Nodes are not treated with RT on this protocol, yet pelvic recurrence remained favorable: pelvic relapse with vs. without chemo 5% vs. 7%.

The conclusion of the initial paper stated that OS was improved with chemotherapy despite OS being reported as nonsignificant. At long term follow-up, chemotherapy lead to benefit in CSS after adjustment in prognostic factors, but again this is no different than a propensity analysis.

These protocols were of the 2D era. Some of the authors eventually published instructions for modern planning (Portner 2021):
CT sim with empty bladder.
Rectum mean <40 Gy
Rectum V50 Gy <50%
Small bowel V50 Gy <98 cc.
The authors recommedned PTV 1.5 cm, but this can lead to hotspots in the small bowel. Consider also small bowel max <53-57 Gy and undercovering the PTV if needed, or using a smaller PTV with daily CBCT.

BCON was a randomized trial assessing hypoxia modification with carbogen and nicotinamide. Neither original trial randomized hypofx vs. conventional fractionation; the regimens were investigator's choice. This means that this study is a propensity analysis. Investigators may have tended to prescribe long course for more advanced tumors. Recognize that after incomplete TURBT for biopsy, a wide variation of tumors, including very large ones and indeterminate T3s, can be categorized as T2. That, and other factors, cannot be completely adjusted for post-hoc. Randomized trials are warranted. Hypofx nevertheless shows generally favorable results prospectively and stands as a useful regimen for many, especially patients who are unfit for long course or have a limited schedule.

These protocols were of the 2D era. Some of the authors eventually published instructions for modern planning (Portner 2021):
CT sim with empty bladder.

trials.commentary:
Cervix summary
-Milan study shows that WPRT+brachy vs surgery have similar OS in early stage cervical cancer. Surgery tends to have more morbidity, so RT becomes standard for many cases
-Trials show OS benefit with chemo in addition to RT for definitive treatment of cervical cancer. This is confirmed in meta-analysis
-Trials have some mixed results regarding the use of coverage of PA fields (EORTC, RTOG 7920). EFRT is generally then restricted for PA N+ only
-The Peters trial shows OS benefit with chemo in post-op cervix with N+, +margin, or +parametria
-The Sedlis trials shows PFS benefit with RT in post-op cervix with intermediate risk factors
-EMBRACE refines the use of image guided HDR brachy for cervical cancer
-Tata Memorial and EORTC 55994 studies showed worse DFS with neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to surgery vs definitive chemoRT
-OUTBACK trial showed no benefit to additional adjuvant chemo after definitive chemoRT
-KEYNOTE A18 integrates pembrolizumab with chemoRT for survival benefit

Median time to relapse 13.5 vs. 11.5 mos (p=0.10)

Worst morbidity with adjuvant RT plus surgery (hydronephrosis, GU incontinence, LE edema, bowel obstruction)

⬆️ OS benefit trend with surgery in adeno, p=0.09

trials.commentary:
This landmark trial established the role of definitive radiation for cervical cancer. It's often quoted to support definitive RT over surgery in early cervical cancer, but its application is more nuanced. Individualized care is called for. Those that would be expected to require post-op RT, especially chemoRT, may be best suited for definitive chemoRT. In the 2017 update there is trend to benefit with surgery in adeno, and trend to benefit with RT in size >4 cm.

Adverse effects. The adverse effects from post op RT are excess here compared to modern therapy and the study should be referenced limitedly in contemporary context. How often do you encounter hydronephrosis, LE edema, and bowel obstruction after adjuvant RT? Adjuvant RT may have been performed too early in the study, or surgical complications may have been mistakenly attributed to RT. Techniques have also advanced. In the EORTC and Tata Memorial studies the neoadjuvant chemo plus surgery arms with post-op RT as indicated did not lead to worse late adverse effects overall compared to definitive radiation, as was shown in the Milan trial. This could be due to less receiving adjuvant RT (64% post-op RT in Milan study vs. 48% post-op CRT in EORTC, 13% post-op CRT & 10% RT alone in Tata Memorial) and/or improved surgical and post-op radiation techniques such as laparoscopy and IMRT. A modern surgical study reported GU incontinence of 11% after radical hysterectomy (Plante 2024). The Peters trial reported grade 4 effects in 4% vs. 17%. The Sedlis trial reported acute grade 3-4 effects 2% vs. 7%. Adverse effects are also low in adjuvant RT studies for endometrial cancer, though these undergo TAH rather than radical hysterectomy, and now have SLNB.
(Commentary last updated 2024, Estes)

trials.commentary:
70% prescribed to point A, and 30% to HRCTV. PET used in only 25%. 40% had IMRT. Lindegaard et al commented that well-conducted brachytherapy replaces the role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Image guided brachy yields LC of 90% in all stages and improves OS by 10% in studies. Ideally the trial would have been performed with high quality brachytherapy delivery, but INTERLACE is the trial that was performed with the resources available. Pembrolizumab in KEYNOTE A18 provides a similar OS beneft and required rx to HR-CTV, which may lead some to favor that regimen.

The authors state that periaortic nodes were excluded because they were not believed to be curable at the time of design.

trials.methods:
➜ WPRT 45-50 Gy
vs.
➜ WPRT with concurrent cisplatin
vs.
➜ 🏆 WPRT with sandwich cisplatin and taxol

Sequential: 2 cycles pre and 2 cycles post RT, q3w cis 60-75 mg/m2 and paclitaxel 135-175 mg/m2

Concurrent: weekly cisplatin 30-40 mg/m2

Neoadj chemo allowed for size >4 cm
trials.results:
DFS, cancer death, and OS significantly improved with sequential vs. RT alone. DFS improved with sequential vs. concurrent

WPRT vs. WPRT con vs. WPRT seq:

3-yr DFS 82% vs. 85% vs. 90%

High risk (+margin, +node) (supp eFig 3)
3-yr DFS 67% vs. 68% vs. 83%
3-yr OS 78% vs. 80% vs. 90%

Int risk only (eFig 3)
3-yr DFS 85% vs. 92% vs. 90%
3-yr OS 90% vs. 94% vs. 90%

results were maintained across subgroups except for size >4 cm or received neoadjuvant chemo

5-yr cancer death 11% vs. 10% vs. 8%
5-yr OS 88% vs. 89% vs. 92%
5-yr DM 11% vs. 11% vs. 7%
trials.interpretation:
Sequential chemotherapy and radiation has superior DFS and risk of cancer death than radiation alone.

On subanalysis, in the high risk group only sandwich chemo gave benefit in DFS and OS. In the intermediate risk group, concurrent and sandwich chemo both gave benefit in DFS and OS.

Sequential also had superior DFS compared to concurrent.
trials.commentary:
Although a well designed trial, it isn't referenced in NCCN 2024 guidelines. The chemo dose was higher in the sandwich arm, which could explain the benefit. 73% completed sandwich and 62% completed concurrent. This study had n=287 with high risk factors, slightly more than Peters et al. The concurrent chemo here was different that in Peters: Peters had two cycles concurrent plus two adjuvant. Patient characteristics were imbalanced, favoring the single modality RT arm, but RT alone was still inferior to sandwich chemotherapy RT. In the RT arm 18% were node positive, and 30% were node positive in each of the chemo arms.

19-23% of patients in each group had neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and the groups were balanced. While this trial was ongoing, a Tata Memorial trial discovered detriment with neoadjuvant chemotherapy compared to definitive chemoRT (Gupta 2018).

Why was chemo not effective in size >4 cm? Most of these received neoadjuvant chemo, which perhaps had some negative effect. The subgroup does not seem underpowered at 246 patients.

Although a risk factor in the Sedlis trial, ≥4 cm was not an eligibility factor in STARS.
trials.reference: 1. Huang H, Feng YL, Wan T, et al. trials.patients: Locally advanced cervical cancer
trials.methods:
Prospective multi-institutional study of MRI image guided BT to the HRCTV. Records practice patterns, characteristics, dose to tumor and OARs, adverse effects

Additional retrospective exploratory analysis of this data (RetroEMBRACE)
trials.results:
•5-yr LC rates
HRCTV size ≤30 cm 96%
HRCTV size >30 cm 87%
Stage IB & IIA 98%
IIB 91%, III 75%, IVA 76%

Nodal control in N+ & III+IVA of 83%
Nodal control in N- & I+II of 93%

5-yr OS overall 67%
5-yr OS 82% in N- and Stage I+II
5-yr OS 49% in N+ and Stage III+IV

Suggested dose constraints
•Rectum
D2cc <69.5 Gy had <10% grade 2+ adverse effects
D2cc ≥75 Gy had 12.5% risk of fistula vs. 0%
D2cc <65 Gy had 2x less proctitis

•Bladder
D2cm3 of 75 Gy vs. 80 Gy risk of 4-yr grade ≥2 cystitis of 8% vs. 13%

•Small bowel with 45 Gy
D2cc < 60 Gy

•Rectovaginal point <65 Gy EQD2
(20% have stenosis with 65 Gy, 27% with 75 Gy, and 34% with 85 Gy)

*Intersitial BT has better LC in size ≥30 cc
*Tandem and ring provides better coverage than T&O
*5 Gy is required to compensate for each 1 week break
*IGBT had less pelvic failures compared to historical controls. IGBT failure is mainly systemic
trials.interpretation: Outcomes and practice patterns of image guided BT to the HRCTV are demonstrated. Dose constraints are recommended.

In their discussion the authors comment that some studies show that CTNNB1mut and L1CAMmut should perhaps be classified as NSMP. NSMP may benefit from further subdivision into ER positive and negative. ER positive have a worse prognosis. Studies have also shown that dMMR may not benefit from radiation or chemotherapy at all, and may be better served with immunotherapy. Further subanalysis would have been very underpowered.

For POLEmut 5-yr VCR was 4.1% vs. 0.9% and determined to be noninferior. However numerically there seems to be a difference, suggesting that the prespecified noninferiority margin could have been too wide.

trials.interpretation:
There is OS and FFS benefit with chemotherapy added to RT on post-hoc analysis with longer f/u. (On initial reporting, there was no OS benefit.)

On subanalysis the benefit is only present in Stage III. On histologic analysis the benefit is in serous, and in molecular analysis the benefit is only in p53abn (mainly in serous). There was no benefit in Stage I-II, POLEmut, dMMR, or NSMP.

De-escalation and further trials may be warranted for some of the molecular groups. OS and RFS were outstanding in POLEmut in both arms.

IMRT had less adverse effects than 3DCRT.
trials.commentary:
PORTEC-3 is a landmark trial that revealed important information as to who benefits from chemotherapy added to WPRT, and began the transition to the molecular subtype era in post-op endometrial cancer.

POLEmut. PORTEC 4a shows that early POLEmut can be observed. PORTEC3 shows no benefit with chemo in Stage I-III. GOG258 did not test POLEmut.

NSMP. There is some trend to benefit with chemotherapy in PORTEC 3, 10-yr RFS p=0.13 and OS p=0.21 that warrants further investigation. There was RFS benefit with WPRT in GOG 258 after adjustment, though OS p=0.26. In NSMP in early stage in PORTEC 1&2, VCB is preferred.

dMMR. There appears to be no benefit in dMMR with chemotherapy or radiation (PORTEC 1-3 and GOG 258). This population may be better treated with immunotherapy (NRG GY018 & RUBY). Per both EEE and ASTRO, omission of chemotherapy can be considered in Stage I-III dMMR; these guidelines were published prior to GOG 258 molecular data.

p53abn. There is benefit from WPRT in p53 early stage (PORTEC 4a) but there seems to be no benefit in advanced stage (GOG 258). p53abn benefits from chemotherapy in PORTEC 3.

Statistics. The authors adjusted the data due to imbalances between arms. Although many may have been taught that adjustment in clinical trials means that the trial is no longer randomized, this is not the consensus among statisticians. On the contrary adjustments are endorsed to increase the power of a study (Kahan & Morris 2012).

Compare to GOG 249 which showed no benefit with chemotherapy added to RT in stage I-II (Randall 2019).

(Commentary last updated Oct 2025, Estes)
trials.notes:
Endometrial advanced summary
-GOG 122 found a survival detriment with whole abdominal radiation therapy. But the trial was poorly designed and the RT technique is outdates
-For years, RT was an option but generally not prioritized
-Results of other studies are mixed, and various sequencing techniques used including chemo alone, sequential chemoRT, "sandwich" chemoRT, RT and adjuvant chemo, or radiation alone
-A phase II trial, RTOG 9708, showed promising results with concurrent chemoRT followed by adjuvant chemoRT
-Over 10 years after GOG 122, GOG 258 re-evaluates the role of radiation with concurrent and adjuvant chemo. Results were mixed. There was no benefit in RFS or OS. RT did decrease pelvic and local relapse
-PORTEC3 showed benefit with chemo in Stage III. Benefit seems to be mainly in p53abn tumors and serous

Primary endpoints

trials.commentary:
This study is conducted by PORTEC and available internationally. The trial investigates the benefit of new agents based on molecular profiles, and makes a few changes in chemo and radiation based on prior molecular analysis. However reconsideration of chemo and radiation in some additional subgroups is still warranted.

POLEmut. Outcomes were outstanding in all arms in PORTEC 1-3 in POLEmut, and in PORTEC 4a these HIR patients were able to be observed. RAINBO doesn't randomize this question. However many clinics don't have access to POLEmut testing.

NSMP. ER is a prognostic factor in NSMP, which is why the trial is evaluating progestin. Re-evaluation of chemo should also be performed since there was no clear benefit in PORTEC 3. In GOG 258 (2024) there was RFS benefit with WPRT after adjustment, but not OS.

dMMR. NRG GY018 and RUBY already show benefit with duralumab in Stage III-IV, and the trial will evaluate if this also extends to Stage II. The trial rationally omits chemo based on no benefit in dMMR in PORTEC 3. But the benefit of WPRT should also be re-evaluated at some point since there was no benefit in GOG 258 (2024).

p53 abn. There is benefit from WPRT in p53 early stage (PORTEC 1, 2, 4a) but WPRT in advanced stage warrants re-evaluation. There was no benefit in GOG 258. p53abn benefits from chemotherapy in PORTEC 3.
(Commentary last updated May 2025, Estes)

trials.commentary:
This trial set a standard of VC brachytherapy for HIR patients. These patients were also included as eligible for GOG 249, which concluded WPRT to be standard (Randall 2019). However eligibility in the study may have been too broad.

A combined analysis (Witlink 2014) showed no increase in 2nd cancers after RT in PORTEC 1, PORTEC 2, and patients who received pelvic RT for rectum after TME.

POLEmut. PORTEC 4a shows that early POLEmut can be observed. PORTEC3 shows no benefit with chemo in Stage I-III. GOG258 did not test POLEmut.

NSMP. There is some trend to benefit with chemotherapy in PORTEC 3, 10-yr RFS p=0.13 and OS p=0.21 that warrants further investigation. There was RFS benefit with WPRT in GOG 258 after adjustment, though OS p=0.26. In NSMP in early stage in PORTEC 1&2, VCB is preferred.

dMMR. There appears to be no benefit in dMMR with chemotherapy or radiation (PORTEC 1-3 and GOG 258). This population may be better treated with immunotherapy (NRG GY018 & RUBY). Per both EEE and ASTRO, omission of chemotherapy can be considered in Stage I-III dMMR; these guidelines were published prior to GOG 258 molecular data.

p53abn. There is benefit from WPRT in p53 early stage (PORTEC 4a) but there seems to be no benefit in advanced stage (GOG 258). p53abn benefits from chemotherapy in PORTEC 3.

trials.notes:
Early endometrial summary:
-Aalders Norwegian trial shows benefit of WPRT+VCB in Stage I, especially in IB grade 3
-GOG99 and PORTEC-1 establish that the benefit with WPRT is in high intermediate risk groups. Most recurrences in vaginal cuff
-PORTEC 2 shows VC brachy is noninferior to WPRT in high int risk
-GOG 249 compared WPRT vs. VC+chemo in high intermediate risk and high risk early stage patients and found that VCB+chemo was not superior and had more pelvic recurrences and worse adverse effects. Thus WPRT remained standard. There is still rationale to treat HIR patients with VCB only per PORTEC II.
-HIR patients were also included in PORTEC 3, which evaluated the benefit of adding chemo to WPRT. There was benefit with chemo in stage III, p53, and serous, but not in early stage

p53abn 10-yr OS 23-25%, not different
dMMR 10-yr OS 56% vs. 67%, not different

Grade 3-5 adverse effects 58% vs. 63%

On subanalysis and sensitivity analysis, no subgroups were favored by either arm
trials.interpretation:
RT with concurrent and adjuvant chemo did not improve RFS or OS compared to chemo alone.

ChemoRT had less VCR, LN recurrence, and adverse effects. Chemo alone had less DM, possibly due to more cycles being given.

On molecular analysis, after adjustment there was RFS improvement in NSMP with WPRT, but otherwise there was no improvement in OS or RFS with radiation in any subgroup.
trials.commentary:
Characteristics. 49% were NSMP, 24% p53abn, and 27% dMMR.  75% in the CRT arm completed therapy. There was 85% completion for chemo alone. 18% of patients were serous, 3% clear cell. The abstract refers to p53wt and dMMR negative as simply p53wt, which I have renamed NSMP here to be more consisent with PORTEC. Note also that POLEmut was not evaluated.

POLEmut. PORTEC 4a shows that early POLEmut can be observed. PORTEC3 shows no benefit with chemo in Stage I-III. GOG258 did not test POLEmut.

NSMP. There is some trend to benefit with chemotherapy in PORTEC 3, 10-yr RFS p=0.13 and OS p=0.21 that warrants further investigation. There was RFS benefit with WPRT in GOG 258 after adjustment, though OS p=0.26. In NSMP in early stage in PORTEC 1&2, VCB is preferred.

dMMR. There appears to be no benefit in dMMR with chemotherapy or radiation (PORTEC 1-3 and GOG 258). This population may be better treated with immunotherapy (NRG GY018 & RUBY). Per both EEE and ASTRO, omission of chemotherapy can be considered in Stage I-III dMMR; these guidelines were published prior to GOG 258 molecular data.

p53abn. There is benefit from WPRT in p53 early stage (PORTEC 4a) but there seems to be no benefit in advanced stage (GOG 258). p53abn benefits from chemotherapy in PORTEC 3.

An alternative approach is "sandwich" chemo → RT → chemo (Lupe 2009, Secord 2009). This approach could warrant further testing. In GOG 258 there was less DM with 6 cycles of chemo alone (although p value not given). Perhaps more cycles of chemo could be delivered with RT with the sandwich method.
(Commentary last updated May 2025, Estes)

Protocol amended to the following after excess failures:

grade 3 adverse effects in 4%

The groin nodes were not contoured fully prior to 2015: only a 5 mm margin around vessels was required. In 2015 the protocol was amended. Furthermore 56% in the LND alone arm (size >2 mm) still received RT for ≥2 nodes positive or ECE. Therefore the trial may be underpowered and it can be difficult to draw conclusions. And since the macromets arm was nonrandomized, there is a possibility for imbalances in the two cohorts even though the stopping rule was met.

The vulva was only included in RT field if specifically indicated. Chemotherapy was optional. The trend to better control with chemoRT suggests that this method should be further investigated.

trials.commentary:
H&N dose overview:
-MDACC Peters initially showed 57.6 Gy needed for post-op low risk neck and 63 Gy for ECE
-Concominant boost becomes standard from RTOG 9003 fx study
-66 Gy used for ECE and +M with concurrent chemo in EORTC and RTOG. Benefit in OS with chemo for ECE and +M
-RTOG 0022 outlines use of IMRT SIB to spare salivary glands, combining MDACC Peters and CCB into an IMRT SIB regimen
-Doses as low as 45-50 Gy may be reasonable for untreated neck in Belgium study

H&N fractionation overview:
-RTOG 9003 results initially show CCB and hyperfx both improve LC; since more convenient, accel-CCB was favored. Split course no longer in use
-CCB goes on to become standard and have OS benefit with chemo
-Long term 9003 follow-up shows hyperfx has best OS, LC and the least late effects
-MARCH HN meta-analysis also confirms hyperfx gives best OS
-Overgaard DAHANCA and later IAEA show better LC with 6 fx per week, compared to conventional, if no chemo
-Transition from 2D to IMRT with RTOG 0222, using SIB technique, like a modified CCB, to spare salivary glands
-Whether IMRT SIB hyperfx with concurrent chemo is better than IMRT SIB qday with concurrent chemo is an open question

2-yr crude LF worse with <54 Gy than with ≥ 57.6 Gy.
No difference between 57.6 Gy and ≥63 Gy overall. ENE results seem best with ≥63 Gy based on crude LR

On UVA, ENE was the only independent risk factor for recurrence (regardless of dose). Trend to worse recurrence with ≥2 nodes, p=0.08. There was increasing recurrence risk with ≥2 risk factors (factors: oral cavity, close or positive margins, PNI, ≥2 nodes, node ≥3cm, delay >6 wks, low PS)
trials.interpretation:
At early interim analysis, LF was worse with <54 Gy and the arm was changed to 57.6 Gy. ENE seems to benefit from dose escalation to ≥63 Gy based on a crude subanalysis at 2 years.

There is no benefit in LRC with dose escalation from 63 Gy → 68.4 Gy in the high risk group or 57.6 → 63 Gy in the low risk group at any point in f/u, up to 20 years. Chemo was not used in this study.
trials.commentary:
This trial laid the foundation for dosing in intermediate and high risk post-op H&N cancer. There are a few important points to note in context of modern statistical approaches and staging. Observe that the trial endorses 63 Gy for ENE, not 66 Gy. Note that ENE was allowed in both groups and not randomized, and the finding that ≥63 Gy is ideal for ENE was determined by subanalysis, which was simply a review of crude recurrence rates by risk factors (Table 9). Today, a subanalysis such as MVA would have been performed with p values. Modern standards in statistical approaches in these situations are much stricter. At the time the trial was not questioned to be underpowered, but from modern standards it seems it could be. There are two randomizations of about 130 patients each.

The late f/u publication used more modern statistical approaches. ENE was analyzed as a prognostic factor in general but the exploratory analysis in the previous publication was not done to determine if ENE specifically benefited from higher dose RT.

"Low risk" and "high risk" were determined by a historical point system. The head vs. neck risks were determined separately. Cobalt era, 1.8 Gy/fx with no chemotherapy.

Lu et al, IJROBP, 2022
trials.patients: post-op H&N with risk factors as above
trials.methods:
Combined analysis of EORTC 22931 and RTOG 9501

A later combined analysis also included RTOG 0234 to evaluate findings with rising nodal count
trials.results:
⬆️ Chemo improved OS in ENE and positive margin
↔️ No OS benefit if int risk factors only (p=0.33 in EORTC and p=0.78 in RTOG)

No interaction between # lymph nodes and benefit with chemo (DM p=0.8, OS p=0.161,  DFS p=0.45) (this analysis also included RTOG 0234)
trials.interpretation: The addition of chemo to adjuvant RT improves OS in post-op H&N tumors with ENE or positive margins. There is no improvement in intermediate risk factors including number of nodes.
trials.commentary: If one considers the combined EORTC 22931 RTOG 9501 analysis as exploratory and limited in its methodology, EORTC 22931 might be used to support an OS benefit with chemotherapy in those with multiple intermediate risk factors. MVA or adjustment for risk factors for example was not performed. Statistical approaches for post-hoc analysis have improved, and plenty of useful ones exist (consider STAMPEDE, EORTC 22881, 9413 & Ottawa, PORTECs, even EBCTCG). One must be cautious of seeing what they want to see in subanalysis, which goes both ways. Nature does not have a clear cutoff for significance, and cancer cells don't know if a human pre- vs post-planned a statistical analysis. It must be acknoweldged that a combined analysis is stronger evidence than a single one. Rad oncs also omit therapy based on exploratory subanalysis (EORTC 22881 breast boost, PORTEC 1). Omission of an intervention becomes more rational when the disease is already curable and there are notable adverse effects, as is often the case in head and neck. On the other hand, LR can be morbid, and both EORTC and RTOG studies showed LRC benefit with chemotherapy, which can support its use in more advanced cases. An updated combined analysis (Lu 2022) shows that there is no benefit with chemo with rising nodal count in OS or DM, which does not support the practice of recommending chemotherapy for ≥5 nodes.  If any investigators, or those who know them are reading, an updated analysis of intermediate risk factors with modern statistical approaches would be welcome.

Statistical approaches for post-hoc analysis have improved, and plenty of useful ones exist (consider STAMPEDE, EORTC 22881, 9413 & Ottawa, PORTECs, even EBCTCG). One must be cautious of seeing what they want to see in subanalysis, which goes both ways. Nature does not have a clear cutoff for significance, and cancer cells don't know if a human pre- vs post-planned a statistical analysis. It must be acknoweldged that a combined analysis is stronger evidence than a single one. Rad oncs also omit therapy based on exploratory subanalysis (EORTC 22881 breast boost, PORTEC 1). Omission of an intervention becomes more rational when the disease is already curable and there are notable adverse effects, as is often the case in head and neck. On the other hand, LR can be morbid, and both EORTC and RTOG studies showed LRC benefit with chemotherapy, which can support its use in more advanced cases. An updated combined analysis (Lu 2022) shows that there is no benefit with chemo with rising nodal count in OS or DM, which does not support the practice of recommending chemotherapy for ≥5 nodes.  If any investigators, or those who know them are reading, an updated analysis of intermediate risk factors with modern statistical approaches would be welcome.

trials.commentary:
Why was this induction trial positive and the others negative? Perhaps HPV epidemiology played role; prevalence may be higher in US and lower in this study. The trials had slightly different regimens. Perhaps cetuximab somehow sensitizes better when delivered after induction chemo as the subanalysis suggests (but this is contradictory to the lower HPV prevalence idea), or perhaps the concurrent chemo is overtreatment. It is unclear what population, if any, truly benefits from induction chemo. Refer also to RTOG 9111, where on long term follow-up the induction chemo arm (with no concurrent chemo) trended to better OS. Otherwise, the MACH-HN meta-analysis shows no OS benefit to induction as a whole.

Given the other 3 negative trials, results should be interpreted with caution. Patient characteristics seemed well balanced. HPV was not assessed in the trial's era. RT was 70 Gy with ≥60 Gy to neck.

vs.

After NACT, five patients did not undergo surgery (one due to CR, who had CRT) and one patient had inoperable disease due to progression. There was 38% PR (n=12) or CR (n= 1).

For upfront patients, surgery entailed segmental mandibulectomy, ipsilateral neck dissection with appropriate reconstruction and adjuvant radiation+chemo (weekly cis) per standard indications (about half received CRT). Two patients did not receive adjuvant treatment due to no adverse features. All neoadjuvant chemotherapy patients underwent adjuvant CRT per protocol unless deemed unfit for chemotherapy (n=3). Oral cavity overview
-There have been few studies for oral cavity specifically. Refer also to post-op trials
-Most randomized trials come from Tata Memorial. They showed than LND improves OS. They also held a phase II study to show that neoadjuvant chemo can help mandibular preservation
-However the Senti MERORL trial and a Japanese trial showed that SLNB and LND are noninferior.
-Much data in oral cavity centers around management of RT field and lymphatics
-Retrospective studies show that ipsilateral RT can be employed for well-lateralized lesions
-The ACRIN 6685 study supports omission of RT in PET negative dissected neck

p16+ T4 N0-2

trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 neoadj pembrolizumab x2 cycles → surgery → adj pembrolizumab x15 cycles plus adjuvant therapy as indicated
vs.
➜ surgery→radiation and/or chemo as indicated

Immunotherapy q21 days
trials.results:
3-yr EFS 60% vs. 46%
est 3-yr OS 68% vs. 61% (data not mature)

12% stopped pembrolizumab due to progression prior to adjuvant phase (Table S2B. 43/361=12%)

pCR ≤5%

CPS-10 pCR 4% vs. 0
CPS-1 pCR 3% vs. 0

Grade ≥3 immune-related adverse effects 10%

Grade ≥3 adverse effects 45% vs. 43%
Grade 5 adverse effects 1.1% vs. 0.3%
trials.interpretation: Neoadjuvant before surgery followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab improved EFS in locally advanced head and neck cancer. pCR was low at <5% but did occur in some.
trials.commentary:
The trial allowed pre-op tumor growth to be deemed a "tumor flare" and was not counted as an EFS event. Table S2B shows that n=43, or 12%, discontinued pembrolizumab prior to the adjuvant phase due to progressive disease. The true number that had progression would be even higher, as some would have continued despite progression. Another trial IMMUNEBOOST-HPV showed similar findings, that 14% had progression after two cycles of nivolumab prior to chemoradiation (Mirghani 2022).

pCR was <5% with immunotherapy but did occur in some after only two cycles, a remarkable finding. CR with chemoradiation in HPV+ is 90%, though impovements are needed in HPV negative. pCR rates were not emphasized in the study but calculated by me from Table 2. It is unclear how much benefit is derived from the neoadjuvant portion, but NIVOPOST-OP shows that there is benefit with adjuvant only nivolumab. Thus far OS data is not mature but appears promising.

Immunotherapy should not be used for a borderline surgical candidate, or to convert a morbid procedure into a less radical one. What if the tumor does not become resectable or progresses and then chemoRT is needed? T4b were not eligible for the trial. About 14% may have progression with immunotherapy. If a tumor does not become resectable, chemoRT then becomes less feasible. The phase II study IMMUNEBOOST-HPV showed that after two cyles of nivolumab prior to chemoRT, 10% of patients required reduced dosing of cisplatin. The study did not meet its feasibility target.

Those p16+ have excellent response to chemoRT already, but more advancements are needed for p16 negative. Although pCRs were low in KEYNOTE 689, a CR after two cycles immunotherapy is an outstanding result and could allow for response adapted treatment to avoid surgery or chemoRT.

vs.
➜ ⭕️ 60 Gy/ 30 fx (6 weeks) + cisplatin
vs.
➜ 60 Gy/ 30 fx (DAHANCA) + nivolumab

60 Gy plus cispatin is not noninferior and this arm is now closed. Futility was reached.

Interim estimated PFS and OS outcomes

2-yr OS 99% vs. 98% vs. 96%

2-yr PFS of 98% in the control arm is outstanding. HN-005 is a cautionary tale of adopting phase II data too quickly. Phase II and prospective data may be reasonable to apply in disease states with poor prognosis in which one is willing to take risks, but one should be more cautious in applying experimental therapy in favorable prognosis. In HPV+ H&N, where LRC is 85-90%, such an approach is probably not appropriate. Some had a goal of reducing adverse effects. HN-005 finally resolved the question.

An interesting feature of RTOG 1016 and HN-005 is that the control used the DAHANCA regimen with concurrent chemotherapy. The original DAHANCA 6&7 and IAEA-ACC trials did not use chemotherapy concurrent with the 6 days per week regimen.

trials.methods:
Phase II
➜ 60 Gy IMRT (54 & 48 Gy SIB)
with weekly cis if N2 by AJCC 7th ed

vs.

➜ TOS (TLM or TORS) of primary site with neck dissection with adjuvant RT based on risk features
int: 50 Gy (LVI, N2, close margin)
high: 60 Gy (+margins or ENE)

Initially planned for 2-yr OS
Terminated early due to deaths
acute grade 5 adverse effects 4% (n=2), all in surgery arm due to post-op hemorrhage

Median f/u 17 mos
OS 100% vs. 89%
PFS 100% vs. 84% (favoring RT)

+margin in 8% of TORS
78% of these received adjuvant RT
trials.interpretation: The trial was terminated early due to deaths in the surgical arm. Primary RT seems to provide favorable outcomes.
trials.commentary:
ENTs have concerns regarding the surgical quality, and rad oncs should have concerns that the RT dose is too low. The trial closed early due to excess rates of G5 post-op hemorrhage. There are concerns regarding surgical quality: 4% mortality in this study (n=2/35). Compare to other studies: In ECOG 3311, there were 1/495 deaths (0.2%) with TORS, and in MC1675, no grade 5 toxicites with n=194. In ECOG there were no further deaths once the protocol was amended to strongly recommend vessel ligation, which was not specified in ORATOR2. Palma comments on Twitter (2022) however that ECOG 3311 outcomes are not representative of US outcomes. In an editorial Teckie notes that if there was just 1 fewer surgical death, ORATOR2 would have still been ongoing.

The trial should have selected 70 Gy for the radiation arm. 60 Gy was chosen prematurely based on phase II findings. After the trial's design, 60 Gy was compared to 70 Gy for HPV+ in NRG-005 and was determined to be not noninferior.

This study has higher rates of positive margins compared to E3311, 8% vs. 3.8%. Mandated prophylactic tracheostomy in the trial is also rarely used in contemporary transoral surgery. Given the variability in surgical quality it may be difficult how to best interpret results. For transoral surgery for HPV OPSCC, one can say that, if surgery is to be performed, careful patient selection and experienced surgeons at high volume centers are strongly preferred; at least while awaiting the results of EORTC 1420 and EORTC 1701-HNCG (PATHOS).

trials.interpretation:
Transoral surgery and adjuvant 50 Gy RT for intermediate risk (close margin <3 mm, 2-4 nodes, ENE ≤1 mm) warrants comparison to definitive chemoRT in a phase III trial

All approaches led to favorable outcomes in HPV+ oropharynx.
trials.commentary:
Surgery. ENTs have concerns regarding the surgical quality. There were no longer any deaths after the protocol was amended to strongly recommend vessel ligation. Palma comments on Twitter (2022) however that ECOG 3311 outcomes are not representative of US outcomes. ENE was the most common reason for allocation to high-risk arm (44%), which typically only can be determined following pathologic assessment, requiring staged surgeries (i.e. upfront neck dissection) to eventually indicate chemoradiotherapy.

Radiation. There is concern regarding high-quality and protocol-compliant radiotherapy delivery. Many patients received less than protocol-intended radiotherapy dose to the primary site (int 50 Gy in only 28%, 60 Gy in only 47%), with some patients not receiving RT to the primary site at all [int 50 Gy (26%), 60 Gy (19%)], which may complicate interpretation of study outcomes. Granted, the AVOID Phase II trial has suggested that RT is not of benefit to a post-operative bed without risk factors (Swisher-McClure 2019).

There was also significant dropoff rate in completion of MDADI and FACT-HN beyond the early post-treatment period which may limit drawing firm conclusions in late QOL.

Eligibility. Why were those with ≥5 resected nodes included in the high risk arm? Data to support this practice is sparse. Some data shows a high risk of DM in this population (Lu 2022, Zhan 2017). However the best evidence, the pooled analysis of EORTC 22931,  RTOG 9501, and RTOG 0234 shows no DM benefit with chemotherapy in increasing nodal count, p=0.8 (Lu 2022). The ECOG authors do not share how many had ≥5 nodes as a single risk factor without ECE or positive margin. 27% had ≥5 nodes, 77% had ENE, and 11% had +M. A randomized trial could be warranted.

trials.notes:
Oropharynx summary
-HPV was discovered as a prognostic factor for response to treatment and OS, validated in RTOG 0129
-Studies sought to de-escalate therapy in HPV+ tumors by various means, but most of these failed under multi institutional randomized trials
-RTOG 1016 and De-Escalate found that chemo cannot be replaced by cetuximab
-A surgical technique, TORS, is developed that leads to less morbidity than standard surgery
-In HN005, 60 Gy was found inferior and the arm was closed
-ECOG 3311 validates TORS and post-op approaches as options in low, int, and high risk HPV
-ORATOR2 compared chemoRT vs surgery in HPV+ and was closed due to deaths in the surgery arm, but some question the surgical quality in the trial
-EORTC "Best of" to evaluate TORS vs. chemoRT in HPV+

trials.commentary:
OS is improved with immunotherapy, but low CR rates show that it is rarely a cure and that further advancements are needed. In addition, on subanalysis there was no benefit in locally recurrent only disease. This comparison could be underpowered or could illustrate that immunotherapy should be combined with local therapy.

It is important to emphasize that immunotherapy and chemotherapy are palliative. Definitive reirradiation is an option for local control while carefully taking into consideration its high rate of adverse effects, and the cure rate with radiation also shows room for improvement. Radiatioin therapy is more useful in those recurrent HPV+. More advancements in this area are needed. Palliative radiation is of course another option.

In the study pembro was not directly compared to pembro-chemo, but it seems that pembro-chemo has the best outcomes.

What is CPS score? In NSCLC, tumor proportion score (TPS) is used, but in other cancers, combined positive score (CPS) is used, which is the positivity of both tumor and surrounding immune cells.

H&N Recurrence summary
-More study is needed in this area
-Various trials including GORTEC and RTOG 9601 evaluated reirradiation. DFS seemed to be improved but not OS. adverse effects can be severe
-A Sun Yat-sen randomized trial compared hyperfractionated RT to daily RT and found that hyperfx reduced late adverse effects and improved OS. Neither regimen used chemo.
-The MIRI retrospective study showed hyperfx RT worsened OS (but this was not protocol, as was in the Sun Yat-sen study) . The study also helps guide use of RT.
-PET-NECK showed that the neck can be salvaged with surgery 3 mos after chemo RT at time of follow-up PET if there is residual disease in the neck
-KEYNOTE 048 established the benefit of immunotherapy. However CR rates are very low at ≤10%, and on subanalysis there was no benefit in locally recurrent only disease

trials.methods:

trials.results:
74 Gy worsened OS
⬇️ Median OS 29 mos vs. 20 mos, p=0.004
2-yr OS 58% vs. 45%
5-yr OS 32% vs. 23%

↗️ 2-yr LF 31% vs. 39%, p=0.13
↗️ 5-yr LF 38% vs. 46%, p=0.068
↗️ 5-yr LRF 35.7% vs. 38.4%, p=0.05
↘️ 5-yr PFS 18% vs. 13%, p=0.055
Median PFS 1.0 vs. 0.8 yrs

5-yr DM 52% vs. 58%, p=0.3

⬆️ Grade ≥3 esophagitis 5% vs. 17%
Grade 5 adverse effects n=3 vs. 9
Grade ≥3 pneumonitis 21% vs. 19%

Cetuximab arm had more adverse effects and no OS difference

Use of IMRT or 3DCRT not associated with outcome

MVA analysis factors associated with OS: rx dose, PTV, heart V5, tumor location, institution accrual, and esophageal adverse effects

Worse contouring in 74 Gy, but this was not associated with worse outcomes
trials.interpretation:
60 Gy is standard for locally advanced NSCLC. Dose escalation to 74 Gy worsened OS.

This also led to acceptance of carboplatin and taxol into common practice rather than cisplatin and etoposide.

Concurrent and maintenance cetuximab has no role in locally advanced NSCLC.

Dosimetric analysis shows the importance of more stringent and specific heart constraints.
trials.commentary:
Overview. Note that 74 Gy didn't even improve LC. In fact, LF, LRF, PFS and DM all trended to better outcome with 60 Gy. Why was 60 Gy superior? Theories include dose to heart, better immune response at 60 Gy, or variations in contouring and RT QA. Regarding RT protocol compliance, although there was slightly worse contouring in the 74 Gy arm, this was not associated with worse outcomes (see the discussion section of the 2019 publication). Per authors, RT protocol compliance was rigorous and every patient was centrally reviewed. It's hard to conceive that a better trial could have been performed. Regarding the immune system, we know that immune cells are affected at even low doses of radiation, and immunotherapy has proven how critical for NSCLC. Heart dose might be representative of dose to the immune system. Since its completion, RTOG 0617 has substantially advanced our knowledge of dosimetry and the immune system in NSCLC.

Dosimetry innovation. 0617 eventually inspired an array of dosimetric goals for heart substructures (Bergom 2021). On a later secondary analysis, atria D45%, mean lung, pericardium mean of hottest % of 55%, and ventricles MOH% 5% predicted OS. Rx dose was actually not predictive of OS, nor was IMRT (Thor 2020), differing from the original MVA analysis. The authors are careful to say that causation cannot be ascertained. IMRT gave less dose to heart and lower grade 3+ pneumonitis but no OS change. LAD V15 <10% was also related to OS (McKenzie 2022). Lung V5 not associated with grade 3+ pneumonitis; V20 was (Chun 2017). How could dose and IMRT not be directly associated with OS? Well, dose has to hit and pass through something. So the answer must be the something it's hitting and the duration, such as lung, heart, or blood pool. 74 Gy IMRT to a point would mean nothing.

Outcomes. Since this study, PACIFIC improved outcomes further to 2-yr OS 66% and 5-yr OS 43% with immunotherapy. And PACIFIC had more Stage IIIB (45%) than RTOG 0617 (~35%). RTOG 9410 had more Stage IIIB of 57%. Note stage IIIC was not an AJCC stage at the time, but included in IIIB.

Lessons. Some hold RTOG 0617 as a cautionary tale against those practicing phase II data before confirmation in phase III. Reality is more nuanced. RTOG 9410, the prior trial, resulted a 5-yr OS of a dismal 15%. The LC benefit of dose escalation was not questioned. In such situations, practicioners and patients may be more willing to take risks with phase II and prospective evidence. For example many treat oligometastasis as per phase II data.

This trial de-escalated RT, but mandated adjuvant escalated chemo in both arms based on low evidence (see CALGB 39801 and HOG trials). Since the publication of PACIFIC this practice has largely discontinued.

trials.patients:
NSCLC Stage II-III, not chemo candidates

Zubrod PS ≥2
>10% weight loss in 6 months
trials.methods:
Superiority

➜ hypofractionated RT 60 Gy/ 15 fx
vs.
➜ conventional fractionated RT 60 Gy/ 30 fx
trials.results:
1-yr OS 38% vs. 45%, p=0.29
Median OS 8.2 mos vs. 10.6 mos, p=0.17
1-yr PFS 6.4 mos vs. 7.3 mos (NS)

Grade 2 esophagitis 22% vs. 8.7% p=.09

On MVA, receipt systemic therapy and max dose to esophagus most associated with OS
trials.interpretation: Accelerated hypofractionated is not superior to conventional fractionation in locally advanced lung cancer, but may represent a viable treatment alternative for those unable to have chemotherapy.
trials.commentary:
The trial was designed to investigate superiority of hypofractionated RT and was not powered to show noninferiority or equivalence (note only 103 patients); given lack of SS difference in endpoints between arms, conventional fractionation is still standard of care.

60 Gy/15 fx was associated with increased Grade 2 AEs, which may be impactful in the more fragile "target" patient population with medical comorbidities and poor KPS who are too deconditioned to tolerate chemotherapy in the first place. The regimen may also serve a role for ultracentral tumors for practitioners who prefer to avoid 5-10 fraction regimens and for patients who would benefit from hypofractionation for whatever reason.

The characteristics were imbalanced against the conventional arm. There were significantly more N1 patients in the hypofractionated RT arm (24.0%) compared with the conventional RT arm (6.5%) p=0.02. There were significantly fewer patients with N3 disease in the hypofractionated RT arm (8.0%) compared with the conventional RT arm (23.9%) p=0.02. It is remarkable that the conventional arm did so well with such a higher percentage of N3. OS and PFS both trended in favor of that arm.

trials.patients:
size ≤2 cm, N0, in outer 3rd of lung

(60% were adenocarcinoma)
trials.methods:
Noninferiority

➜ lobectomy
vs.
➜ 🏆 sublobar resection (segmentectomy in 38%, or wedge in 59%)

Mediastinal sampling and PET in all

~80% had VATS
trials.results:
✅ 5-yr DSF 64% both arms, noninferior
5-yr OS ~80% both arms

No difference in recurrence patterns
5-yr RFS ~70% both arms
5-yr LRR 13% vs. 10%
5-yr RR ~2%
5-yr DM ~16%

Sublobar had 2% benefit in median predicted FEV1

90-day mortality 1.7% vs. 1.2%
trials.interpretation: Sublobar resection for early NSCLC size ≤2cm in outer 3rd of lung is now standard. The procedure was noninferior to lobectomy.
trials.commentary:
CALGB/Alliance 140503 and JCOG0802 dispelled a 30-year-old finding that lobectomy was superior to wedge (LCSG 821 Ginsberg 1995) in Western and Eastern populations respectively. The studies are representative of modern surgical outcomes. CALGB had 0.6-1.7% 30 to 90-day post-op moratlity, and JCOG had 0% post-op deaths. In CALGB 80% had VATS, and all had PET and mediastinal sampling. In JCOG 90% had VATS, all had mediastinal sampling, and PET was not required. There is room for further improvement in RFS/DFS. In CALGB these tumors of size ≤2 cm still have a DM rate of 16%.  But caution cross comparing to SBRT: DFS is higher here than in SBRT trials RTOG 0236, RTOG 0915 and SPACE, where it is 19-42%. SBRT trials allow inclusion of larger size tumors and inoperable patients with poorer performance. Selection bias is inherent; propensity analyses have otherwise already been done, and randomized trials are the next stage.  Immunotherapy for Stage IA warrants investigation in both surgery and SBRT.

Stations 4 and 7 could be sampled either pre-op or intra-op, and the following stations required sampling intra-op otherwise: stations 4, 7, and 10 in right sided, and stations 5 or 6, 7, and 10 for left sided. One would think that LR could be calculated by LRR - RR, but these were defined differently: RR was medastinal nodal recurrence, and LRR was LR or hilar recurrence.

trials.patients: T1-2N0M0 operable NSCLC
trials.methods:
SBRT→ VATS lobectomy or sublobar resection after 10 weeks

(SBRT doses: 54 Gy/3 fx if peripheral, 55 Gy/5 fx for chest wall contact or size >3 cm, 60 Gy/8 fx if within 2 cm of MS or brachial plexus)
trials.results:
Of those who had surgery:
pCR 60%, major pCR 63%
5-yr LC 94%
5-yr RC 80%
5-yr DM 18%
2-yr OS 77%, 5-yr OS 67%
No 30- or 90-day post op deaths
Grade 3-5 adverse effects in 17%
trials.interpretation:
With SBRT followed by VATS resection, the pCR rate was lower than expected, but higher than in many pre-op chemoimmunotherapy trials. adverse effects and post op deaths were similar to surgical series.

Randomized trials are warranted to detect if pre-op SBRT results in any survival or DM benefit.
trials.commentary: The pCR rate is lower than expected compared to LC seen in SBRT studies, but markedly higher than that in pre-op chemoimmunotherapy trials. On Twitter David Palma (2019) comments that a pCR of 60% may not represent active tumor in all cases; tumor can be alive but not mitotically active to cause LF later, undergoing a slow senescent death. Ten weeks may be early to assess response surgically. This time point was chosen for surgical purposes to avoid fibrosis during resection. Yet in view of other pre-op therapy studies, 60% pCR actually is an achievement, and is among the highest of any trial so far including those evaluating pre-op chemoRT and pre-op immunotherapy, and matches pCR of those with PDL1 ≥50% (Checkmate 77T, Checkmate 816, AEGEAN). The DM rate is similar to other early stage SBRT and surgical trials and may indicate a role for adjuvant treatment (CHISEL, RTOG 0236, CALGB 140503).

Chemotherapy and chemoimmunotherapy do not improve the resection rate, but rather decrease it.
trials.commentary:
For eligibility patients were required to be resectable upfront, but note that at the end of the trials evaluating neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy that resectability was decreased. Only 75% to 83% finally underwent surgery in either arm, and about 5-10% were due to progression.

Poor response or progression from chemoimmunotherapy in a patient who was resectable upfront or borderline resectable places the patient in a worse position: they then must complete chemoradiation, which will be more difficult with already impaired bone marrow. PET images can be difficult to interpret after immunotherapy due to indeterminate findings and often call for repeat EBUS (see the LYRIC criteria in lymphoma for example, Cheson 2016).

The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Expert Consensus (2025) states "Patients who are deemed initially with unresectable disease should not be treated with neoadjuvant therapy in an attempt to render it resectable. This will only serve to delay or compromise definitive nonsurgical therapy."

The above are valid reasons to avoid the neoadjuvant portion, especially those with low PDL1, and treat with the adjuvant portion only. It's unclear if peri-op chemoimmunotherapy has benefit over adjuvant only; there is no randomized trial comparing the two. Reasons to use the neoadjuvant portion would be to follow the protocol as-is, and that most studies thus far showing OS benefit included neoadjuvant, regardless of the risk of what could happen.

Only one study, the phase II NADIM trial, had pCR >50%. Observe also that a meta-analysis of three trials in advanced/metastatic NSCLC showed that immunotherapy improves OS even in those PDL1 negative (Cancer 2009), and there is still DFS benefit across the surgical studies.

trials.patients: Stage IIIA N2 NSCLC s/p surgery + platinum chemo x4 cycles
trials.methods:
➜ post-op ≤50 Gy/ 2 Gy per fx
vs.
➜ 🏆 no RT

RT given ≤6 weeks after chemo

CTV: ipsilateral hilum and MS, subcarina, stump

89% had IMRT
trials.results:
↗️ ITT 3-yr DFS 41% vs. 33%, p=0.20
PP 3-yr DFS 43% vs. 31%
ITT median DFS 22.1 mos vs. 18.6 mos

⬇️ 3-yr LRR 10% vs. 18%
⬆️ 3-yr LRFS 67% vs. 60%, p=0.03

3-yr ITT OS ~80%, not different
PP OS also not different

In RT arm, 24% did not receive RT

3-yr DM ~40%, not different
trials.interpretation:
Post-op RT for N2 disease in NSCLC should not be routinely recommended. There was no OS benefit. There is some LC benefit, and no significant DFS benefit.

There was 24% noncompliance in the RT arm. In the per protocol analysis, post-op RT for N2 disease led to benefit in DFS but not OS, but these results could be biased.
trials.commentary:
Increased deaths in LUNG-ART, which were not seen in PORT-C, might be accounted for by IMRT in only 11% and/or higher RT compliance in LUNG-ART that could have led to more exposure to heart, ENI, or blood pool; less may be more. LRR was improved in both trials. Perhaps more targeted radiation to only the involved stations with IMRT might lead to a better ratio of risk benefit. ENI often shows an OS detriment (Yuan 2007), and that finding seems to be reproduced here.

11% had IMRT in LUNG-ART, and 89% had IMRT in PORT-C. There was poor protocol adherence in the RT group: 24% did not receive any RT, which makes the results of the trial difficult to interpret.  Although the per protocol analysis was pre-planned, this does not eliminate issues that arise from any per protocol analysis.

There is a possibility that a subgroup analysis could show benefit with RT with higher nodal burden. A future trial design might be to target only the involved nodal stations, to wait longer for healing after surgery, and to require arc IMRT.
trials.reference: 1. Hui Z, Men Y, Hu C, et al. trials.methods:
Dose escalation: SBRT 10, 10.5, 11, 11.5, 12 Gy x 5 fx

Endpoint: 1-yr grade ≥3 adverse effects <20%
trials.results:
12 Gy was MTD with 1-yr grade 3+ adverse effects of 7.2%

Within one year, total 9% deaths (!):

11.5 Gy had 3/25 die (esophageal ulcer that eroded into vessel and 2 bronchopulmonary hemorrhages).

12 Gy had 1/21 die (bronchopulmonary hemorrhage)

trials.interpretation:
The highest dose level allowed, 12 Gy x 5 fx, was tolerated as defined by the predetermined endpoint of grade 3+ adverse effects <20% at short f/u of 1 year.

However after 1 year there were deaths with 11.5 and 12 Gy due to hemorrhage and ulceration. The trial was not powered to compare local control.

[Editorialization: Consider anticoagulants a contraindication for higher doses, and only treating peripheral lesions with higher dose.]
trials.commentary:
The interpretation here is an editorialization and differs from the original conclusion. Follow-up of one year is too short (such a f/u length would never be accepted in a hypofractionation or omission of RT trial). In the HILUS trial, hemorrhage continued to occur until 2 years later. The primary endpoint was grade ≥3 adverse effects at 1 year. Even at 1-yr f/u, many will find the risk of grade 5 adverse effects unacceptable. The authors replied that more tumors in the higher dose levels were located adjacent to bronchi (Bezjak 2019). The HILUS trial, a phase II evaluting 56 Gy/ 8 fx to ultracentral tumors, also led to deaths related to bronchopulmonary hemorrhage. Perhaps dose escalation could be safe in peripheral tumors in those who are not taking anticoagulants. The arms weren't powered to compare LC - this was a phase I study - so there's also no proof that higher dose is needed.

Few patients were "ultra" central. Dose was D95 to 100% and fractions were every other day. When a trial changes its endpoints post-hoc, it generally triggers a negative reaction. But here, with loss aversion, it's the inverse effect: there is an impression that the endpoint should be changed post-hoc, or was misplaced initially, to describe the therapy appropriately. Adverse effects with RT can occur after one year.
