trials.interpretation:
In this propensity matched analysis, SBRT was noninferior to VATS in OS, but LR, DM, and RR trended to favor surgery. The analysis is likely underpowered. Randomized trials are ongoing.

trials.commentary:
This is a propensity matched analysis, which cannot replace a randomized trial. A strength of the study is that it was guided by protocol, and those who received SBRT would have had consistent workup and treatment. The revised STARS trial seems underpowered at 80 patients. Recurrence rates seem to trend higher for SBRT. The VALOR randomized trial is ongoing, where planned n=670 (NCT02984761).

In the VATS group, 60% had EBUS, and in the SBRT group, 90% had EBUS. In the VATS group there was a rate of 10% occult nodal metastasis on LND, followed by less eventual regional recurrences after VATS treatment over SBRT. And salvage therapy in the form of chemoRT for nodal recurrence after SBRT is not ideal. Despite this, OS was similar; possibly due to salvage therapies eventually equalizing OS, or adverse effects, or other factors including underpower.

Since the trial is nonrandomized, there could be selection bias toward poor performance status patients with SBRT, which would favor the surgery arm; this would not be able to be completely corrected for in propensity matching. Despite this, OS results seem similar, and this strengthens the idea that SBRT could be equivalent in some way, at least in regards to eventual OS.

trials.methods:
NSCLC EGFR+ s/p complete resection

➜ 🏆 osimertinib x3 years
vs.
➜ placebo x3 years (23% crossed-over to osimertinib)

post-op RT not permitted
trials.results:
Stage II-IIIA 5-yr OS 85% vs. 73%
overall 5-yr OS 88% vs. 78%
Median OS not reached in either arm

Stage II-IIIA 4-yr DFS 70% vs. 29%
overall 4-yr DFS 73% vs. 38%

Stage II-IIIA 4-yr CNS recurrence 8% vs. 14%
overall 4-yr CNS recurrence 6% vs. 11%

Looking at Figs 1 & 3, it seems that DFS eventually begins to merge at about 5-6 years f/u
trials.interpretation: Osimertinib improves OS, DFS and reduces CNS relapse in completely resected EGFR+ NSCLC vs. control with minimal crossover.
trials.commentary:
Osimertinib is tumorostatic rather than tumorocidal. In a pre-op study, there were zero pCRs with osimertinib, and major path responses were 15% (Blakely 2024). Still osimertinib is a landmark discovery in personalized medicine, a drug that greatly extends outcomes with minimal adverse effects. There is controversy regarding whether all need the drug in the adjuvant setting, for what duration and the design of the control arm.

Role of radiation. The findings of later disease failure and lack of pCR may lend for a tandem role of radiation alongside osimertinib for recurrence, especially for brain metastasis and oligometastatic disease. The SINDAS and NROGC 002 trials showed OS benefit with RT for EGFR+ oligometastatic disease treated by earlier generation EGFR inhibitors (of note osimertinib was not included in the studies).

DFS statistics. In the DFS and CNS DFS figures there seems to be eventual merging of the curves at about 5-6 years (Willers 2023 and West 2023). This suggests that disease recurrence might eventually rapidly "catch-up" to control. The answer for some could be simply that the drug should be continued indefinitely until failure. Yet 33% discontinued the drug in the study.

Although the authors do report what they call cumulative DFSs of HRs 0.23-0.27 at "data cutoff" - when all had completed therapy - it is impossible that these could be the final DFS outcomes. They are DFSs during the time which the drug was given, not cumulative - it would be better termed as "on-trial-therapy DFS HRs". The authors wrote that because DFS was significant, no further formal statistical testing was done, and p values after are not provided. The statistical approach raises concerns that data is being withheld. The 4 year values nonetheless are excellent, and may be all that some need, especially those with limited life expectancy or who wish to avoid other types of treatment.

Design controversy. A debate centers around the control arm - the argument is that the control arm should have had 100% salvage crossover to osimertinib (similar to the adjuvant vs salvage prostate trials) when it was approved as SOC first line therapy for metastasis by the FDA on 4/18/18 (FDA and FLAURA). The trial began enrollment 10/2015 and closed 1/2020, however note also that recurrence takes time. West and Prasad comment that AztraZenica was urged to make the drug available to the control arm, but did not, even while promoting the drug as standard (West 2023, Prasad 2023). Instead only 39% in the control arm with progression crossed-over (Prasad 2020, 2023 & Olivier 2023). MRI brain and PET were not required, which passively biases the trial to occult disease, and again may overstate the benefit of the drug.  West, Akhade, and Gyawali (2023) write "We submit that oncologists and patients should expect that phase III trials are conducted in a way that aspires to more than the lowest threshold of what a lenient regulatory authority will accept. Rather, the oncology community should seek that key trials enroll appropriately staged patients and ensure they receive access to the best treatments as defined by the contemporary practice in health care systems in which the experimental therapy would be marketed."

trials.interpretation: Subablative SBRT for oligoprogessive disease improved local control of the treated lesions, but not PFS or OS.
trials.commentary:
Review and future directions. Why was this trial negative when others were positive? The answer could be due to choice of endpoints, sequencing, radiation doses, or that there is no benefit. A strength of LU002 and STOP are their multi institutional reach. Neither LU002 or STOP used ablative doses.

The SBRT doses used in LU002 and STOP were BEDs <100. The IAEA study used similar doses as LU002. IAEA was a positive study, although phase II and used different sequencing. The 34 Gy/5 fractions permitted in LU002 is a departure from the 34 Gy/1 fraction determined safe in RTOG 0915.

The NSCLC oligometastasis trials used different sequencing, and there is a possibility that specific sequencing must take place to achieve benefit from RT. NRG LU002 randomized upfront local therapy to all lesions vs. none, which is unique amongst the trials. Definitive upfront 60 Gy chemoRT was not permitted. In IAEA and OliGomez, chemo was given first, then, if no progression, patients were randomized to local therapy to oligomets. In CURB & STOP chemo was given first followed by SBRT to oligoprogressive masses. In SABR COMET, those eligible already received definitive treatment to primary, then were randomized to SBRT to oligomets vs none. If sequencing is the answer, perhaps definitive chemoRT should be first, or local therapy is only of benefit after induction chemotherapy challenge.

Future directions. Perhaps oligometastasis should be conceptualized similar to limited vs extensive stage SCLC and treated with definitive chemoradiation followed by immunotherapy when feasible, an already well established regimen. There has never been a positive induction chemo trial for definitive chemoradiation. Metastasis that are not feasible to treat simultaneously could be treated with ablative SBRT using doses already established in dose escalation trials.

Phase II practice. Should clinicians be applying phase II data before confirmation in phase III? The choices one's willing to make are based on risk tolerance. In Stage III-IV NSCLC, which despite advances still has poor survival rates, clinicians and patients may be willing to take on more risk. Phase II trials for oligomets showed unexpectedly impressive and consistent results.

NSCLC EGFR+, 1-5 oligometastasis

Excluded: brain metastasis

no prior therapy
trials.methods:
Phase III

➜ 🏆 25-40 Gy in 1-5 fx to all sites (primary, nodes, & oligomets) then TKI
vs.
➜ TKI (later palliative RT allowed)

(VMAT, IMRT, and SBRT were allowed. Most used ~500 MU dose rate)
trials.results:
⬆️ Median OS 25.5 vs. 17.4 mos, p<0.001

⬆️ Median PFS 20.2 vs. 12.5 mos, p<0.001
⬆️ 6-mos PFS 99% vs. 95%

⬆️ LC 91% vs. 55%

Grade 3-4 pneumonitis 6% with RT+TKI
no grade 5 adverse effects
trials.interpretation: Upfront RT in 5 or less fractions to primary and oligometastatic disease in EGFR+ oligometastatic NSCLC improves OS and PFS. This approach should be a standard of care treatment option.
trials.commentary:
Radiation is cytotoxic and osimeritiib is tumorostatic. In a pre-op study, there were zero pCRs with osimertinib, and major path responses were only 15% (Blakely 2024). DFS can be extented with osimeritinib, but other treatment is required to eradicate disease.

VMAT, IMRT, and SBRT were allowed. 3DCRT was not. Most institutions used ~500 MU dose rate (Zeng M, email communication, Feb 2022).

Although 6-mos PFS, the primary endpoint, does not show a large difference, later median PFS and OS show impressive separations. This suggests that the benefit of RT continues to manifest and evolve with time. The trial was ended early at interim analysis due to benefit: observe the miniscule p values. Patient characteristics favored the TKI arm: the RT arm had more mets. <10% had 5 mets.

Some might ask if RT can be delayed until progression. In the TKI only arm, RT was only allowed for later palliation, and not for eventual possible oligoprogression as crossover. Delay in RT until progression is not necessarily ruled out as an appropriate strategy, but it also doesn't have the same level of validation as the SINDAS approach, which seems very reasonable for those with good life expectancy.

SINDAS was prior to osimertinib. TKIs permitted in SINDAS were gefitinib, erlotinib, or icotinib. Still we know that osimertinib does not produce pCR. SINDAS was conducted primarily in the Sichuan and Chengdu provinces of China.

Dose constraints: trachea/large bronchus mean <16.5 Gy, heart/ribs/esophagus V30 <5cc

5-yr OS 42% vs. 18%, p=0.006
8-yr OS 27% vs. 14%
grade 5 toxicity 4.5% (n=3) vs. none

trials.interpretation:

Overall results, including power, applicability by # mets and reproducibility in individual histologies, are to be validated in Phase III trials.
trials.commentary: Note that PFS was definitive (p<0.005), and OS was nearly definitive per the statistical design. Results should eventually be evaluated in individual histologies. The median PFS of 6 mos and LC of 63% suggests that the improvement in OS was in part a result of continuing salvage SBRT and potentially reduced future spread due to lower tumor burden, and possible immune response. There were more prostate cancer patients in the SBRT arm (21% vs. 6%). A post-hoc sensitivity analysis of other histologies showed consistent results. Although there were perhaps more favorable histologies in the SBRT arm, there were also some typically more aggressive histologies that did well. Note also that results are similar in the IAEA and Oligomez trials. Also note remarkable changes in OS with moderate LC of 63%. LC was different per met location: adrenal 100%, bone 72%, lung 51%, liver 50%, possibly due to low power in subanalysis, or other factors. The results should eventually be confirmed in phase III trials in individual histologies. Consider also that the majority of oncologic drugs approved by the FDA are approved based on PFS, but this remains controversial and OS is preferred. There were treatment deaths of 4.5% in this study, which is high, however there were no treatment deaths in the OliGomez and IAEA studies.

trials.commentary:
SCLC dose summary
-Early trials show an OS benefit with RT, and this is confirmed on meta-analysis
-INT 0096 establishes 45 Gy/ 30 fx BID as standard
-Over 15 years later, CONVERT compares 45 Gy BID regimen to 60 Gy and did not show superiority. Trends in results support 45 Gy BID
-CALGB is an ongoing trial to also evaluate dose

SCLC PCI cognitive benefit summary
-There was previously a debate as to whether PCI caused cognitive decline
-Early trials were mixed on whether PCI causes neuroadverse effects (INT and UKCCR/EORTC)
-SRS trials looking at addition of WBRT (EORTC, MDACC, Alliance NCI), or WBRT vs. SRS (RTOG 1270) showed improved QOL and cognitive function without WBRT.
-See also the PCI study in NSCLC, NVALT-11/DLCRG-02, that does show cognitive impairment with PCI but similar QOL later.
-Hippocampus sparing with IMRT in 30 Gy WBRT has shown improvement in cognitive function and seems translatable to PCI.
-PCI specific IMRT trials are ongoing.

trials.interpretation: 70 Gy QD did not improve OS compared to 45 Gy BID. Since the trial was designed to show superiority and did not, BID RT remains standard of care per the prespecified design. Daily RT is a reasonable alternative.
trials.commentary:
CONVERT results trended in favor of BID, and there was worse esophageal adverse effects with daily fractionation, so BID is preferred. For those strictly following pre-specified design, CALGB and CONVERT were superiority studies - not noninferiority - so per the prespecifed design the conclusion is that 66-70 Gy is not superior and 45 Gy BID remains standard of care. It is important also to keep in mind that design of superiority and noninferiority, especially selection of noninferiority margins, is somewhat arbitrary (Dunn 2018). Treating SCLC with 60-70 Gy does demonstrate favorable results and is an option alongside 45 Gy BID, especially for patients with a limited schedule. OS in CALGB and CONVERT was much improved over the INT trial, perhaps due to stepwise improvements such as PET, MRI, no ENI, IMRT, better 2nd line options, and more experienced use of chemo.

In the 70 Gy and 61.2 Gy arms, initial volume to 44 Gy includes ipsilateral hilum. Then resim and boost are optional.

Cord max <41 Gy for BID
Other dose constraints similar to conventional

trials.methods:
Phase II
➜ 54 Gy BID to GTV with SIB 45 Gy to PTV/ 30 fx
vs.
➜ past phase II cohort of 45 Gy BID/30 fx

cisplatin/etoposide x4-6 cycles
trials.results:
median PFS 13.3 vs. 11.1 mos, p=0.08
2-yr OS 66% vs. 39%

grade 2 esophagitis worse with SIB, but grade ≥3 no different
grade ≥2 pneumonitis not different
trials.interpretation: In this phase II dose escalation study, dose escalation to 54 Gy BID in 30 fx had improved OS with similar adverse effects. Findings require validation in phase III.
trials.commentary:
Although the CONVERT and CALGB studies were negative for dose escalation, the THORA and Sun-Yat Sen University studies provide some evidence for benefit of dose-escalation with BID or hyperfx approaches. In this study, given that these were two separate phase II trials that are being compared, there is a possibility of imbalances. The THORA authors make the point that doses without phase III evidence have a history of being employed in SCLC (e.g. 60-66 Gy daily, 70 Gy daily before their Phase III studies, etc). The data for RT for oligometastasis in NSCLC is phase II and widely implemented. SCLC continues to have poor survival rates. Some may be willing to take on more risk.

The abstract does not provide details regarding what margins were used for SIB targeting, but it seems that the high dose was delivered to a PTV that was added to the GTV, and the low dose was given to a PTV from the CTV.

trials.results:
2-yr OS 48% vs. 74%, p=0.0005
5-yr OS 28% vs. 39%
Median OS 22.5 vs. 43.5 mos
Median PFS 15.0 vs. 18.6 mos, p=0.13

Disease progression 63-64%, not different
LC 23% vs. 37%, p=0.037
DM ~45%, not different
Brain mets 12% vs. 20%, p=0.17

n=2 esophgeal strictures, only with 60 Gy

grade 3-4 pneumonitis 0% vs. 3%
trials.interpretation: In this phase II dose escalation study, 60 Gy BID had improved OS with similar adverse effects. Randomized trials are warranted.
trials.commentary:
Although the CONVERT and CALGB studies were negative for dose escalation with daily dosing, the THORA and Sun-Yat Sen University studies provide some evidence for benefit of dose-escalation with BID. In THORA four patients in the 60 Gy arm received 45 Gy when constraints were not achieved, and one by mistake. Per protocol outcomes were similar. Information is not provided regarding how many had 54 Gy. Stratification was by T and N staging, reducing imbalance by tumor volume. 85% had PCI. It is unusual to see an OS benefit without a PFS benefit, but not an impossibility. PFS did have a trend to benefit. Perhaps worse or faster progression would have occured without escalation. As always, phase III trials are required to fully confirm a phase II finding. In endorsement of use of 60 Gy BID, the authors make the point that doses without phase III evidence have a history of being employed in SCLC (e.g. 60-66 Gy daily, 70 Gy daily before their Phase III studies, etc). In syndromes of poor prognosis, it is reasonable to have a higher risk tolerance and accept interventions of limited evidence. The data for RT for oligometastasis in NSCLC is phase II and widely implemented.

GTVs were gross disease and PET avid lesions. CTV 5 mm.

trials.methods:
Phase II:
➜ 45 Gy BID/30 fx (BED 52)
 vs.
➜ hypofx 65 Gy QD/26 fx (BED 66.4)

cis/etoposide x4-6 cycles

1⁰ Endpoint: PFS

IMRT
RT starts with cycle 1-3 of chemo
No ENI
PCI for good response
trials.results:
Median OS 33.6 vs. 39.3 mos, p=0.137
(OS data still maturing)

Median PFS 13.4 vs. 17.2 mos, p=0.031
2-yr PFS 28% vs. 42%

Median LPFS 23.9 mos vs. not reached
2-yr LPFS 50% vs. 69%, p=0.017

- More grade 3+ acute lymphopenia with QD RT 40% vs. 72%

- No differences on grade 3-4 esophagitis, pneumonitis, or death

Treatment compliance similar between both groups
trials.interpretation: Moderately hypofractionated QD RT to 65 Gy/26 fx showed improved PFS & LPFS with similar toxicities compared with SOC standard 45 Gy BID RT in LS-SCLC. This regimen should be evaluated in a phase III study.
trials.commentary:
Although the CONVERT and CALGB studies were negative for dose escalation with daily dosing, the THORA and Sun-Yat Sen University studies provide some evidence for benefit of dose-escalation with BID. This study was designed to test slightly higher BED than CONVERT 70 Gy arm (BED of 66.4 Gy here vs. 64.6), but within shorter period of overall treatment time based on data showing worse outcomes in those with prolonged treatment time. The authors also cite preclinical data suggesting that hypofx RT may improve the efficacy of immunotherapy. As always, phase III trials are required to fully confirm a phase II finding. The THORA authors make the point that doses without phase III evidence have a history of being employed in SCLC (e.g. 60-66 Gy daily, 70 Gy daily before their Phase III studies, etc). The data for RT for oligometastasis in NSCLC is phase II and widely implemented. SCLC continues to have poor survival rates. Some may be willing to take on more risk.

Interestingly, the majority of patients initiated RT with cycle 3 rather than cycles 1 or 2 of chemo, under the idea that tumor shrinkage from upfront chemo might allow for RT dose escalation, with stratification of pts based on chemo response for those who might need more intensive RT regimens or further adjuvant tx (immunotherapy).

PCI rate was lower than other trials (71.4%) due to patient choice.

Omitted ECOG 2 patients

-Early trials were mixed on whether PCI causes neuroadverse effects (INT and UKCCR/EORTC)
-SRS trials looking at addition of WBRT (EORTC, MDACC, Alliance NCI), or WBRT vs. SRS (RTOG 1270) showed improved QOL and cognitive function without WBRT.
-See also the PCI study in NSCLC, NVALT-11/DLCRG-02, that does show cognitive impairment with PCI but similar QOL later.
-Hippocampus sparing with IMRT in 30 Gy WBRT has shown improvement in cognitive function and seems translatable to PCI.
-PREMER and NRG CC003 show some benefit with hippocampal sparing PCI, although CC003's primary endpoint was not met

trials.citation:
Slotman et al, Lancet, 2015
Slotman et al, Lancet, 2015
trials.patients: Extensive stage SCLC, no brain mets, who responded to 4-6 cycles chemo, ECOG 0-2
trials.methods:
➜ 🏆 30 Gy thoracic RT + PCI
vs.
➜ PCI

Primary endpoint: 1-yr OS
trials.results:
⬆️ 2-yr OS 13% vs. 3%, p=0.004
↗️ 1-yr OS 33% vs. 28%, p=0.066
⬆️ 6-mo PFS 24% vs. 7%
⬇️ Thoracic failure 44% vs. 80%
CR only 5% in both arms

Post-hoc analysis in author's reply: No benefit in CR. Benefit was only in those with residual disease. 95% had residual disease
-OS and PFS in residual disease very similar to above. Stats not provided for those with CR
trials.interpretation: Consolidative thoracic RT improves OS in extensive stage SCLC that responded to chemo. However the primary endpoint of 1-yr OS was not met.
trials.commentary:
This trial confirmed the survival benefit of consolidative RT in extensive SCLC, a condition with poor prognosis and few innovations over years other than immunotherapy. For some the role of RT is controversial - so much so that even the author Slotman published an accompanying editorial doubting his own results! The role of radiotherapy could be in priming an immune response, cytoreduction, or LC reducing future pulmonary complications. The trial reproduced the results of a smaller Yugoslavia trial six years prior. Opponents to consolidative thoracic RT might respond that CR to chemotherapy doesn't benefit, that immunotherapy may negate the benefit of RT or be too toxic together, or that the primary endpoint was not met. Two year OS is obviously an important time point for patients. Some question whether RT is still of benefit with atezolizumab or durvalumab (Goldman 2020), which can have adverse effects of pneumonitis. A clinical trial must be performed to show this. Pneumonitis is low in ADRIATIC. The ADRIATIC, CAPSIAN, and IMpower studies have shown that SCLC is immunogenic.

Slotman speculated that RT only works in residual disease and not CR. This CREST subanalysis was post-hoc and likely underpowered for those with CR, which were only 5%. Now practioners often assess response by PET, which could overestimate the response rate compared to RECIST criteria. Recognize also that a radiologic CR is very different from a pathologic CR, and a CR on imaging is no indication of cure. In IMpower and CASPIAN, immunotherapy improved median OS by only 2 months, and CR rate with immunotherapy was only 3% (measured by RECIST). If CR is what is needed to avoid RT, this is not resolved with immunotherapy, and the improvement in outcomes offered by immunotherpy is not enough.  Consider for example the noninferiority trials in CR in favorable early stage Hodgkin lymphoma that show superiority with RT. SCLC has poor survival rates, and is not yet at a status in which practitioners should be omitting therapy or de-escalating. NCCN's 2024 recommendation that chest radiation should only be recommended for those with poor response in the chest seems misguided. Canadian and UK guidelines recommend the opposite, that radiation should be given for those with response to chemotherapy (Melosky 2023 & NICE 2024).

Thoracic RT and PCI were given simultaneously. RT volume was post-chemo volume of involved nodal levels with 1.5 cm margin. Involved levels were treated whether CR occurred there or not. Thoracic failure was still high after RT, raising a hypothesis if control can be further improved with dose escalation.

trials.patients: Extensive stage SCLC with PR or stable disease by RECIST after 4-6 cycles chemo plus atezolizumab
trials.methods:
➜ RT to up to 5 sites, 5 fx simultaneously on days 1-5 only
Thorax or liver: 45 or 30 Gy
Extrathoracic RT: 30 or 20 Gy
followed by atezolizumab
vs.
➜ atezolizumab
trials.results:
ongoing study

Primary endpoints: PFS (phase II), and OS (phase III)
trials.commentary:
The CREST study showed benefit with RT to thorax. On an exploratory analysis the benefit was only in residual disease, but that analysis was likely under powered (see CREST commentary). In CASPIAN and Impower133, only 3% in the immunotherapy arms had CR, which may indicate a continuing role for consolidative RT with immunotherapy. PET may overestimate CR compared to RECIST. The immunotherapy trials withheld standard of care therapy with thoracic RT.

The RAPTOR trial would benefit from a dose constraint for blood pool, or separation of radiation courses, as 5 courses of radiation or even 3 is a large area to treat simultaneously and risks negating the benefit of radiation, especially when a similar trial, RTOG 0937 was negative.

This trial differs from the negative trial RTOG 0937 in that RAPTOR prescribes radiation for those with PR or stable disease, while 0937 gave radiation for CR/PR.

trials.trial: National Kyushu Cancer Center, Fukuoka, Japan
trials.patients: Extensive stage SCLC who responded to platinum chemotherapy. No brain metastases on MRI
trials.methods:
➜ PCI 25 Gy/10 fx
vs.
➜ observation
trials.results:
No OS benefit with PCI. BM improved
1-yr OS 54% vs. 48% (NS, p=0.094)
2-yr OS 15% vs. 19%
Median OS 11.6 mos PCI vs. 13.7 mos
1-yr brain mets 33% vs. 59%
Overall brain mets 48% vs. 69%
trials.interpretation:
PCI did not improve OS in extensive stage SCLC staged with MRI.

The incidence of future brain metastases was reduced.
trials.commentary:
This is the first trial to require MRI for eligibility. PCI did reduce the incidence of new brain mets. The study at hand may be used to support close observation of patients with MRI followed by WBRT when brain metastases present, or potentially even SRS. Some might choose to offer PCI based on improvement in LC. adverse effects should also be considered: some studies stress that there are few to no cognitive changes with PCI UKCCR/EORTC, Gregor 1987), while those in support of hippocampal sparing (PREMER) or SRS (NRG CC009) caution of its potential hazards.

Compare to the EORTC study (Slotman 2007). Interestingly, OS was higher despite the same treatment. EORTC evaluated symptomatic brain mets only, and Japan scanned for any brain mets.

trials.patients:
Extensive stage SCLC with no prior therapy

Ineligible: prior chest consolidative RT or palliative radiation
trials.methods:
atezolizumab (anti PD-L1) + carbo/etop x4 →

➜ atezolizumab
vs.
➜ 🏆atezolizumab plus lurbinectedin

PCI permitted as discretion, but not chest or palliative radiation
trials.results:
⬆️ 1-yr IRF PFS 12% vs. 21%
⬆️ 1-yr OS 44% vs. 56%, p=0.017

Grade 3-4 adverse effects 38% vs. 22%

Lurbinectedin had more cytopenias
trials.interpretation: Lurbinectedin added to maintenance atezolizumab in extensive SCLC improves IRF and OS.
trials.commentary:
Lurbinectedin is an alkylating drug that binds guanine residues in the minor groove of DNA. Those with brain metastasis were excluded. 27% were not randomized after four cycles of chemo.

After years of stalled progress, lurbinectedin and immunotherapy finally managed to improve OS in extensive SCLC, and CREST showed an OS benefit with consolidative chest radiation. Since lurbinectedin was already available as second line treatment at the time of the study, the trial perhaps should have been crossover design. Some advocate or choose to employ lurbinectedin after failure of atezolizumab (Choudhury and Garassino 2025). The bottom line is that the study shows an OS benfit.

Consolidative chest radiation was not permitted in the study. 1-yr OS is 56% still leaves much room for improvement, and continuing use of radiation is probably warranted in these poor prognosis patients.
trials.reference: 1. Paz-Ares L, Borghaei H, Liu SV, et al. trials.methods:

→ ABVD (x1 for F, x2 for U) + 30-36 Gy INRT

Primary endpoint: noninferiority of PFS, delta of 10%. Superiority stats also included

Positive PET was defined as Deauville 3-5
trials.results:
-In favorable 86% achieved negative PET2.
-In unfavorable 75% had negative PET2
-PET negative arm stopped early at 1-yr analysis

🏿 Fav PET negatives
3ABVD + INRT vs. 4ABVD:
5-yr PFS 99% vs. 87%
⬆️ 10-yr PFS 99% vs. 85%, superior
10-yr OS 100% vs. 98%, not different

🏿 Unfav PET negatives
4ADVD + INRT vs. 6ABVD:
5-yr PFS 92% vs. 90%
5-yr OS 100% in both arms
✅ 10-yr PFS 91% vs. 86%, not noninferior
10-yr OS 95%, not different
10-yr 2nd cancer 6.8% vs. 6.5%
-With ABVD alone, 73% failures were soley at original sites

No difference in 10-yr adverse effects or 2nd cancer

🎗️ PET positive SER (standard vs. directed):
ABVD+INRT vs. BEACOPPesc+INRT
5-yr PFS 77%  vs. 91%
10-yr PFS 79% vs. 85%
trials.interpretation:
Observation is not noninferior to INRT in early stage HL, both favorable and unfavorable, with negative PET2. The PET negative arms were closed early due to futility.

PFS with INRT was superior in favorable PET negative. Additional cycles of chemotherapy do not replace INRT in this setting.

There is no difference in 10-yr adverse effects or second cancer.

There is no OS benefit to INRT in CR, but INRT spares some from salvage therapy.

In SER PET2 positive, BEACOPPesc improves PFS over ABVD. Chemo and INRT shows good results and allows some to be spared transplant.
trials.commentary:
Since this study, SWOG 1826 showed 3-yr PFS of 98% in Stage III HL in peds treated with N+AVD x6. Thus there may no longer be a role for routine ISRT for PET2+ in Stage I-III HL treated with this regimen, but there is still a role for ISRT for refactory PET6+. Two to three cycles of chemo followed by ISRT may be useful for those who want less chemotherarpy.

This trial's 10 year follow-up confirms long term PFS benefit with INRT in PET2 negative, without detriment to OS or increase in secondary cancer. The study also shows that additional cycles of chemo cannot replace INRT. There is no benefit in OS, likely due to salvage therapy. For comparison HD17 did show noninferiority without INRT in PET negative unfavorable HL when BEACOPP is used. GHSG HD10 used a slightly de-escalated regimen, ABVD x2 plus 20 Gy.

PET2 positive. These trials not only ask who can avoid radiation, but also give data on who can avoid death and transplant when using RT for PET positive at cycle 2-3. In H10, RAPID, and HD16, PFS was 80-95%, allowing a large majority to avoid salvage therapy and transplant. Some prefer treatment with response adapted chemotherapy, but this is mainly studied in advanced HL, not early stage.

Adverse effects and 2nd malignancy. In HL for some there is a careful balance between cure, adverse effects, and secondary malignancy. There was no increase in secondary malignancy in EORTC with RT - small INRT fields were used. Effects past ten years are unknown for this specific study, but ten years is a good follow-up period. Increasing doses of doxorubicin, ASCT, and CAR-T also increase 2nd cancer risk (Neppelenbroek 2024, McDonald 2023). CAR T cell has reported secondary malignancies of 4-16%, and consequently FDA now requires boxed warnings (Cappell & Kochenderfer 2023, Suran 2024). Neither ASCT nor CAR T have shown improvement in OS in randomized trials in HL (Schmitz 2022 and Linch 1993).  Concerning cancer survivorship, female patients who undergo radiation are required to undergo more frequent screenings for breast cancer (NCCN 2024). It is unclear if this is needed with INRT; site of 2nd cancer was not reported in H10. Would a patient rather have INRT or "go through this again" with the chance of salvage chemo with ASCT or CAR-T? Patients should be offered INRT.

Radiation planning. INRT volumes in the study strictly covered the initial volume of nodes prior to chemotherapy, also taking into account anatomical displacement. There was no allowance for extra elective volume per expert opinion. In other words the smallest volumes possible should be implemented to reproduce these results.

trials.patients: Pediatric and adult HL Stage I-II favorable or unfavorable per adult staging, bulky allowed, age 5-60
trials.methods:
ABVD x2 → PET →

RER Favorable/Unfav
➜ ABVDx2 for F, AVDx4 for U
vs.
➜ Brentuximab + nivolumab x4

SER Favorable/Unfav
➜ escBEACOPPx2 + 30 Gy ISRT IMRT or protons
vs.
➜ Brentuximab + nivolumab x4 + 30 Gy ISRT IMRT or protons
trials.results:
Ongoing protocol

Primary endpoint: PFS

Secondary endpoints: noninferiority of 12-yr OS, 12-yr EFS, adverse effects, QOL
trials.commentary:
Background. Both pediatric and adult patients are eligible. In order to preserve fertility and reduce late effects, adult HL regimens are now being trialed in the pediatric population.

SER. As in essentially all other clinical trials for early stage HL, RT remains mandated for those with SER, anticipated in 15%. The investigators write "Therefore, there is no data to support omitting radiotherapy among patients with SER for patients with Stage I/II disease." RT for SER shows good results in studies, and there is no evidence that response adapted chemo for something that already seems chemo resistant is superior. In H10, RAPID, and HD16, PFS in PET2-3 SERs treated with RT was 80-95%. In AHOD0431, when ISRT was required for low risk relapse after CR, 84% avoided transplant. In RATHL in adults, 91% who had optional radiation for refractory were able to avoid transplant. In the HD12+9 combined analysis in advanced lymphoma there was PFS and OS benefit with radiation for refractory disease.

RER. This study was designed prior to the publication of long term follow-up of EORTC H10 in adults, which showed superiority of INRT in CR in favorable HL and not-noninferiority of removal INRT in CR in unfavorable. An amendment adding ISRT to the RER arms in AHOD2131 seems called for, at least for favorable HL in adults in the control arm, though perhaps COG anticipates that mainly young adults will be enrolled. In AHOD0031, an analogous study to H10 evaluating IFRT in RER in pediatrics, the benefit with IFRT in CR at four year was p=0.11, and the trial does not yet have the long term follow up that EORTC H10 does. In H10 additional cycles did not compensate for omission of ISRT. HD17 showed no benefit with RT in unfavorable HL with RT after PET CR when BEACOPP is used, but HD16 did not show noninferiority in with omission of RT in PET negative favorable early stage. In AHOD0431 for low risk pediatric lymphoma, a post-hoc analysis showed benefit with IFRT in RER, but this was non randomized. Concerning the experimental arm, in SWOG 1826, evaluating nivolumab in Stage III-IV lymphoma ages ≥12, only ≤1% were treated with radiation, but this trial had extremely strict criteria for allowing RT. In SWOG 12% in the nivolumab arm were still Deauville 4-5.

Radiation planning. IMRT, VMAT, and protons are now recommended. ISRT is now 30 Gy. For age <15, 21 Gy with 9-10 Gy boost to SER sites can be given. Prior COG protocols showed risk of in field relapse with 21 Gy in SER, suggesting a role for dose escalation. The trial recommends to follow ILROG guidelines for CTV.

Improved OS and EFS with chemotherapy, and improved FFP with RT:

trials.commentary:
This trial was used by some in the past to support omission of RT in Hodgkin lymphoma for years. Radiation techniques have since modernized to much smaller fields than STLI, and the trial is now historical since the publications of UK RAPID, EORTC H10, and HD16. Those trials showed that IFRT/INRT improves PFS in PET negative HL. EORTC H10 has ten year f/u.

In HL there is a careful balance between cure, adverse effects, and secondary malignancy, with a focus for some on de-escalation. There is admittedly excellent OS for the ABVD alone arm in NCIC ECOG HD6. Differences in OS were partly due to 2nd cancer in this study. There is long term data elsewhere that shows evidence of increase in secondary malignancy with RT (Schaapveld 2015), but this should be reduced with ISRT. In the modern era, CAR T cell has reported secondary malignancies of 4-16% (Cappell & Kochenderfer 2023). ACST has also been shown to increase the risk of secondary malignancy (McDonald 2023). Increased doses of doxorubicin also increase the risk of second malignancy (Neppelenbroek 2024).

Older patients in STLI arm. HR in trial reached 0.99 for OS and FFP, very close to 1. Chemo improved OS and EFS, RT improved FFP (Straus 2012). Cardiac events were increased with RT, but modern RT is more likely to avoid heart.

BEACOPP is not commonly applied in some regions due to adverse effects and added complexity, and PFS benefit without OS benefit. On subanalysis, those with bulky masses or elevated ESR tended to have better outcomes with escBEACOPP but the trial was not powered for this analysis. Some practicioners instead elect to use 6-8 cycles ABVD in bulky HL. But an advantage of the 2+2 regimen is that there are fewer cycles. The trial did not confirm long term adverse effects with escBEACOPP. And even if that's the case, BEACOPP does spare patients from long term adverse effects of salvage chemo and BMT.

In the US, generally intensification of treatment is less accepted if it increases PFS and adverse effects without OS benefit. This includes both escBEACOPP and radiation.

trials.interpretation:
RT improves FFTF in advanced HL with refractory compared to no further treatment. These were able to avoid transplant. BEACOPPesc seems preferred to BEACOPPbase.

A combined analysis of HD9 and HD12 at ten years shows PFS and OS benefit with radiation for residual disease.
trials.commentary:
HD15 and onward incorporate PET guided RT as standard based on HD12. A long term combined analysis of HD12+9 showed PFS & OS benefit with radiation. The HD9 portion was not randomized, which could lead to imbalances in the analysis. The mechanism of radiation might be cytoreductive and could also stimulate an immune response. The use of nivolumab in lymphoma shows that lymphoma can be immunogenic (Ansell 2023).

Dose & field. Although some guidelines endorse 36-40 Gy for PR (ILROG, Constine 2018), 30 Gy is what was established in HD12 and incorporated into HD15. In HD9 IFRT was given for bulky or residual disease to 30 Gy or 40 Gy respectively. A benefit of 30 Gy is shorter time without systemic therapy and its actual use in the randomization. ISRT to limited areas may reduce adverse effects. An enlightening TLI study for relapse shows that even TLI + IFRT boost doesn't always completely eradicate disease (Paudeal 2019). Investigation into other radiation techniques or systemic therapy is still warranted. Nonetheless there is PFS and OS benefit in the combined HD9 and H12 analysis with RT for disease refractory to chemo.

Adverse effects and 2nd malignancy overview. There are variations in practice patterns. In HL for some there is a balance between cure, adverse effects, and secondary malignancy with a focus on de-escalation (Gisselbrecht 2018). In HD12+9 late causes of death from 2nd malignancy and adverse effects were about double that of death from the disease itself regardless of RT use. ASCT and CAR T don't have the same length of f/u. Note that there is long term data elsewhere that shows evidence of increase in 2nd malignancy with RT and total 40-yr incidence of second cancer of possibly 49% in HL. But there is some bias in that some may not present for f/u (Schaapveld 2015). This should be reduced with lower RT dose and volume. Increasing doses of doxorubicin and ASCT also increase the risk of second malignancy (Neppelenbroek 2024, McDonald 2023). CAR T cell has reported secondary malignancies of 4-16%, and consequently FDA now requires boxed warnings (Cappell & Kochenderfer 2023, Suran 2024). There was no increase in secondary malignancy with INRT in EORTC H10 in early stage HL at ten years.
trials.notes:
Advanced HL summary
-HD12 showed FFTF with RT in PET+ refractory. EORTC 20884 also showed that RT maintained outcomes in PET+
-There seems to be no benefit thus far with RT after CR per EORTC 20884
-RATHL established use of AVD
-ECHELON showed an OS benefit with Br+AVD over ABVD. Few studies have shown an OS benefit to any intervention
-HD21 showed a PFS benefit with BrECADD over escBEACOPP. RT was used in PET+ refractory
-SWOG1826 showed a PFS benefit with N+AVD over Br+AVD. SWOG's protocol had very strict criteria for the use of RT, thus it was used only in 1% in both arms
-Some now use N+AVD in early stage as well based on SWOG1826 and NIVAHL

trials.commentary:
EORTC 20884 is likely underpowered. GITIL/FIL HD0607 delivered IFRT to bulky only CR, but was intentionally not powered to test the role of RT, since according to the authors, lack of published reports were available. In EORTC IFRT to multiple areas may have been too large of a field. EORTC H10, the trial that showed PFS benefit with INRT after CR in early stage HL, had higher powerer wth n=1137, while EORTC 20884 had n=421.

Out of concern for high late adverse effects many are hesitant to escalate. In HD12+9 late causes of death from 2nd malignancy and adverse effects were about double that of death from the disease regardless of RT use. However IFRT was in use.

A new trial with higher power and smaller INRT fields may be reasonable. It's possible that RT in CR could improve outcomes by mechanism of cytoreduction or stimulating an immune response. Until possibly then, there is not yet good evidence to suggest RT provides benefit in CR in advanced HL.

🏿 Entire cohort
⬆️ 2-yr PFS 83% vs. 92%

PFS for PR not yet reported

Grade ≥3 neutropenia 26% vs. 48%
Grade ≥3 peripheral neuropathy 8% (Br) vs. 1%

Hypothyroidism 7% and hyperthyroid 3% with N+AVD. Approx 0 thyroid disorders with Br+AVD

🏿 Pediatric cohort, ages 12-17
3-yr PFS 82% vs. 93%
⭐Stage III 3-yr PFS 91% vs. 98%
Stage IV 3-yr PFS 76% vs. 89%
Stage IVB 3-yr PFS 70% vs. 86%

Deauville 4-5 3-yr PFS of 37% vs. 43%

Protocol specified RT in 1.3% (n=2 vs. 1)
n=7 met criteria for RT but did not receive it

Grade ≥3 peripheral neuropathy 14% (Br) vs. 7%

trials.interpretation:
Nivolumab + AVD improves PFS compared to Br+AVD.

Similar results of pediatric cohort to the entire cohort shows that HL trials and regimens can include both adult and pediatric patients.

Consolidative radiation was only used in ≤1%, though the criteria for allowing radiation in the study were extremely strict.
trials.commentary:
SWOG 1826 and HD21 are groundbreaking clinical trials in advanced HL, showing 2 and 4-yr PFS of ≥90%. Adolescents and adults were eligible in SWOG 1826, ages ≥12. 68% had IPI 0-3, and 32% had IPI 4-7. Stage III had an outstanding 3-yr PFS of 98% in pediatrics! This does seem to validate omission of RT in this group and also in Stage I-II treated with this regimen.

The use of RT was low in the study. 3-yr PFS in Deauville 4-5 in peds was 43%. In the overall population 12% in the N arm were still Deauville 4-5. This could have been improved with broader use of RT, including less strict criteria for it.  An easy way to reduce the role of radiation is to require extremely strict criteria for it. It is to be acknowledged that the eventual goal in adult and pediatric trials is to increase cure while reducing late adverse effects, which involves reducing the use of radiation, though not at the cost of cure and risk of more other adverse effects later. We also need to develop transplant free protocols, which may entail consolidative radiation, especially in adults.

There were no instructions in the protocol for radiation planning. RT might be cytoreductive or also stimulate and immune response similar to nivolumab. RT was allowed, but not required, if all of the below specific criteria were met. The size criteria seem perhaps too restrictive. If all criteria were met, physicians were also optionally allowed to follow the LYRIC criteria, which propose instructions for assessing indeterminate response after immunotherapy (see Cheson 2016 - the LYRIC criteria are too lengthy to outline here). Clinicians however should use caution in applying the LYRIC criteria too liberally as confirmation bias to exclude RT. The LYRIC authors themselves write in their proposal that "There are not at present sufficient data to rigorously support the details of the choices made here."

All criteria must have been met to consider radiation:
1) Residual nodal mass ≥2.5 cm axial, or residual extranodal lesion >1 cm axial (e.g. lung or splenic nodule)
2) Deauville score 4-5
3) ≥30% reduction axial compared to pre-treatment
4) Only 1-2 nodal sites involved

HD21, which resulted 4-yr PFS of 94% with BrECADDx4, treated 14% with radiation. HD12+9 combined analysis showed improvement in PFS and OS with radiation for partial response.

Commentary last updated Jan 2026, Estes

trials.interpretation:
BrECADD has better efficacy than escBEACOPP and less adverse effects.

RT was required for refractory.

Results in PET+ were also excellent. This approach with radiation for refractory and PET4+ allowed many to avoid transplant.
trials.commentary:
SWOG 1826 and HD21 are groundbreaking clinical trials in advanced HL, showing 2 and 4-yr PFS of ≥90%, an achievement unthinkable not so many years ago.

41% were PET2+ and had six cycles. 30 Gy RT was required in refractory (in 15%) and the high PFS shows that many were able to avoid transplant with this approach. BrECADD plus RT for PR in HD21 has higher PFS than Br+AVD and optional RT in ECHELON - again even those PET positive in HD21 had higher PFS than Br+AVD!

In HD21, 54% were IPS 0-2, 47% were ≥3. In ECHELON 21% had IPS 0-1, 53% 2-3, and 26% had ≥4. In SWOG 1826, 68% had IPI 0-3, and 32% had IPI 4-7.

Compared to BEACOPP, BrECADD removes bleomycin and vincristine, and exchanges procarbazine for dacarbazine, and prednisone for dexamethasone. HD21 maintains RT as standard for PET PR refractory disease based on PFS benefit in HD12, and PFS and OS benefit in HD9 + 12 combined analysis.

For radiation planning the protocol recommends to follow the S3 guidelines, which recommend ISRT (Leitlinienprogramm Onkologie 2022).

trials.results:
Negative PET: ABVD vs. AVD

7-yr PFS 81.0% vs. 79.2%

7-yr 2nd malignancy 5.1% vs. 5.8%

trials.interpretation: AVD is noninferior to ABVD for interim PET negative advanced Hodgkin's lymphoma. RT was optional for refractory.
trials.commentary:
On the initial publication, 3-yr PFS was not noninferior, but with additional follow-up the 3-yr outcomes eventually became noninferior. RT was 30-36 Gy IFRT and given in 6.6%. Only 9% of those that received radiation relapsed, while the 7-yr PFS of the entire PET+ group was 66% (AHOD2131 protocol, 2023). Interestingly, BEACOPP for those PET+ had less secondary malignancy in this study.

The regimen has been adapted by some for use in early stage Hodgkin Lymphoma. However since long term results of EORTC H10 showed that radiotherapy should not be omitted, the regimen is less appropriate. In EORTC H10 the control arm in unfavorable used ABVDx6, a regimen not unlike RATHL's AVDx6 - meaning that RATHL also cannot replace radiotherapy. And using AVDx4 - a regimen designed for advanced Hodgkin - for favorable would seem to be over treatment compared to 2-3x ABVD plus INRT.

Since thus study, some use N+AVD + ISRT for unfavorable early stage HL per the phase II NIVAHL trial. In this study ISRT was required.
(Commentary last updated Oct 2025, Estes)

trials.patients: Biopsy proven relapsed or refractory HL
trials.methods:
Phase I/II: Salvage chemo → TLI + IFRT to 150 cGy BID → HD CIV chemo and ASCT

TLI was given in AM to 1500 cGy total and IFRT in PM to 3000-3400 cGy total
trials.results:
Most failures were within RT field
5- and 10-yr LC 78%

14/33 infield failures were at sites PET positive after salvage chemo

CR to chemo associated with improved OS and PFS

5/10/15-yr OS 73/68/58%
5/10/15-yr PFS 73/69/59%
5/10/15-yr EFS 72/68/58%

Secondary malignancy in 9%
(5 heme and 3 solid)
trials.interpretation:
TLI has favorable OS in refractory/relapsed HL, especially with CR to chemo.

However most failures were in field, and PFS continues to fall long term. New approaches should continue to be investigated.
trials.commentary:
This study is an eye opening evaluation concerning what occurs when radiation is given to biopsy proven relapsed or refractory disease. Given that this was TLI, it makes sense that most failures would be infield, but this is an indication that radiation is not eradicating the relapsed disease. This may mean that some dose escalation would be of benefit, that radiation should be TBI, or that some HL is resistant to radiation. The study is not showing that there is no benefit to radiation - as it is not randomized - but does illustrate that even TLI may not be a cure. HD12 and the HD12+9 analysis showed benefit with ISRT to refractory disease (not TLI). The mechanism of radiation might be cytoreductive and could also stimulate an immune response. The use of nivolumab in lymphoma suggest that lymphoma can be immunogenic (Ansell 2023).

TLI was to mantle, inverted Y, and spleen.

Interestingly OS, EFS, and PFS values are nearly identical. This suggests that any event will lead to soon death.

48% were PET positive after chemo

trials.interpretation: Administering RT only for PET positive refractory disease, and omitting for PET negative, maintains outcomes compared to RICOVER-60. This approach allows some to be spared CAR T.
trials.commentary:
Since this study, German guidelines now recommend radiation only for all refractory (PET positive, PRs) in DLBCL, and no RT for CR, regardless of bulky, extranodal status or age (Oertel 2023). The rationale is further justified by the British Colombia retrospective study (Freeman 2021). And in LYSA/ GOELAMS those with refractory disease on PET treated with RT had similar EFS and OS to those who had CR. This allows patients to be spared CAR T.

The study is a cohort comparison and not randomized. Patient characteristics were worse in OPTIMAL, with more IPI 3-5. Despite this results were maintained, and more were able to be spared RT when only treating those who were PET positive. The press release contains some additional findings not included in the abstracts.

The OPTIMAL interim analysis was considered to be firmly positive and continuation futile. A full publication was never submitted. I reached out to the authors for comment but did not receive a response. The British Colombia and LYSA/ GOELAMS studies also strengthen the approach.

🏿 RT randomization
Closed early due to excess failures without RT

(mainly due to lower PR rate in RT arm)
PR 11% vs. 2%
CR 79% vs. 90%

trials.interpretation:
In early bulky or extranodal NHL in ages 18-60, RT improves EFS, but not PFS or OS.

RT seemed to compenstate for refractory: these had identical survival to CRs and were able to avoid salvage therapy.

There was no benefit with RT in CRs. This study was performed prior to PET era.

In PMBCL RT improved EFS but not PFS or OS.

Results were consistent in extranodal.

There is no difference in RCHOP q14 days or q21 days.
trials.commentary:
DSHNHL: Deutsche (German) Study Group for NHL

This trial is the largest to assess the benefit of RT in extranodal and bulky disease in ages 18-60 in NHL in R era. It was conducted prior to PET era. About 70-75% had PET. Whether PET was obtained or not, response was assessed by CT.

Secondary malignancy was increased in the obs arm. Salvage therapies could have increased the risk of 2nd cancer. CAR T cell has reported secondary malignancies of 4-16% (Cappell & Kochenderfer 2023). Information is not provided on what salvage therapies were given.

The authors write that RT may have helped maintain PFS and OS in those with PR. After the interim analysis showing benefit with RT, the no RT arms were closed. RT was then mandated in those with bulky or extranodal disease, and RT for PR was not counted as an event.

It's unclear to me if PR triggering RT in the obs arm was counted as an event at the time of the interim analysis. In a commentary by Oertel and Eich (2024), their interpretation is that this was not counted as an event in the obs arm, which would bias favor to that arm. I reached out to the authors for clarification but did not receive a response. Although the reporting may be unclear, the point may be irrelevant: based on the OPTIMAL>60 study, German guidelines since then recommend RT for all with refractory disease, i.e. PET positive PR - and observation of CR - regardless of bulky or extranodal status or age (Oertel 2023).  The rationale is further justified by the British Colombia retrospective study (Freeman 2021).

This trial evaluates CR at 2 weeks after last RCHOP or at the time of first f/u after radiation. If PR or uCR after 6 cycles of chemo, perform additional testing in 4 weeks.

NHL summary
-Prior to rituxan, three studies looked at benefit of RT. SWOG showed OS benefit, ECOG showed PFS benefit, and GELA found no benefit with RT
-With rituxan, RT use has declined

-RICOVER shows PFS with RT in extranodal in ages >60.
-UNFOLDER found EFS benefit with RT in bulky and extranodal in ages 18-60 and in PMBCL. RT seemed to maintain outcomes when being used for PR
-GHSG meta-analysis shows benefit with RT in bony involvement in R era

trials.results:
OS improved with use of RT
Estimated 5-yr OS 82% chemoRT vs. 75% chemo

trials.interpretation: Chemo alone was associated with worse OS compared to when RT was given with chemo. Randomized trials are required for confirmation as adjustments for imbalances in database studies cannot remove all confounding variables.
trials.commentary: NCDB provides OS data only and no info on EFS, FFP, etc. Although an intriguing study, there is no information here regarding CR, PR, or bulky disease. The eras are hand selected and must guestimate was treatments were employed. Caution using large population observational studies: A review found that the conclusions of these were not better than chance at matching randomized trials, and no factors were found to improve conclusions (Soni 2019). This does not necessarily mean the reports worthless - they still contain more data than a single insitution retrospective report for example - but that the eras and parameters should be carefully selected, that the results should be considered something in the realm of hypothesis generating and exploratory, and that results absolutely cannot replace or disprove a randomized trial unless perhaps it was poorly undertaken.

trials.commentary: NCDB provides OS data only and no info on EFS, FFP, etc. Caution using large population observational studies: A review found that the conclusions of these were not better than chance at matching randomized trials, and no factors were found to improve conclusions (Soni et al, JCO, 2019). This does not necessarily mean the reports worthless - they still contain more data than a single insitution retrospective report for example - but that the eras and parameters should be carefully selected, that the results should be considered something in the realm of hypothesis generating and exploratory, and that results absolutely cannot replace or disprove a randomized trial unless perhaps it was poorly undertaken.

trials.commentary:
The EFS for those who had PR and received radiation was numerically higher than those who had CR with omission of RT, which should give caution to the findings. The authors' conclusion was that radiation could be omitted in CR, but the trial did not meet its endpoint for the CR portion. RT is still recommended for PR. PR was defined strictly at the time, as Deauville 1-2. Both EuroNet-PHL-C1 and AHOD0431 are nonrandomized trials regarding the radiation analysis. On 10-yr f/u of AHOD0431 for low risk pediatrics, there was benefit with IFRT in RER and SER at PET1 after AVPC. A prior COG randomized trial, CCG5942, also showed benefit in EFS with IFRT in low risk after CR from COPP/ABVx2. Likewise in adult early stage HL, some omitted radiation based on early results of EORTC H10, HD16, and UK RAPID, but 10-yr f/u of H10 showed that radiation improved PFS. There are concerns in pediatrics regarding late effects of radiation, and some oncologists favor a risk vs benefit approach.

Radiation planning. Although called IFRT in the protocol, the method is more similar to AP/PA INRT, as I have labeled it here. The protocol has detailed instructions for radiation planning.

Similar results of pediatric cohort to the entire cohort shows that HL trials and regimens can include both adult and pediatric patients.

Consolidative radiation was only used in ≤1%, though the criteria for allowing radiation in the study were extremely strict.
trials.commentary:
SWOG 1826 and HD21 are groundbreaking clinical trials in advanced HL, showing 2 and 4-yr PFS of ≥90%. Adolescents and adults were eligible in SWOG 1826, ages ≥12. 68% had IPI 0-3, and 32% had IPI 4-7. Stage III had an outstanding 3-yr PFS of 98% in pediatrics! This does seem to validate omission of RT in this group and also in Stage I-II treated with this regimen.

The use of RT was low in the study. 3-yr PFS in Deauville 4-5 in peds was 43%. In the overall population 12% in the N arm were still Deauville 4-5. This could have been improved with broader use of RT, including less strict criteria for it.  An easy way to reduce the role of radiation is to require extremely strict criteria for it. It is to be acknowledged that the eventual goal in adult and pediatric trials is to increase cure while reducing late adverse effects, which involves reducing the use of radiation, though not at the cost of cure and risk of more other adverse effects later. We also need to develop transplant free protocols, which may entail consolidative radiation, especially in adults.

There were no instructions in the protocol for radiation planning. RT might be cytoreductive or also stimulate and immune response similar to nivolumab. RT was allowed, but not required, if all of the below specific criteria were met. The size criteria seem perhaps too restrictive. If all criteria were met, physicians were also optionally allowed to follow the LYRIC criteria, which propose instructions for assessing indeterminate response after immunotherapy (see Cheson 2016 - the LYRIC criteria are too lengthy to outline here). Clinicians however should use caution in applying the LYRIC criteria too liberally as confirmation bias to exclude RT. The LYRIC authors themselves write in their proposal that "There are not at present sufficient data to rigorously support the details of the choices made here."

All criteria must have been met to consider radiation:
1) Residual nodal mass ≥2.5 cm axial, or residual extranodal lesion >1 cm axial (e.g. lung or splenic nodule)
2) Deauville score 4-5
3) ≥30% reduction axial compared to pre-treatment
4) Only 1-2 nodal sites involved

HD21, which resulted 4-yr PFS of 94% with BrECADDx4, treated 14% with radiation. HD12+9 combined analysis showed improvement in PFS and OS with radiation for partial response.

High response rates were observed with nivolumab plus BV in relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma.

trials.commentary:
Although phase II thus far, some are interested in this approach to omit radiation.

Radiation for low risk relapsed and refractory disease allowed 84% to avoid SCT in AHOD0431, and ISRT is still required for SER in open protocol AHOD2131. The Checkmate 744 approach does not allow those with standard risk and good response to avoid transplant.

Response can be difficult to assess after nivolumab. The LYRIC criteria propose instructions for assessing indeterminate response from immunotherapy (see Cheson 2016 - the criteria are too lengthy to outline here). Clinicians however should use caution in applying the LYRIC criteria too liberally as an excuse to exclude RT without evidence. The LYRIC authors themselves write in their proposal that "There are not at present sufficient data to rigorously support the details of the choices made here."

trials.interpretation:
VAC/VI chemotherapy has less adverse effects than VAC and maintains EFS and OS.

LF with VAC/VI was unexplainably worse in ARST 0531 than in D9803; this may be due to confounders.

In the subsequent trial ARST 1431, VAC/VI is the chemo regimen. Boost is allowed for size >5 cm. Week 13 is chosen for RT to allow for assessment of feasibility of temsirolimus, complex RT planning, and possible delayed primary excision.

In a post-hoc analysis of reduced dose RT after CR in 0531 & 1431, reduced dose radiation to 36 Gy had improved EFS and OS and similar LC.
trials.commentary:
Even though LF was worse in 0531 than D9803, VAC/VI chemo is incorporated into new protocol ARST 1431. The authors are uncertain as to why LF was worse than in D9803. There was no change in LF in the 0531 or D9803 randomizations themselves. This trial illustrates the problem with historical controls. This method of analysis is reasonable in pediatrics because pediatric patients tend to be more uniform and without other comorbidites, whereas randomized trials are preferred in adults due to more confounding variables. The authors admit it can be problematic to compare outcomes from two different trials using adjustments, but reinforce that their intention was indeed to improve LC on 0531 from D9803, which was not achieved. In the next trial, 1431, boost is allowed for tumors >5 cm and delayed primary excision encouraged. No difference in outcomes in timing of RT.

-At 15 years, with RT vs. surgery, there is no difference in PCM, DM, disease progression, ADT salvage, or all deaths.

-AS had worse DM, disease progression, and ADT compared to RP and RT. However 15-yr PCM and all cause mortality were similar.

15-yr clinical progression 21% vs. 8.0% vs. 8.4%

10-yr all deaths 11% vs. 10% vs. 10%
15-yr all deaths 16% vs. 15% vs. 15%
Results similar in per protocol analysis

•Subanalysis
No difference by PSA, stage, Gleason grade group, or risk stratification (2023)

•QOL
6-yr ED 53% vs. 85% vs. 74% (35% at start)
7-yr erections 30% vs. 18% vs. 27%
ED converges at 12 years
immediate ED 95% RP vs. 69% RT+ADT

6-yr fecal incontinence 4% AS vs. 10% EBRT
6-yr loose stools 13% AS vs. 16% EBRT
EBRT 6-yr bloody stool 6%
RP 6-yr GU incontinence 20% (none with RT)
Nocturia initially worse with RT, but similar to AS by year 6
trials.interpretation:
RT+ADT and radical prostatectomy show no difference in prostate cancer mortality or DM. Active surveillance had worse DM and ADT salvage, but this did not lead to worse PCM at 15 years.

RT+ADT and surgery have differing adverse effect profiles. Surgery has worse incontinence and sexual dysfunction. RT+ADT also leads to some ED at mid term f/u, then ED eventually converges.

RT has slightly worse long term loose stool, blood in stool, and GI incontinence compared to AS. Late nocturia is similar between RT and AS. 12-yr adverse effects results were similar.
trials.commentary:
Patient characteristics & effects. There was no difference on subanalysis by Gleason grade group, showing that the results apply to both low and intermediate risk. Most of the patients fit low risk criteria. 77% were Gleason 6, 20% had Gleason 7, 2% had Gleason 8-10.  <1% were black.

Active surveillance. There was selection bias favoring the AS group: it featured more favorable tumors. But despite the better characteristics handicap, plus the crossovers in the group to treatment, the AS group still performed worse. In AS, 55% eventually received treatment. Of these, 49% had surgery, 33% had protocol RT, 9% had non-protocol RT, 8% had brachythearpy, 1% (n=3) had HIFU. Use caution comparing efficacy to other active surveillance series as not all patients were low risk. Remember, the trial included 20% Gleason 7, which are less suitable for AS than Gleason 6.

Methods. 78% were randomized, and the remainder chose their therapy. The randomized and choice cohorts were analyzed separately (most of the data displayed here is from the randomized cohort or combined cohorts).

Radiation. Dose escalation was not used. IMRT and dose escalation should be expected to produce even better results.

ADT. ADT was added to RT in this trial, but it does not have clear benefit in low or favorable intermediate risk, and thus should not have biased those results. ADT may have improved some outcomes for the few higher risk patients. Sexual adverse effects with RT in the study may be over-represented due to use of ADT.

Sexual function. Sexual function was better with radiation over RP. Some of the worsening of ED in the RT group could be attributed to the 3-6 months of ADT included with RT. Recognize also that some of the impairment of sexual function in the AS group is not all due to aging and will be due to eventual receipt of treatment, especially RP (49% had RP). Most of the prostatectomies were nerve-sparing (205 were bilateral, 53 unilateral, and 12 unspecified out of 324). In the PACE-A trial, which compared SBRT without ADT to RP (86% nerve sparing), radiation had less sexual dysfunction compared to RP (As 2023).

Salvage therapies. Salvage radiation was given in only 5 patients. Salvage surgery was given after radiation in 3 patients. ADT salvage was in 6-9%.
(Commentary last updated 2024, Estes)

Grade 3-4 adverse effects 40% vs. 31%
Urinary incontinence grade 1-2 in about 50% both arms
Urinary incontinence grade 3 in 1-2% both arms

Median time to testosterone recovery from end of 12 mos ADT 8.1 vs. 6.6 mos

Testosterone recovery in ~82% in both arms

Any subsequent therapy 42% vs. 57%

Post op radiation 11% vs. 21% (of all patients)
(Calculated from Table s4 by me)
Post op radiation 27% vs. 37% (of those who had any additional treatment)
trials.interpretation: Peri-op apalutamide added to ADT improved response rates, downstaging, R1, MFS, and EFS.
trials.commentary:
There was no standard of care arm without any ADT or comparison to radiation + ADT. Pre or peri-op ADT has not shown benefit over surgery only in a randomized trial. Note the eligibility criteria - not all high risk were eligible.

The need for adjuvant or salvage radiation was reduced, but radiation therapy was at discretion. There were no RT planning instructions of any kind in the protocol or reporting of any RT details in the manuscript. Therefore the rate of salvage RT is more of an exploratory endpoint. ADT did reduce positive margins.

ADT can cause cell death through necrosis and other mechanisms and delay recurrence, but does not completely eradicate disease. It may also begin a path toward early androgen pathway modulation resistance (Zhang 2011). pCR was not an endpoint, and "pCR or MRD" was low in both arms. R0 was improved with ADT. In contrast SBRT to 40 Gy in five fractions leads to a pCR of 92% (Zelefsky 2019). One might respond that prolonged time to recurrence is also meaningful; however, this may not be worth the worsening of QOL from ADT, lack of cure, and potential earlier androgen pathway modulation resistance. 18% had long lasting testosterone deficiency (which would also occur with RT+ADT). Results may continue to change with additional follow-up.

MFS was detected by conventional imaging or PSMA PET. Freedom from disease was also reported, but MFS was an appropriate and better primary endpoint (Basak 2021). PSMA PET was used in most, 65% vs. 72%. After biochemical failure imaging was then performed every six months. Some have made the assertion that MFS early detection with PSMA PET is essentially an EFS endpoint and may not be a surrogate for OS (Kishan and Vapiwala 2026). Or in other words, stage migration minimized the effect. However if PSMA PET was not used, the study would have been criticized as outdated. PSMA PET has a role to detect oligometastatic disease early for treatment with SBRT for PFS benefit  (EXTEND, ARTO, STOMP, ORIOLE). An OS benefit may not occur until later f/u, and additional salvage therapies in both arms can lead to similar survival. Likewise for example FLAME and ASCENDE showed a benefit in DFS and BPFS only respectively, not OS or DM. SBRT for oligometastatic disease improves PFS but there is low evidence thus far for OS benefit. Point being that PSMA PET MFS is a good endpoint - a radiation trial with improved MFS would be celebrated. But the bigger picture still must be considered.

The authors reported adverse effects during treatment but not late adverse effects. Only about 50-55% experienced urinary incontinence during treatment.

Results do appear promising overall, though ultimately there was no standard of care arm of surgery without ADT or radiation + ADT. ADT did reduce positive margins. pCR was not reported, and pCR+MRD was very low. 18% did not recover testosterone. A comparison to surgery alone and radiation + ADT is of interest. The authors are applauded for their contributions and this large trial.
(Commentary last updated Aug 2026, Estes)

trials.commentary:
Dose escalation summary
-A number of single and multi institutional studies show improvement in BPFS with dose escalation (MDACC, GETUG, Dutch CKVO, MRC, Ontario, Fox Chase)
-RTOG designed a multi-institutional protocol somewhat later: RTOG 0126. The protocol allowed IMRT in an amendment. Some of its publications focus on the effects of IMRT
-Further increase in dose esclation is sought out with brachytherapy boost. Again, there is a conflict between increase in adverse effects, improved BPFS, and no confirmed OS benefit. (ASCENDE-RT, RTOG 0232, McMaster University, Mount Vernon)
-SBRT is also investigated as a means of dose escalation (HYPO-RT-PC, PACE B, RTOG 0938)
-FLAME showed a bDFS benefit in MRI guided boost to the nodule

Why dose escalate if there is no survival benefit and adverse effects are increased? RTOG 0126 and MDACC showed benefit in DM, and PCSM benefit in the MDACC study, but of uncertain validity. BPFS is believed by some to be a surrogate for OS (Buyyounouski 2012, Denham 2008, Shilkrut 2016). However, these sorts of effects of surrogates would not be expected to manifest until later f/u or require higher power. The increase in adverse effects with dose escalation with EBRT is considered to still be low, with benefits outweighing the risks.

trials.interpretation: Focal boost to tumor on MRI improves bDFS. Late GU adverse effects may be slightly higher. There was no benefit in DMFS or OS.
trials.commentary:
Only 20% actually reached 95 Gy. There was no CTV or PTV margin from the GTV nodule for the high dose SIB. Sparing of OARs was prioritized over covering the nodule with high dose. Dose constraints were by institution and are located in the supplemental appendix. None employed a urethral constraint. IMRT or VMAT was used in all. Because of this, there might be some question regarding the reproducibility or future consistency of the results. Nonetheless it would seem that very good results should still be achieved if one maintains adequate constraints in planning, though there could be some uncertainty regarding the urethra. High dose escalation is already employed in SBRT. An important metric, DMFS, was not different though could possibly show improvement with additional follow-up. Although not significant, adverse effects were slightly worse with dose escalation - and without DM or OS benefit. An argument could be made that dose escalation should not be employed without a DM or OS benefit with increased adverse effects. Some consider BPFS to be a surrogate for DM and OS, but this was not the case in ASCENDE, likely due to salvage therapy, but may help avoid later ADT.

Urethra dosimetry. On secondary analysis, the authors found that increasing urethra dose correlated to GU adverse effects, without threshhold (Groen 2021). They recommended urethra D0.1cc ≤ 80 Gy and bladder D2cc ≤ 80 Gy. However, one can also see that this suggestion seems to conflict in some way with the existence of SBRT for prostate cancer, which has BED doses much greater that 80 Gy, and thus far has been shown to be safe but with slightly increased mild adverse effects (PACE B, As, 2024).

The initial 4 field phase consisted of 11 x 11 cm A/P beams and 11 x 9 cm laterals. In the 70 Gy arm, the boost was a 9 x 9 cm box. In the 78 Gy arm, the  boost was 3D CRT with CTV to block edge margin of 1.25-1.5 cm ant/inf and 0.75-1.0 cm post/sup.
trials.notes:
Dose escalation summary
-A number of single and multi institutional studies show improvement in BPFS with dose escalation (MDACC, GETUG, Dutch CKVO, MRC, Ontario, Fox Chase)
-RTOG designed a multi-institutional protocol somewhat later: RTOG 0126. The protocol allowed IMRT in an amendment. Some of its publications focus on the effects of IMRT
-Further increase in dose esclation is sought out with brachytherapy boost. Again, there is a conflict between increase in adverse effects, improved BPFS, and no confirmed OS benefit. (ASCENDE-RT, RTOG 0232, McMaster University, Mount Vernon)
-SBRT is also investigated as a means of dose escalation (HYPO-RT-PC, PACE B, RTOG 0938)
-FLAME showed a bDFS benefit in MRI guided boost to the nodule

Why dose escalate if there is no survival benefit and adverse effects are increased? RTOG 0126 and MDACC showed benefit in DM, and PCSM benefit in the MDACC study, but of uncertain validity. BPFS is believed by some to be a surrogate for OS (Buyyounouski 2012, Denham 2008, Shilkrut 2016). However, these sorts of effects of surrogates would not be expected to manifest until later f/u or require higher power. The increase in adverse effects with dose escalation with EBRT is considered to still be low, with benefits outweighing the risks.

trials.citation:
Morris et al, IJROBP, 2017
Rodda et al, IJROBP, 2017
Oh et al, IJROBP, 2022
trials.patients:
intermediate and high risk prostate cancer

(66% high risk and 33% int risk)

Excluded: T3b, T4, PSA>40, prior TURP
trials.methods:
12 mos ADT + 46 Gy WPRT then:

➜ LDR boost (115 Gy I-125)
vs.
➜ EBRT boost (78 Gy total)
trials.results:
No difference in OS, CSS, or DM
BPFS improved
10-yr MFS 88% vs. 86%, p=0.56
10-yr CSS 94% vs. 91%, p=0.26
10-yr OS ~75%, not different
15-yr bPFS 85% vs. 67%

Worse adverse effects with LDR
5-yr cumulative grade 3 GU adverse effects 18% vs. 5% (SS), prevalence of grade 3 GU adverse effects 8.6% vs. 2.2% (p=.58),
5-yr any pad usage 16% vs. 3% (SS),
5-yr late catheterization 12% vs. 3% (SS)

cumulative grade 3 GI adverse effects 8.1% vs. 3.2% (p=.124), prevalence grade 3 GI 1.0% vs. 2.2%

Similar erectile function 45% vs. 37% (p=.30)
trials.interpretation:
LDR boost with EBRT substantially improved BC compared to EBRT alone. However there was no improvement in long term MFS, CSS, or OS.

LDR led to a marked increase in GU adverse effects and trended towards worse GI adverse effects.
trials.commentary:
BF was improved and there was some trend to benefit in CSS, p=0.26. Adverse effects were significantly increased. ASCENDE and GETUG P05 did use dose escalated EBRT in their control arms, unlike the McMaster and Mt Vernon trials. There is no benefit in 15-yr DM. Even if there is no benefit in DM, OS, or CSS long term, improved BF may still be useful to avoid or delay more ADT and it's adverse effects for some, but the increase in adverse effects from brachy may not be worth the risk.

For those who do recommend brachytherapy, another question concerns whether intermediate risk really need an escalation in dose. In PACE B 70% of patients were unfavorable intermediate risk, excluding Gleason 4+3=7, and had excellent bPFS without any ADT, suggesting SBRT is sufficient. RTOG 0924 showed no benefit with WPRT, thus the WPRT portion is not needed for most. POP RT did show benefit with WPRT in those staged with PSMA PET but may be underpowered.

Sleep is one of the most important functions the body performs, and a meta-analysis showed that nocturia probably increases the RR of death by 1.3 (Pesonen 2020, see also TROG RAVES and GETUG AFU 17), which could have washed out benefit. One view is that since adverse effects are highly increased in ASCENDE, GETUG P05, and the McMaster and Mt Vernon trials, without improvement in OS or DM, that other regimens should instead be used that have much lower adverse effects and identical OS/DM, even if BPFS is inferior to brachy (Hamstra 2017).

The other view is that cure is the primary goal, and that escalation of therapy for optimal cure is key. BPFS is believed by some to be a surrogate for for OS or DM (Buyyounouski 2012, Denham 2008, Shilkrut 2016). However the trial does not show this at 10-15 years, perhaps due to ADT salvage and deconditioning from nocturia. If one asks practitioners who perform brachytherapy, some might claim it is technique dependent and not their brachytherapy. ("The king is dead - long live the king"). However other trials reproduced findings of increased adverse effects. These studies would be expected to be performed at expert centers. The urethra, bladder, and rectum will always be within or adjacent to the prostate to some degree - minimizing a max dose of a large number is still a large number. Some of the adverse effects in LDR are due to the needles themselves and their quanity (Eapen 2004, Ohashi 2006).

The BC Cancer Agency Candadian study compared HDR vs LDR boost. LDR had faster GU recovery initially, but GU QOL was similar at 18 months (Crook 2024). SpaceOAR could reduce bowel adverse effects.
(Commentary last updated Oct 2026, Estes)

Meta-analysis of ten phase III trials

Patient characteristics were balanced, though ADT use differed
trials.methods:
Meta-analysis of phase III trials

➜ conventional RT (some dose-escalated, some not)
vs.
➜ hypofractionated RT (various BEDs)
trials.results:
No differences in BF, BCF, OS, PCSM, acute GU, or late GU or late GI
F/u of 5 years for most studies

There was heterogeneity in acute and late GI adverse effects.
No heterogeneity in BF, BCF, OS, PCSM, or acute or late GU adverse effects.

trials.interpretation: Hypofx RT leads to similar outcomes as conventional RT in this meta-analysis. However acute GI adverse effects are increased with ADT or inclusion of SV.
trials.commentary:
Caution in the applicability of these results. Regimen designs differed among individual trials. Some trials used non-dose-escalated RT as the standard arm, others used dose escalated. The hypofractionated regimens were designed with various purposes: either to be isoeffective to late tissue effects, to non-dose escalated RT, or to dose escalated RT. There is heterogeneity in GI acute and late effects. There was no heterogeneity in BCF or OS. GI late effects may be able to be mitigated with IMRT and rectal spacer, though the urethra and bladder neck cannot be avoided.

Adverse effects may be unmasked more with wider difference in hypofractionation: PACE B, published after this study, showed about 10% worsening of Grade ≥2 GU and GI adverse effects with SBRT (Fig S10). The authors still considered the results noninferior, but some may wish to ask the patient for their opinion.

Follow-up lengths at the time of this meta-analysis were 5 years. There is a possibility that outcomes could differ at later timepoints. Conventional dose escalation studies show benefit in DM, PCSM, and OS in various studies. Hypofractionated schedules found to be equivalent or noninferior to non-dose-escalated conventional RT should not be routinely adopted.
