trials.commentary:
In PCS 5 acute and late adverse effects were the primary endpoints; efficacy outcomes were secondary endpoints. After low adverse effects events in both arms, the noninferiority analysis was determined to be underpowered and dropped. Indeed, the trial seems as though it could be underpowered at 329 patients (FLAME had n=571, PACE 874, PROFIT 1200, and CHHIP 3200). RTOG 0415 used similar dosing to prostate only, 70 Gy/ 28 fx, and had slight increases in late adverse effects. Still, outcomes seem favorable and may be satisfactory enough to offer this hypofractionated regimen for some, though a formal conclusion cannot be determined. GI late effects may be able to be mitigated with IMRT and rectal spacer, though the urethra and bladder neck cannot be avoided. POP-RT used a similar WPRT SIB regimen.

The control arm used 76 Gy, a fraction lower than traditional dose escalation. Past dose escalation studies that showed OS, DM, and PSCM benefit used 78-80 Gy. The MDACC trial showed benefit in late 15- and 20-yr DM and PSCM. RTOG 0126 showed benefit in 10- and 15-yr DM. GETUG 18 showed benefit in 10-yr CSS and OS.

trials.commentary:
Out of the hypofractionation trials for prostate cancer, PROFIT has the best results: the control arm was dose escalated, it was a noninferiority trial rather than superiority, BPFS was noninferior, and adverse effects were not increased. GI QOL and adverse effects favor hypofractionation. No other hypofx trial holds these criteria.

If one wanted to form an argument to support long course radiation, it can be noted that RTOG 0415 showed a small but present increase in adverse effects, as did PACE B compared to long course radiation.  The fractionation regimen in PROFIT is more hypofractionated than in RTOG 0415. The investigators considered the adverse effects to not be clinically significant. The CHiPP trial was powered more (n=3216) than PROFIT and showed noninferiority of 60 Gy in 20 fx vs non dose escalated radiation. But if 60 Gy represents a dose escalated regimen, one would think it should display some superiority to non dose escalated radiation.  Still the PROFIT regimen has excellent evidence in support and is a reasonable alternative. One might consider recommending long course radiation in those with high AUA scores or diabetes.

PROFIT and the other hypofx trials including SBRT are important contributions to making prostate cancer therapy more convenient for patients.

trials.commentary:
Late adverse effects were slightly increased in the hypofractionated arm. Some effects may be able to be mitigated with rectal spacer and IMRT, though the urethra and bladder neck will not be able to be avoided. The standard arm in this trial was not dose escalated, though BED of the hypofx arm is similar to conventional dose escalation. Conventional dose escalation studies show benefit in DM, PCSM, and OS in various studies (RTOG 0126, MDACC, GETUG 17). Hypofractionated schedules found to be equivalent or noninferior to non-dose-escalated conventional RT should be carefully considered.

Dose constraints are each 1 Gy different from conventional: https://ascopubs.org/doi/suppl/10.1200/jco.2016.67.0448/suppl_file/Protocol_2016.670448.pdf#page=18

The study also shows possible limitations of QOL as an endpoint. Even though QOL did not differ, physician assessed late effects did. Amdur and Chera (2019) write that QOL measurements can display the fallacy of reification: although treated as an objective value, ultimately it is still subjective. QOL also follows the adaptation principle, which means that people tend to see their state in view of their recent baseline, not from where they began.

trials.commentary:
This randomized trial finally established SBRT as a standard treatment option. Surprisingly extra dose escalation doesn't offer an additional benefit in bFPS, but could at later follow-up. There is some increased risk of acute and late adverse effects with 5 fractions. Conventional fractionation can be useful for patients who want the lowest risk of adverse effects possible, but the increased risk is not enough to only offer conventional. Clinicians should also be mindful of deciding for the patient that grade 1-2 adverse effects don't matter: sleep is one of the most important functions the body performs, and a meta-analysis showed that nocturia probably increases the RR of death by 1.3 (Pesonen 2020, see also TROG RAVES and GETUG AFU 17). The information should merely be presented as-is, and only the patient can decide. SBRT is a remarkable innovation to make treatment more approachable.

ADT was not permitted and DM was only 1%. 70% of all patients were unfavorable intermediate, though Gleason 4+3=7 was excluded. Genetic testing is probably warranted to stratify patients for ADT. SpaceOAR was not in use, and there were no grade ≥3 GI late effects. See also PACE A reproducing the results.

BPFS. PACE created a new definition of biochemical failure: before 24 months, PSA failure requires confirmation with 3 consecutive rises to rule out PSA bounce. Efficacy or toxicity findings could change with longer follow-up, but five years is a very good period. There is evidence that SBRT lowers PSA absolute value more than prolonged fractionation (Moore 2023), but whether this has an effect on BPFS, DM, or OS remains to be elucidated (In ASCENDE there was benefit in BPFS, but not OS or DM). There are no randomized trials as of yet comparing SBRT vs brachy boost.

Radiaton planning. Fiducials were used in 73% of SBRT and 57% of VMAT. Treatment was on alternating days in 75%, and daily in 25%. There's no report thus far on if late effects differ with scheduling. There were actually worse adverse effects with fiducial use (Ratnakumaran 2023). Alison Tree commented on X (2024) that use of alpha blockers in grade 2 can lead to confounding findings, but that she actually treats most patients now without fiducials with MRI guidance. trials.interpretation: Sequencing ADT adjuvantly results in better DM, PFS, and BF than neoadjuvant or concurrent treatment.
trials.commentary:
This combined reanalysis of two trials delivers a result that challenges conventional wisdom, that ADT should be administered after radiation. Such a method may cause practitioners anxiety, that start to treatment is being delayed while fiducials and radiation planning are underway, or while healing takes place for adjuvant radiation when PSA is perhaps even as low as 0.05.

Should the results be doubted because the combined analysis wasn't preplanned? Cancer cells don't know if an analysis was planned or not. "P hacking" is an artifact of human imagination, a term for inevitable type 1 and 2 errors that one hopes for a result they don't like. Yet in this case, the new analysis does match the original randomizations.

How could delay in ADT be beneficial? From a radiation biology standpoint, perhaps cells need to be mitotically active to experience cell death from radiation. Another theory is that the benefit with radiation in prostate cancer is partially due to stimulating an immune reaction, and for this to be successful, cells may need to be present. We know from sipuleucel-T (Provenge, Kantoff 2010) that prostate cancer cells are indeed immunogenic. In node positive patients neoadjuvant ADT can lead to less accurate radiation planning if nodes are difficult to identify. This wouldn't be the only kind of cancer that shows a detriment or no benefit with neoadjuvant systemic therapy (EORTC 55994 in definitive cervix; PARADIGM, DeCIDE in H&N; CALGB 39801 in lung, to reference a few). If oncologists continue to doubt the findings, randomized trials are urgently called for. Otherwise, we can speed up our time to fiducials and treatment while providing careful reassurance to the patient and other oncologists.

trials.interpretation:
On the prespecified analysis, WPRT improved 4-yr PFS over PO RT, but the effect was lost at later follow-up.

ADT can be delivered neoadj-concurrent or adjuvant. There were no differences in PFS between delivery times in the prespecified analysis.

There was no benefit in DM at any follow-up point.

Post-hoc analyses to compare the four arms together at long term f/u resulted in unexpected interactions. WPRT+adj ADT led to worse PFS and OS. At 10 years the best PFS was seen in PO RT + adj ADT and WPRT + NC ADT. The trial was not powered or designed for this comparison.
trials.commentary:
This trial has a history of controversy due to its statistical approaches. An important finding of 9413 that is often overlooked was that ADT can be administered either before or after radiation without differences. A later combined analysis of 9413 and an Ottawa trial reported that outcomes are superior when ADT is delivered after radiation (Spratt 2020). The WPRT randomization was later repeated in RTOG 0924 with stricter eligibility criteria and reproduced no difference. PSMA PET was not used in the study. POP-RT had higher risk patients than 9413 and used PSMA PET staging. The trial found a benefit with WPRT, but may have been underpowered.

28% had Gleason <7, "mini" WPRT was allowed, and PSMA PET was not yet in use, which all likely confounded this study. No DM benefit was ever detected at any point in any arm, a key endpoint. This study was not powered to find differences between 4 arms. A popular criticism of the study surrounds its post-hoc subanalyses and statistical approach toward them, leading to inconsistent and nonintuitive results. The p values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. It seems illogical that if a 2x2 comparison was nonsignificant, then a full 4 arm comparison could then somehow be significant. To conclude from the discussion that unplanned subanalyses are worthless however would be an oversight. The term "unplanned" is too pejorative - they're better labeled as post-hoc or exploratory. The rationales, p values, and CIs will tell the story. Underpowered analyses and subanalyses, both prespecified and post-hoc/unplanned, are common to see in studies, past and present. Beware of bias - it can be tempting to accept an unpowered or unplanned subanalysis when it meets ones views, and dismiss it when it does not. Beware listening to the loudest voices. The standards for post-hoc analysis have improved, and plenty of useful ones exist (consider STAMPEDE, NSABP B51, 9413, 9413 & Ottawa, PORTECs, even EBCTCG), some of which lack modern standards (EORTC 22931 RTOG 9501). Nature does not have a clear cutoff for significance, and cancer cells don't know whether a sentient human pre- vs post-planned a statistical analysis. A p value of ≤.05 is often standard, but a professional gambler would be elated to say the least of a p value of .06. In any case, results are descriptive.

A secondary analysis showed that there was a step-wise improvement in PFS with prostate only, "mini-pelvis", and whole pelvis radiation. Since this study, PSMA mapping has shown that 25% of nodes are actually periaortic (Schiller 2020).

The compliance rate of 36 mos ADT was only 53%, further reinforcing the realistically low feasibility of the approach.

The trial might have been better designed as noninferiority. Some have interpreted the trial in such a way, and consider 18 mos ADT for high risk prostate cancer as a risk vs adverse effects decision. Quadshot editors comment that if the trial was designed as noninferiority, it does not appear that the delta range would have been reached at the five year timepoint. ADT leads to a change in QOL with significant adverse effects, and recovery is markedly prolonged with 36 mos ADT.

trials.methods:
Meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials

➜ RT alone
vs.
➜ 🏆 RT with ≤6 mos ADT
trials.results:

OS HR 0.88, BF HR 0.50, BF+bPFS HR 0.54

On subgroup analysis, ADT duration, RT dose, and Gleason score were associated with improved PSA response, but no factor was associated with OS
trials.interpretation: Adding short term ADT to radiation for intermediate risk prostate cancer improves OS, PFS, and BF.
trials.commentary:
This meta analysis provides very good evidence for an OS benefit for ADT in intermediate risk prostate cancer, shortly after RTOG 0815 showed a 5-yr DM benefit but no benefit in 5-yr OS. All trials were prior to the widespread implementation of PSMA PET, therefore some tumors could be understaged and show more than expected benefit. Similarly in all prostate trials and meta-analyses innovations will advance faster than the trials, and more next line therapies are now available since the publication of the individual trials, lengthening OS in both arms.

It's unclear if the results apply to all intermediate risk or if the group should be further stratified. The study authors wrote that separating into favorable and unfavorable intermediate risk in the study was not possible. DM was unable to be analyzed due incomplete reporting. Although there are mixed results from randomized trials for the existance of favorable vs unfavorable intermediate risk (see RTOG 0815), conceptually it is difficult to rationalize active surveillance in low risk followed by immediate escalation to radiation plus short term ADT as soon as the patient upstages. On the other hand the idea that RT and ADT are best in combination should also not be dismissed. QOL must also be taken into account, and some patients may not even consider a 2-5% benefit in OS worth the adverse effects, especially if they have a friend or family member who had a negative experience. The meta analysis does suggest that effects differ by Gleason score for PSA response, but not for OS. The bottom line is that there appears to be an OS benefit. Today genomic testing is likely the future of prognostication in prostate cancer, in combination with PSMA PET.

The trials included RTOG 9408, DFCI 95-096, TROG 96.01, PCS III, EORTC 22991, RTOG 0815, and GETUG-14

trials.commentary:
This trial was prior to the era of PSMA PET. Patient characteristics are not yet shared. There are some nuances regarding who were eligible. T staging was by palpation only. Even at the time of presentation of this abstract, the staging system is in need of an update to integrate PSMA PET and MRI (if PET or MRI detects SVI, would that not change your management?). In the study T2c-T4 were considered too advanced and were ineligible unless Gleason 6 only. However, Gleason 9-10 T1c-2b were allowed. Because this trial did not allow PSMA PET and MRI for staging, hypothetical image-only-detected T3a-b, N+, and M1 would have met eligibility and lessened the power of the study. In summary many high risk were excluded, and others, even those N+ or metastatic by today's precision PSMA PET imaging, would have reached eligibility. Medicine often moves faster than outcomes of clinical trials, which is not a fault, and only descriptive.

In the modern era, PSMA PET may be what is needed to reasonably stratify those who will benefit from WPRT, although there is suggestion of benefit with WPRT in negative PSMA PET from POP-RT. In POP-RT 80% had PSMA PET, and the study had higher risk patients than 9413 and GETUG, but the trial enrolled only n=224 and may have been underpowered. One could rationalize elective WPRT for T3-4, highest Gleason scores, and high Decipher score, but RTOG 0924 certainly narrows support for elective WPRT. WPRT may warrant another randomized trial, next time with higher risk patients, PSMA staging, and perhaps genetic and molecular staging.
(Commentary last updated Oct 2025, Estes)

trials.commentary:
The trial may be underpowered. A strength is that PSMA PET staging was used. How was this study possibly positive when RTOG 9413 was not? The estimated pelvic nodal risk in this study (55% had >35% LN risk) was higher than in RTOG 9413 (25% had >35% risk) and GETUG (10%). 80% had PSMA PET. 90% had Gleason 7-10 and 49% had Gleason 8-10. (In 9413, 72% were Gleason 7-10, and in GETUG, 51% were 7-10 and 11% were Gleason 8-10.) RTOG 0924 enrolled lower risk patients than POP RT and did not use PSMA PET. But again, the trial could be underpowered.

The Roach formula would allow for inclusion of an intermediate risk patient with a PSA of >15, but does not differentiate between 3+4 and 4+3=7. It is unclear if 4+3=7 needs WPRT. Other methods such as genetic testing may better help to stratify patients in the future.

Note that the dose was hypofractionated. A similar regimen was later tested in PCS V and found to be noninferior, but results may be underpowered. ADT was given for ≥24 mos duration. About 20% had orchiectomy.

trials.commentary:
Trial hypothesis. Is there a difference in efficacy between starting RT at PSA of 0 vs. PSA of 0.2? Other than reducing adverse effects and sparing some from radiation, the answer is no.

Background. Urologists believed a positive margin or EPE could be benign, and rad oncs worried the worst cells could be growing for months. A meta-analysis of timing of salvage radiation had shown worse prognosis with rising PSA, particularly above 0.2 (King 2012). Obviously those with rising PSA will have worse outcomes, but the study did not show evidence against observation and selecting those with actual progression. Urologists hesitated due to complications they observed, eventually leading to the studies at hand.

High risk. Since relatively few high and very high risk were included, do these apply? Estes's opinion: Shoulda said no (to adjuvant). Since the adverse effects from early adjuvant radiation is so profound, delay to radiation is strongly preferred if feasible. ADT after surgery should provide a safe method to delay radiation for a high risk patient while healing proceeds. Additionally, adapt to modern diagnostic methods and use PET imaging to assess whether only a focal area of gross disease could be targeted.

Compare the results here to that of SPPORT: the EFS values in SPPORT are not as favorable. The SPPORT population was somewhat worse prognosis because they were true salvage pts with higher PSAs. Some may remark that the results may not apply to higher Gleason grades due to lower numbers included in the trial. However observe that there were similar higher risk Gleason scores in RAVES, GETUG, and RADICALS as in prior SWOG, EORTC, and ARO.

There is actually trend to benefit in DM with adjuvant radiation, but results are statistically insignificant, and there is no benefit in 10-yr PFS.

Does ADT improve outcomes in salvage RT? Results are mixed but seem to favor 24 mos ADT. In RADICALS, the largest trial, 24 mos ADT vs. none improved MFS, but 6 mos ADT vs. none showed no improvement. There was no difference in benefit based on subanalysis of PSA, Gleason score, or margins. There was no benefit in OS. In RTOG 9601, 24 mos bicalutamide improved DM and OS. In RTOG SPORT, 6 mos ADT + prostate bed RT vs. prostate bed RT did not improve DM, but 6 mos ADT + WPRT did. In GETUG 16, 6 mos ADT improved DM but not OS.

Apparently whole pelvic radiation to 46 Gy could be integrated with either dose regimen. Thus the hypofractionated regimen would have been 23 fractions if whole pelvis was also treated.

Adjuvant and Salvage RT summary
-ARO, EORTC, and SWOG  trials validated the use of RT in the "adjuvant" setting, however many of those patients would now be classifed as salvage. Only SWOG showed DM and OS benefit. Others BF benefit.

-RAVES and RADICALS, and ARTISTIC combined analysis show that early salvage is safe (compared to immediate adjuvant)
-RTOG SPORT shows DM benefit to WPRT in salvage
-Above studies show that 24 mos ADT is optimal, but 6 months also provides benefit
-PSMA PET further helps guide decision making in salvage prostate

Secondary endpoints of DM, BF, androgen pathway modulation resistance, and regional failure are also improved.
trials.commentary:
The authors chose the Phoenix definition to define BF, and also report results with 0.4. Which one is better? Good luck explaining to your patients that 2 above the nadir is failure when they've been meticulously monitoring it up to 0.2, which is what they were told was failure before starting. Failure rates are increased when using a more conservative definition of ≥0.4: BF with prostate only RT was 30%! See also in the figures that failures continue to rise. PSMA PET has changed our definition of failure. New oligometastasis could be potentially detected with PSMA PET at PSA of 0.5 (or even lower) that could be ablated with SBRT. In addition POP RT showed benefit with WPRT in those PSMA PET negative.

FFP may not be an ideal primary endpoint, but secondary endpoints in the study of DM, RF, and androgen pathway modulation resistance did show improvement. In the results section the authors point out that FFP becomes significant with PSA ≥0.35, but futher elaboration is possible such as with Gleason score, PSA velocity or genetic testing. Holding a value of 0.35 also risks "splitting" (Zeno's Paradox). If you split your data points enough, you can find infinite regions that are underpowered.

IMRT used in 87%. The trial showed no increase in late grade 2+ adverse effects, however recall that the POP-RT trial did. Whatever the increase in adverse effects, it seems to be minimal. Note that this study allowed entry even if no bladder constraints were met (a variation acceptable). GU adverse effects was not increased. Info is not provided regarding what bladder dosimetry was achieved.

The authors openly share a wealth of information analyzed by different statistical methods. A few different p-values systems were used in the paper; selected data is shown here. The statistical design required p<0.0125 for significance. Not all p-values were provided for 5-yr endpoints, but they are all given for the cumulative data (Table 2). The significance for FFP and DM here are from Figure 2B, and those for the other metrics are from Table 2. See also supplemental table S8. Cumulative data reporting however seems premature; it is not usually shown until final f/u.

The accuracy of the findings is limited due to self reporting from the patient, no randomization for node positive, optional WPRT, no nodal boost specifications in the protocol, and many of those who were planned to receive RT offered no reporting. Still it provides some preliminary support for radiation in node positive.

For node positive, receipt of RT and field were apparently self reported by the patient per my interpretation of the manuscript (I reached out to the authors but did not receive a response). The protocol states directly that it's not their objective to collect RT details. About 1/3 node positive planned to receive RT did not report receiving it. 82% of those who reported radiation reported receiving it to the prostate and pelvis. Various fractionations including WPRT were allowed for non metastatic disease. Recommended doses were 74 Gy/ 37 fx to prostate and 46-50 Gy to WPRT, or 55 Gy/ 37 fractions WPRT SIB. Nodal boost instructions were not specified. Regional nodes could be boosted, but we have no information regarding this (James 2016).

The findings suggesting benefit of RT in regional node positive disease perhaps suggest that regional nodes should not be considered stage IV. For the rest of the STAMPEDE findings, see its entry in the metastatic category. Selected data is shown here for node positive patients.

The protocol allowed 3D, IMRT, and "equivalent coplanar techniques" that use MLCs. This permits some coplanar versions of SBRT.

In this phase II trial, p<0.005 was prespecified as definitive. A p of <0.05 requires validation in phase III.
trials.results:
Median OS 50 vs. 28 mos
5-yr OS 42% vs. 18%, p=0.006
8-yr OS 27% vs. 14%
grade 5 toxicity 4.5% (n=3) vs. none

Median PFS 12 vs. 6.0 mos
8-yr PFS 21% vs. 0, p=0.001

Grade 4 adverse effects 0

trials.interpretation:
SBRT in oligometastatic disease of varying histologies improved PFS and OS as per phase II statistical design. Results are maintainted long term.

Overall results, including power, applicability by # mets and reproducibility in individual histologies, are to be validated in Phase III trials.
trials.commentary: Note that PFS was definitive (p<0.005), and OS was nearly definitive per the statistical design. Results should eventually be evaluated in individual histologies. The median PFS of 6 mos and LC of 63% suggests that the improvement in OS was in part a result of continuing salvage SBRT and potentially reduced future spread due to lower tumor burden, and possible immune response. There were more prostate cancer patients in the SBRT arm (21% vs. 6%). A post-hoc sensitivity analysis of other histologies showed consistent results. Although there were perhaps more favorable histologies in the SBRT arm, there were also some typically more aggressive histologies that did well. Note also that results are similar in the IAEA and Oligomez trials. Also note remarkable changes in OS with moderate LC of 63%. LC was different per met location: adrenal 100%, bone 72%, lung 51%, liver 50%, possibly due to low power in subanalysis, or other factors. The results should eventually be confirmed in phase III trials in individual histologies. Consider also that the majority of oncologic drugs approved by the FDA are approved based on PFS, but this remains controversial and OS is preferred. There were treatment deaths of 4.5% in this study, which is high, however there were no treatment deaths in the OliGomez and IAEA studies.

trials.patients:
operable localized retroperitoneal soft tissue sarcoma

Exclusion: expected R2

(subtype characteristics: 33% well differentiated LPS, 39% dedifferentiated LPS, 2% other LPS, 14% leiomyosarcoma, 11% other)
trials.methods:
➜ pre-op RT to 50.4 Gy then en bloc surgery in 4-8 weeks
vs.
➜ en bloc surgery

Primary endpoint: abdominal RFS (composite of LR or DM progression during or after RT based on CT 2 weeks after RT, 3 on ASA scale, R2, sarcomatosis, or LR following R0/R1 resection)

Dose constraints and margins:
https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1002%2Fcncr.34239&file=cncr34239-sup-0001-TableS1-S6.pdf
trials.results:
No difference in abdominal RFS, OS, DM
3-yr abdominal RFS ~60%
Median abd RFS 4.5-5.0 yrs
5-yr OS 80%, DMFS 68% both arms
No change in operability, re-operations

-various sensitivity analyses found no differences in abd RFS
-in subanalysis of liposarcoma, CI crosses to 1.02 and p not provided, but curves appear to begin to separate. Trial not powered for subtypes

Selected sub-endpoints of abd RFS:
-LR following R0/R1: 13% vs. 29%
-LR/DM progression during/after RT 14% (12% were LR, 2% DM)
(supp p6-7, calculated by myself)

-Serious adverse effects 24% vs. 10%
-In RT group, lymphopenia in 77%, anemia in 12%

OS in RT QA compliant vs. noncompliant
3-yr abd RFS 67% vs. 50%
LR after CR 15% vs. 6%
trials.interpretation:
Pre-op RT in RP sarcoma did not improve abdominal RFS. There may be benefit in the sub-endpoint of LR following R0/R1.

The trial was not powered to evaluate specific subtypes.

RT QA noncompliance was associated with worse OS.
trials.commentary:
STRASS was an impressive undertaking for an uncommon malignancy. Concerns about the trial center around its choice of endpoints and radiation planning. The authors are commended for their extensive reporting and appendix, though a few more points of information could be useful. Abd RFS is a broad composite endpoint and is not necessarily validated - its components are enlightening. The sub-endpoint of LR/DM progression during/after RT of 14% seems to be the culprit that led to no difference in abd RFS (supp p6-7), and this was mostly due to LR "during" RT. Are these tumors actually truly recurring during RT? This metric was determined by CT performed 2 weeks after RT. This is too early for response assessment; there is a possibility of treatment effect rather than LR. And 100% of those declared to have LR "during" RT underwent complete resection regardless. It is not reported what subtypes had so-called LR during RT. An important sub-endpoint, LR following R0/R1, does appear significantly in favor of RT and is implied as so in the text (p6). Interesting endpoints would have been LC alone and path response, but these were not reported. Recall that the purpose here is control, not operability - the tumors were already operable upfront, not borderline.

The sensitivity analyses in the paper could be expanded. There may be some benefit with RT in specific subtypes and not in others: on subanalysis of 3-yr abd RFS in LPS (fig 3), the curves seem to separate, but CI crosses to 1.02, p not provided. Some have commented that the K-M curves should have been truncated (Gillespie 2021) and that if done so a p value may have been significant and CI may not have crossed 1 (Scarbrough 2021). Results may also change with longer f/u. Although not specifically powered for this, the exploratory information is valuable for futher investigation. See also the STREXIT propensity analysis here, which showed improved abd RFS in well-differentiated liposarcoma and grade 1-2 dedifferentiated liposarcoma.

Radiation planning. 95% had IMRT. PTVs seem excessive at 9-12 mm. Those with poor RT compliance had worse outcomes. RT compliance was defined as PTV coverage, target delineation, dose received, and treatment time. Poor RT compliance could indicate that the trial could have been better designed, such as with narrower PTV margins and more achievable OAR constraints, that rad oncs were overly cautious in their planning, that RT is less feasible for larger tumors, and/or that better techniques are needed such as protons and arcs. Larger and more invasive tumors can lead to worse dosimetry and OS as well - especially if the trial is not designed optimally - a self-fulfilling prophecy. Poor QA is sometimes a feature of a trial and honest reporting, other times a bug.

trials.methods:
Propensity matched analysis of STRASS and STREXIT cohorts

➜ pre-op RT to 50.4 Gy then en bloc surgery in 4-8 weeks
vs.

trials.results:
RT improved abdominal RFS in well-differentiated liposarcoma and grade 1-2 dedifferentiated liposarcoma

trials.interpretation: In this propensity matched analysis, pre-op RT was associated with improved abdominal RFS in well-differentiated liposarcoma and grade 1-2 dedifferentiated liposarcoma. A randomized trial focused on this subgroup may be warranted.
trials.commentary:
In the STRASS trial, subanalysis hinted towards a benefit with pre-operative RT in liposarcoma, but the analysis was not powered.

This STREXIT propensity analysis, published by many of the same authors, further investigates. Although a propensity analyses is not a replacement for a randomized trial (Soni 2019), the study at hand does provide a fair degree of evidence, especially considering that it sources data of those actually treated on protocol plus a non-enrolled cohort from STRASS credentialed protocol centers where high quality treatment was presumably provided.

trials.commentary:
A second course may have helped prolong the benefit.

On X Koneru writes that there are no randomized trials comparing total knee replacement vs placebo or sham. On the other hand, LDRT has two positive two positive sham controlled trials (LORD-KNEA and Iranian), extensive prospective evidence, 4.5x difference in pain scores at 36 months across every domain (pain, stiffness, function, quality of life), and plain-film radiography and MRI at 10 years showing a statistically significant reduction in marked progression.

Other OA treatments have significant downsides: NSAIDs: known cardiovascular, renal, and Gl harm at chronic doses. Corticosteroid injections: evidence of accelerated cartilage loss with repeat use (Wernicke 2025).

boards.title: General
fields:
H&P with palpation of axillary/infraclav/SCV nodes and breast

(extra history: prior RT, collagen vascular dz, menopausal status, pregnancy status)

Labs: CBC, LFTs, alk phos, beta-HCG. BRCA for age ≤45 or direct family history (see BRCA section for full details)

Imaging primary: diagnostic mammogram (magnification for calcs, spot compression for questionable mass), US with core needle bx. Evaluation of ER/PR/Her2. In invasive breast cancer patients with ER/PR+ and tumor size 0.5 cm or greater, order Oncotype

MRI potential indications: DCIS, unknown primary (axillary node or pageats), dense breasts, to assess for extent of multicentric or multifocal disease especially if unsure about lumpectomy

Imaging staging: CXR. Bone scan and CT only for Stage III. PET scan increasing in use

Assess if patient is candidate for lumpectomy and if so offer breast conservation therapy vs. mastectomy.  Lumpectomy and mastectomy OS is identical (some studies actually show better OS with lumpectomy).

Contraindications for lumpectomy that would require radiation
Absolute: radiation would be given during pregnancy, expected poor cosmetic results from a large surgery, diffusely positive margins. ("Diffuse calcifications" is also classically quoted but needs to be confirmed as disease. Node positive is not a contraindiation!)

Relative: prior RT (catheter PBI is an option, or could consider re-RT for long interval), active connective tissue disease of the skin (esp scleroderma and lupus), T3 category 2B, positive margin (prefer re-excision), BRCA or other genetic predisposition

fields: Indication: situations when using tangents with SCV field, but the desired tangent field size exceeds limit of 20 cm superiorly to inferiorly (most machines' field size is 40 cm max total, thus maximum size in a half beam block would be 20 cm)

Oral narrative: The patient would be placed in the supine position with breast board. A supraclavicular field would be created using a half beam block at the inferior edge with the isocenter placed at this level. For the tangent field, a second isocenter would be placed at the midpath of the tangents, about 1 cm anterior to the chest wall. For the tangents, the couch would be moved away from the gantry and collimator rotated to align the cranial edge of the tangents with the supraclavicular field. The lung would be blocked using MLCs.

Alternatively, a less optimal technique involves rotating the collimator so that the jaw of the collimator blocks the lung in the tangent field. Then use MLCs to block the portion of the tangents overlapping the SCV field. The matchline in this technique is less homogenous.

I would first bring the patient to the clinic for transrectal ultrasound guided volume study of the prostate. The patient would have had a bowel prep. the night before. I would place the patient in the dorsal lithotomy position and prep and drape. I would then insert a foley with aerated jelly. Using a transrectal ultrasound with US gel, I would take images every 1 mm. I would assess for any pubic arch interference and record the angles of the probe and legs once finished. I would use these images to create a pre-plan using a peripheral loading technique with PTV of 3 mm laterally and 0 mm anteriorly and posteriorly.

I would then take the patient to the OR and position the patient as done in the pre-plan with general anesthesia. I would prep and drape the patient, place the templates, and load the seeds according to the plan. Once finished I would obtain AP and lateral orthogonal films in the OR to assess the placement of the seeds, and perform a rectal examination. I would have the patient return one month later for post-implant CT and dosimetry.

Anatomical 3D contouring: Goal of local control. The radial border is the true mesorectal fascia (note the RTOG atlas definition of the "mesorectum" is not the anatomical mesorectum). Optional to include sacral hollow. Expand from GTV 1-2 cm superior and inferior. Allows for more sparing of bladder. Some use a smaller 1 cm margin. Inclusion of nodes? Protocols and guidelines vary whether nodes should be included. If the goal is reducing risk of LR, this suggests nodes need not be included in the boost. They will be removed surgically.

PROSPECT trial 3 cm total margin from GTV and include sacral hollow but not all mesorectum. This method can result in unusually large volumes.

H&P with pap and cold conization, sexual history

Pelvic exam (inspection, bimanual palpation. See general section for parametrial and sidewall involvement), rectovaginal exam, palpation of inguinal nodes, abdomen

Labs: CBC, CMP, CA-125, possibly BHCG,

If very young, consider oophoropexy to preserve hormonal function

Imaging: CT A/P, MRI, PET
Special: consider EUA, cystoscopy, sigmoidoscopy

Surgery: radical hysterectomy with nodal dissection. Ex lap with palpation of liver and cytology. Sample omentum if advanced or sarcoma

Options:
1) neoadjuvant carbo/taxol x6 then definitive RT + cisplatin (INTERLACE)
2) Definitive chemoRT + concurrent and adjuvant pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE A18)
3) combo of above

Point based HDR (see respective sections for 3D and interstitial):
45 Gy/25 fx to whole pelvis using 3D RT with HDR using tandem and ovoids to deliver 80-90 Gy to Point A (5x6 Gy = EQD2 of 84. See guidelines for other fractionation). Treat 1-2 times per week. Rx to point A. Boost gross nodes to 54-60 Gy. Boost parametrium by HDR or EBRT if involved.

(Some details may vary by institution)
"I would take the patient to the OR place them in the dorsal lithotomy position and administer general anesthesia. I’d perform and EUA to assess response. After prepping the patient with betadine, a gold  seed would be placed at the anterior cervix. A foley catheter would then be inserted to drain the bladder and the foley bulb inflated with 7cc half saline half contrast. The uterus would be sounded to assess distance to the fundus and flexion, and the appropriate tandem inserted with the largest ovoids that could be accommodated. Packing (option: soaked with saline, clindamycin, or contrast) would be placed anteriorly and posteriorly to the device to pack away from the bladder and rectum. I would then take AP and lateral orthogonal films to ensure adequate positioning and packing."

Supine, vac loc, full bladder

If doing IMRT for PA nodes, some sim on full and empty bladder and contour in the two phases to account for motion (but may not be necessary if you ask the patient to drink the same amount of water each day prior to sim and confirm with CBCT. Or, an ITV that is less than full to empty bladder may be useful)

Some first place gold seed at cervix and some use vaginal marker (however, the patient will not be treated every day with the vaginal marker, which may disrupt dosimetry).

WPRT/EFRT 45 Gy

HDR boost 5-6 Gy x 5

=total EQD2 80-90 Gy

IMRT whole pelvis: common, external and internal iliacs, presacral nodes, entire cervix and uterus, 3 cm upper vagina

Vaginal ITV: For IMRT, some guidelines instruct to contour with both a full and empty bladder and fuse images. May not be necessary with CBCT. Or, choose an ITV that is less than full and empty bladder

Periaortic nodes: If node positive, include PA up to T11/T12. In RTOG 0724, if common iliac nodes are positive then PA nodes are treated up to L1/L2. If PA nodes are positive, treated up to T11/T12. (Some might include PA nodes for multiple pelvic nodes or in Stage IIIB or IVA)

Tandem: Rx to point A. On a 5 cm tandem, there are 10 dwell points. ~5 to 10 points may be used. Points are 0.5 cm apart. Dose 10/10/15 mg rad equiv from sup to inferior. On ovoids dose each 10. Ovoids have 3-4 dwell points. (see LDR section for more on rad equiv, such as for ovoids)

Consider induction carbo/taxol x6 (INTERLACE) and/or adjuvant pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE A18)

cisplatin 40 weekly, 5-6 cycles. CBC weekly, and some transfuse if needed to keep Hb>10 (mixed data)

ICRU bladder point and rectal points <3.7 Gy/fx
rectovaginal point: at midline level of ovoids on lateral imaging, 5 mm dorsal to posterior vaginal wall on body axial plane. ICRU goal is <140% of point A
Bladder point: posterior edge of foley bulb

Ir-192. Starts at ~10 Ci. Half life 74 days, 300kEV, change out source every 3 months, 1% decay/day

Larger ovoids give lower mucosal dose rate and better dose depth

For the 6-cm tandem, dose points are specified along the x-axis 12– 20 mm from the tandem (12 mm from dwell position #1, 14 mm from #2, 16 mm from #3, 18 mm from #4, and 20 mm from all subsequent dwells to the level of point A). One hundred and forty percent of the prescription dose is optimized to dose points placed lateral to the intravaginal applicator.

Goal: complete entire therapy in 8 weeks. (After 5 weeks EBRT, 3 weeks remain.) Scheduling preference varies by institution.

Weekly or biweekly T&O. Do not give chemo or EBRT on T&O days.

Medium and large sized tumors usually start later in RT or even immediately after RT and receive T&O twice weekly. For small tumors some may start early at week 3.

Reading tandem and ovoid films:
On Laterals: ovoids bisected by seeds and tandem, tandem halfway between bladder and sacrum, adequate packing, no packing above ovoids
on AP: flange between ovoids, ovoids 0.5-1cm from tandem

boards.title: Cervix 3D based brachytherapy
fields:
(Some details may vary by institution)
"I would take the patient to the OR and place her in the dorsal lithotomy position and administer general anesthesia. I’d perform an EUA to assess response. I would prep with betadine. A foley catheter would then be inserted to drain the bladder and the foley bulb inflated with 10cc 1:9 gadolinium/saline (1cc gadolinium+9 cc saline). The uterus would be sounded to assess distance to the fundus and flexion, and the appropriate tandem inserted with the largest ovoids/ring that could be accommodated. Packing would be placed anteriorly and posteriorly to the device with gauze (option: soaked with saline or clindamycin) to pack away from the bladder and rectum. (Optional: small amount of gadolinum at cervix before placing packing). I would then transfer the patient to radiology for MRI (For some applicators: I would insert dummy catheters with water into the applicator for visualization)"

MRI based planning: Obtain MRI prior to start of EBRT and prior to each brachytherapy treatment. Tumor and organs are best seen on T2.

Also appropriate to contour based off CT, but CT can overestimate size of tumor and cervix.

HRCTV: (80-90 Gy EQD2, 5.5-6 Gy x 5) Include whole cervix, GTV at time of brachy, and presumed tumor extension (residual grey zones on MRI, clinical judgement, consider margin on GTV)

IRCTV: (60 Gy EQD2) Initial tumor volume at diagnosis. Use at least 10 cm margin on GTV except 5 mm anterior and posterior.

(However since dose to HRCTV by itself correlates to outcomes, many do not contour IRCTV. Also, many find that the IRCTV is mostly covered by dose fall-off regardless.)
MRI prior to start of treatment and with each treatment fraction. Fuse with CT sim to assist with contouring.

WPRT/EFRT 45 Gy

HDR boost 5-6 Gy x 5

=total EQD2 80-90 Gy

EBRT field as above

Tandem and ovoids: Begin point based planning first as above, then modify weighting and dwell positions as guided by 3D contours. Additional types of applicators may be employed for expanded dwell points and positions.

Consider induction carbo/taxol x6 (INTERLACE)

cisplatin 40 weekly, 5-6 cycles. CBC weekly, and some transfuse if needed to keep Hb>10 (mixed data)

On 3D imaging, look for 100% line to cover 90% of HRCTV volume. Goal D90 of 80-90 Gy EQD2 total and D90 of 100% on DVH.

For large tumors, one strategy is to modify dosing as mass shrinks. For example a smaller dose when the mass is large to spare organs, then once it has decreased in size give a larger dose since there is more room from organs at risk.

2cc bladder<90 Gy (ideal <80)
ICRU bladder pt <75 Gy (Ideal <65)
2cc sigmoid<75 Gy (ideal <70)
2 cc small bowel<60 Gy
rectovaginal point<75 Gy (ideal <65)
vaginal wall <108 Gy

EMBRACE study: rectum D2cc<69.5 gives <10% risk grade 2+ toxicity.

Goal: complete entire therapy in 8 weeks. (After 5 weeks EBRT, 3 weeks remain.) Scheduling preference varies by institution.

Weekly or biweekly T&O. Do not give chemo or EBRT on T&O days.

Medium and large sized tumors usually start later in RT or even immediately after RT and receive T&O twice weekly. For small tumors some may start early at week 3.

Tandem and ring has better coverage than T&O (EMBRACE)

Does the entire endometrium need to be treated along the tandem?

According to the GEC-ESTRO definition of HR-CTV and IR-CTV, it is NOT required. For example, refer to the images displaying these volumes, such as in Pötter 2006.

boards.title: Cervix adjuvant RT
fields:
As above, followed by surgery

Radical hysterectomy and lymph node dissection. Entails mobilization of ureters, bladder, and rectum to dissect parametria out to pelvic sidewall and remove 1/2 to 1/3 of upper vagina

Post-op RT indications:
Use GOG nomogram to determine risk of recurrence (Levinson 2021)

Or, for a simpler method, use Sedlis criteria:
≥2 Sedlis factors: LVSI, size >4 cm, or ≥2/3 stromal invasion.

If ≥1 of positive margin, parametrial invasion, node positive, treat with RT plus chemo

Post-op cheno indications below

50.4 Gy/ 28 fx
or 45 Gy/25 fx

May boost vaginal cuff 6 Gy x 2 to surface, especially for LVSI or parametrial involvement

Sandwich chemotherapy (STARS) for deep stromal invasion or LVSI (not size >4 cm)
supine, vac loc, full bladder, empty rectum. Sim prone if large amount of bowel in field

Parametrium borders: superior: bowel, lateral: pelvic wall, anterior: 1 cm into bladder, posterior: uterosacral ligaments (know location). Inferior border at bottom of obturator foramen or UG diaphragm.

boards.title: Cervix parametrial or sidewall boost
fields: Indication: parametrial involvement when treating definitive cervix that cannot be covered with HDR

Ideally include the involved parametrium in routine HDR if the appropriate applicator is available.

If not, consider 5.4-9 Gy EBRT or IMRT boost after 45 Gy WPRT. Intersperse HDR to complete in 8 weeks.
Pay special care to dosimetry of bowel and bladder.

HDR: contour the involved parametrium in the brachy HRCTV if an adequate applicator is available

EBRT: Fuse with MRI to contour GTV. Create conformal fields. In the era of 3D and MRI, historical 2D blocks - especially bilateral - are outdated.

Parametrium borders: superior: bowel, lateral: pelvic wall, anterior: 1 cm into bladder, posterior: uterosacral ligaments (know location). Inferior border at bottom of obturator foramen or UG diaphragm
Pay special attention to rectum and bladder dosing
Begin after whole pelvis phase is complete. Remember to complete therapy in 8 weeks.

2D historical fields:
AP/PA midline block. Lateral borders to point A. Superior border mid SI.

Traditionally the bilateral parametrium is included, but this is overtreatment if the parametrial extention is only on one side per exam or MRI.

fields:
Deauville PET scan scoring
1. No uptake above background
2. Uptake ≤mediastinum
3. Uptake >MS but ≤liver
4. Uptake moderately >liver
5. Uptake markedly >>liver

Score of 4 and 5 are always positive. In some situations, 3 is considered positive.

-------------------
Favorable vs. unfavorable

Ann Arbor sites are used for staging and GHSG sites are used for fav/unfav. Their definitions of sites are different.

GHSG unfavorable factors: ≥3 nodal sites, bulky ≥1/3 chest, extranodal involvement, ESR ≥30 with B and ≥50 without B

NCCN unfavorable factors: ≥4 nodal sites, bulky disease >10 cm or mediastinal mass ratio >1/3, ANY B symptoms. Not counted: extranodal disease

MMR= maximal width of mass/maximum intrathoractic diameter

Field is INRT or ISRT
"ISRT targets the originally involved lymph nodes, accounting for inaccuracies in pre-chemotherapy imaging and anatomical changes after chemotherapy."

Main point of ISRT: cover pre/post gross disease with smallest CTV margin possible. Consideration for errors due to position and shrinking after chemo. ISRT is a further clarification of INRT, and a form of it.

Clinical judgment may entail: allowance for shrinking anatomic boundaries, contouring pre-chemo volume to best ability, possibly with margin for uncertainty, extra margin for ECE or organ infiltration, inclusion of partial elective nodal region of the node (avoid if possible: this leads to fields not unlike IFRT). PTV and sim per institution. Note the 1.5 cm vertical CTV described in the initial rec (Hoskin) is not required in later guidelines.

ISRT guidelines allow some freedom of interpretation. What is the "correct" volume to contour? ISRT interpretations differ even among experts (Maraldo 2015 and Hoppe 2015). The only strong indicator that an ISRT contour is incorrect is that the size is equal to or larger than the corresponding IFRT field.

INRT and ISRT are essentially the same thing - ISRT is simply an evolved guideline to allow for more modifications. ISRT is now the term that is used internationally, even by GHSG.

Sim per site
H&N: do dental eval first. Use bite block to divert tongue away from field if possible. Mask.
Chest: 4DCT, vac loc. Breath hold increasing in use to spare heart and lung
Abdomen: 4DCT. Empty stomach and treat at same time each day. If using oral contrast also sim without contrast. Daily CBCT. In the past many did renal testing but with modern technique kidneys should be spared.
Pelvis: If young age, do pregnancy testing and fertility testing. Consider sperm banking, egg banking, ovarian transposition, testicular clamshell

-Ann Arbor sites are used for staging and GHSG sites are used for fav/unfav in HL. Their definitions of sites are different.

Lugano staging tips for HL and DLBCL
-PET is adequate to assess bone marrow involvement and can be highly suggestive for extralymphatic involvement
-Routine bone marrow biopsy no longer indicated for HL and DLBCL.
-Consider bone marrow biopsy in HL if cytopopenias present and consider in DLBCL if suspecting a different histology
-BM biopsy still required in follicular, MZL, burkitt's

-Use A and B status only for Hodgkin, not NHL
-For bulky, add the word "bulky" to the stage, not letter X
-Bulky disease in HL is >10 cm or >1/3 the transthoracic diameter. CT is appropriate; CXR not required

-For extranodal, use letter E modifier. Extranodal is only applicable for Stage I-II per Lugano. No such thing as Stage IIIE or IVE. Just Stage III and IV.

-Splenomegaly is defined as size >13 cm. PET avidity is not relevant when determining splenomegaly

-Hepatomegaly is focal or disseminated PET avidity

-Bulky in NHL is definted as ≥7.5 cm per NCCN and RICOVER and UNFOLDER (not defined in Lugano)

-Why are some lymphoma fields so large?
Lymphoma nodes have a tendancy to appear in outside the typical confined nodal regions such as in neck, breast, and lung atlases. Contouring toward an INRT concept can help reduce the volume.

What is Lugano? A town in southern Switzerland, near Italy. Majority speak Italian.

"I would position the patient at 3 m SSD with beam spoiler 1 cm thick placed in front of the patient. I would treat 3, out of total 6, positions per day for 4 days per week, delivering 1 Gy per day, ensuring to boost areas of possible underdosage including soles, perineum, scalp, under breasts and pannus. Treat in 6 positions to cover total skin, 3 positions per day, 4 days per week. Boost to soles, perineum, and scalp. Also need to boost "shadow areas" under breast, pannus, etc. Can shield eyes. Can intermittently shield nail beds and tops of feet to reduce risk of edema. A beam spoiler 1 cm thick is placed in front of patient to increase large angle scatter and improve dose homogeneity. The beam is positioned 3 m SSD and moved +/- 20 degrees (angles reduce photon contamination to less than 1%). "Goal is to achieve dose homogeneity in the coronal plane.
